sections.section_path: Pr 18421 Multipart File Validation Limits
sections.heading: Pr 18421 Multipart File Validation Limits
sections.content:
Motivation: users integrating tool/function calling and file uploads via the OpenAI-compatibility endpoints were sending a wide variety of content-types and very large multipart requests which caused inconsistent runtime behavior, high memory pressure, and unexpected acceptance of unsupported payloads. This PR introduces a focused, backwards-compatible implementation for multipart/form-data parsing on the OpenAI-compatibility path, strict Content-Type validation for tool/file inputs, and deterministic payload limits both per-file and per-request. Summary of changes: 1) Add a streaming-safe multipart parser that yields parts rather than buffering entire requests; 2) Validate Content-Type of each part (whitelist: text/*, image/*, application/json, application/octet-stream with explicit size checks); 3) Enforce configurable limits: max_file_size (default 10MiB), max_total_request_size (default 50MiB), max_parts_count (default 20). These defaults are conservative and documented; they can be overridden at tenant or route level via API config. 4) Hook validation into the OpenAI-compat layer so existing client integrations get predictable errors (400/413) with structured error bodies when inputs are rejected. 5) Add detailed unit and integration tests and end-to-end tests for streaming uploads and for the dedicated Dedicated/Private ingress paths. Backwards compatibility notes: this does not change the non-multipart JSON body semantics. Existing users who relied on accepting arbitrary large file uploads should update their tenant config or use Redwood Dedicated with higher quotas. Rollout plan: feature-flagged behind feature.enable_multipart_input (off by default); staged rollout to internal dogfood tenants, then gradual roll to 10%, 50%, 100% via config rollout. Checklist: - [x] Streaming-safe multipart parser implemented - [x] Content-Type whitelist + validation errors - [x] Per-file and per-request size enforcement + configurable defaults - [x] OpenAI-compat error mapping and structured error shapes - [x] Tests: unit, integration, e2e - [x] Docs: compatibility notes and config guide - [x] Telemetry: counters for rejected parts and throttled requests - [x] Migration & rollout plan included Testing notes: the multipart parser uses a small constant memory footprint for each active part and yields part metadata to the handler; large parts trigger a streaming drain with early termination (413 response) to avoid OOM. Integration tests exercise combination of binary and text parts, wrong content-types, and boundary cases around the configured limits. Telemetry: added metrics api.multipart.rejected_content_type, api.multipart.rejected_size, api.multipart.accepted_parts and a hist for part sizes. Implementation details: - parser: runtime/multipart/stream_parser.py - validator: api/validation/multipart_validator.py - compat layer: api/openai_compat/input_adapter.py - config: config/defaults/multipart.yaml - docs: docs/openai-compat/multipart.md - tests: tests/unit/test_multipart_parser.py, tests/integration/test_openai_compat_multipart.py Error shape examples (structured output): when a part is rejected we return 413 with a JSON body {"error":{"type":"request_too_large","message":"part exceeds max_file_size","meta":{"part_name":"file","limit_bytes":10485760}}} and 400 for unsupported content-types with type unsupported_media_type. Observability: trace spans added around parse->validate->route dispatch to help pinpoint latency regressions. Related items: Linear ENG-2728 (multipart uploader stability), PM-146 (OpenAI compat feature parity).
Liam Chen: key question — do we need to special-case application/pdf? many partners send PDFs as application/pdf; current whitelist would block it. Suggest adding application/pdf or making whitelist configurable per-tenant.
Aisha Patel: replied — agreed, added application/pdf to tenant_whitelist in config and made default conservative. Added test case + note in docs explaining why binary blobs should be limited.

sections.section_path: Pr 129874 Timebox Abort Idempotency Resume Openai Compat
sections.heading: Pr 129874 Timebox Abort Idempotency Resume Openai Compat
sections.content:
Context: production customers observed cases where long lived streaming sessions (tool calls + structured output) were left in indeterminate states after a client network disconnect or a client-initiated Cancel. Motivation: we need a predictable server-side safety net that bounds resource residency time, ensures tool-call idempotency when retries/resume occur, and provides a clear fallback path (trimmed response + final event) that OpenAI-compatible clients can rely on. This PR implements a server-side streaming timebox (configurable per-route) that gracefully converts oversized/inflight streams into a final 'timeboxed' terminal event, augments client-cancel handling to be idempotent across reconnect/resume windows, and plumbs a compact resume token that includes tool-call idempotency metadata. Summary of changes: 1) stream manager: add configurable timebox_ms and a deterministic finalization path that emits a structured terminal event ("__redwood_timeboxed__") with a compact summary; 2) openai adapter: interpret Cancel events as idempotent markers tied to resume tokens; retries within the resume window will deduplicate tool calls using a request-level id; 3) tooling: map function-call invocations to idempotency keys and persist minimal call metadata to the stream checkpoint to support safe resume; 4) API: extend the OpenAI-compat streaming spec with two optional fields in the final event (timeboxed=true, resume_hint) without breaking existing clients; 5) tests & docs: integration tests for flaky network simulated disconnects and release notes for the behavior and recommended operational knobs. Rollout plan: feature guarded behind a runtime flag and route-level config. Backwards compatibility: default behavior is unchanged unless a route opts-in. Checklist: [x] unit tests for stream finalizer [x] integration test that simulates disconnect + resume [x] docs page and compatibility notes [x] change log entry. Related: ENG-1023 (stream lifecycle SLO), SUP-4572 (customer incident replicant).
stream: add timebox lifecycle and finalizer logic (runtime)
compat: interpret cancel as idempotent marker with resume token (openai adapter)
stream: persist minimal tool-call idempotency metadata to checkpoints
api: add 'timeboxed' and 'resume_hint' flags to streaming final event schema
tests: integration tests for disconnect/resume/timebox behavior
docs: add streaming-lifecycle/timebox operational runbook
Ava Chen (2026-02-19): Nice approach. Two asks: 1) can we make the default timebox conservative (eg 30s) and 2) add metrics for timebox-triggered finalizations so SRE can track this?
Marcus Li (2026-02-19): Thanks Ava. Default is 30s in the flags; added metric 'stream.timebox_finalized' with labels route/model; will push change.
Diego Martinez (2026-02-20): Concern about persisting tool-call metadata on every request path. How big can the checkpoint grow? What retention semantics?
Marcus Li (2026-02-20): Checkpoints store only a 64-bit idempotency hash + 3-field small metadata (call name, timestamp, status). We GC per-checkpoint on successful terminalization. Size is bounded and measured in tests.
Priya Nair (2026-02-21): Integration test flaky on first run, failure in 'resume-after-disconnect' when the simulated retry arrives slightly after timebox expiry. Can we make the test deterministic?
Marcus Li (2026-02-21): Fixed by injecting a deterministic clock to the stream finalizer and making the resume window configurable for tests. Reran CI locally.
SRE Team (CI bot) (2026-02-24): One lint failure in openai_compat_stream.go for an unused variable — fixed in follow-up commit.
Ava Chen (2026-02-24): Approved after last fixes. Marking as ready to merge.

sections.section_path: Sup 18510 Streaming Throughput Metric Mismatch
sections.heading: Sup 18510 Streaming Throughput Metric Mismatch
sections.content:
Sup 18510 Streaming Throughput Metric Mismatch

Source type: jira
Document ID: dsid_a5a5235d973e421c870e11ceea4887ed
Release: v1.0.0
Benchmark: EnterpriseRAG-Bench synthetic upstream data
Streaming throughput metric mismatch (customer dashboard vs Redwood export) — suspected token accounting double-count in streaming

Customer (Vidorama) reports inconsistent throughput numbers for their Dedicated deployment when using streaming responses.

Issue summary

- Vidorama is comparing:
  1) Redwood Console throughput panel (tokens/sec) for their Dedicated deployment, and
  2) Their internal measurement based on streamed tokens (client-side) + Redwood usage export.
- They see Redwood Console tokens/sec ~1.8–2.1x higher than their client-side computed throughput for the same time windows.
- Discrepancy appears only for streaming (non-streaming requests match within ~5–10%).

Impact

- Customer confusion + concern about Dedicated throughput SLO reporting accuracy.
- Potential false positives/negatives in SLO compliance if the canonical throughput metric is inflated for streaming.

Customer-provided details

- Workload: chat completions, streaming enabled (server-sent events).
- Typical request: prompt 1–2k tokens, completion 150–400 tokens, 20–60 concurrent streams.
- Sampling window: 5-min rolling, comparing against their Prometheus counters.

Redwood initial checks (Support)

- Confirmed customer is hitting the correct deployment_id and region (us-east).
- Confirmed they are not mixing model variants in the comparison window (pinned to llama-3.1-70b-instruct; occasional mixtral bursts were excluded by customer).
- Confirmed they are not counting input tokens in their client throughput metric (they only count generated tokens).

Steps to reproduce (internal)
1) Run load test against a Dedicated deployment with streaming enabled.
2) Compare:

   - streaming token counter used by throughput dashboard (server-side), vs
   - sum(completion_tokens) from request final usage events (server-side) and/or reconstructed deltas.

3) Observe that for streaming requests, the dashboard-aligned metric increases faster than final usage totals.

Investigation notes (SRE/Obs)

- Hypothesis A: double-counting streamed completion tokens (both per-chunk deltas and final usage event contribute to the same counter).
- Hypothesis B: retries/resumes on stream reconnects cause duplicated deltas.
- Hypothesis C: mixed attribution labels (route vs deployment) cause aggregation overlap.

Findings

- We can reproduce consistent ~2x inflation when streaming is enabled and client consumes the full stream.
- Root cause identified in telemetry emission path:
  - For streaming responses, we emit per-chunk token deltas (used for near-real-time throughput).
  - At stream termination, a final usage event is emitted.
  - In the current pipeline, the dashboard throughput counter was incremented by BOTH the per-chunk deltas and the final usage event for the same request.
- This does NOT affect billing totals (billing uses finalized usage only). It affects the real-time throughput metric used in dashboards and SLO evaluation.

Workaround (until fix rollout)

- For customer reporting, use finalized completion token metrics (request end) for streaming workloads:
  - completion_tokens_total (finalized) / wall time
- Avoid using real-time streaming throughput panel for contractual/SLO comparisons until patched.

Next actions

sections.heading: Des 72681 Develop Interactive Tone Derivatives And Kappa Elevation Scale For Data Grids
sections.content:
Des 72681 Develop Interactive Tone Derivatives And Kappa Elevation Scale For Data Grids

Source type: linear
Document ID: dsid_3fd6af404fae48e6b8ea5a57875ef78f
Release: v1.0.0
Benchmark: EnterpriseRAG-Bench synthetic upstream data
Develop interactive tone derivatives and Kappa elevation scale for data grids

Objective: Create a deterministic system for producing interactive color derivatives (hover/focus/pressed/disabled) from the base semantic palette and introduce a physics-inspired elevation scale ("Kappa") tuned for dense data surfaces such as DataGrid, compact tables, and inline action bars.

Scope:

- Define algorithmic transforms to derive interactive tones from semantic base tokens (primary, neutral, success, caution, critical). The transforms must preserve WCAG contrast for actionable states and offer predictable deltas for designers and engineers.
- Introduce a Kappa elevation token family (kappa-0..kappa-6) with mapped umbra/penumbra/ambient values and matching colorized overlays for dark/light themes optimized for high-density rows.
- Propose spacing/radius adjustments for compact rows to align with new elevation cues while retaining hit-target accessibility.
- Update Figma token library and token spec (CSS vars + JSON token artifacts) and provide migration guidance for DataGrid, Table, Button, and InlineAction components.

Goals & Acceptance criteria:
1) Token spec: produce a stable token spec file (design JSON) that includes base palette, interactive derivatives (e.g., color.interactive.primary.hover), and elevation.kappa.{0..6} with explicit shadow parameters.
2) Implementation-ready: frontend repo receives a tokens PR implementing variables; DataGrid and Table components consume new tokens behind a feature flag.
3) Accessibility: automated contrast checks pass for all interactive states against 3:1 where applicable and 4.5:1 for primary actionable text.
4) Visual regression: add per-component visual snapshots and tolerances; no regressions beyond approved deltas.
5) Figma: updated design kit with tokenized components and guidance notes.
6) Rollout plan: canary on internal analytics dashboards -> staged rollout -> full migration with a fallback.

Design notes and trade-offs:

- Algorithmic derivation reduces token sprawl (fewer manual swatches) but requires deterministic tuning. We will prefer per-hue perceptual adjustments (Lab-space tweaks) over fixed lightness deltas to avoid color shifts across hues.
- Kappa elevation prioritizes subtle penumbra for dense rows; larger elevations are intentionally muted to avoid visual clutter. This might reduce perceived separation in extreme cases; provide an override token for high-contrast surfaces.
- Implementation should use runtime CSS variables for quick theming and a build-time compiled fallback for older clients. There are performance trade-offs when shipping many tokens; we will group tokens under semantic prefixes to keep runtime size manageable.

Migration plan:
1) Finalize tokens in design JSON and Figma (this ticket).
2) Engineered tokens PR (feature-flagged).
3) Update DataGrid/Table to read tokens; create opt-in toggle for compact Kappa mode.
4) Run automated visual diffs and accessibility scans.
5) QA and UAT with PM/Analytics team, then canary-release on internal dashboards for 2 weeks before full rollout.

Links and artifacts: see attachments.

GCP Marketplace onboarding + billing review (Redwood Inference)

Redwood and the GCP Marketplace team reviewed how Redwood’s new marketplace SKUs map to GCP billing dimensions (usage-based token/embedding meters vs subscription/commit dimensions), and what identifiers must be carried end-to-end (consumerId/entitlement) to ensure correct metering. GCP emphasized keeping dimension names stable, ensuring aggregation and rounding are consistent, and making the onboarding flow resilient to entitlement propagation delays. The group aligned on a staging test plan: subscribe with a test buyer account, validate entitlement lookup, provision/link a Redwood org, generate an API key, send test inference traffic, confirm metering events appear with the expected dimensions, and verify cancellation/plan change behavior. Redwood will send a proposed dimension list and sample metering payloads for review.

- Google Cloud Marketplace: Priya Shah, Anika Desai, Miguel Alvarez

[00:00] Stephanie Nguyen: Cool, thanks everyone for making time. This is Stephanie from Redwood, I run a lot of the enterprise motion, and we’ve got Cole and Nadia on billing and metering, Ben on onboarding funnel. We wanted to do a sanity pass on the GCP marketplace requirements, specifically billing dimensions and the onboarding UX expectations before we submit.

[00:18] Priya Shah: Sounds good. Thanks Stephanie. Priya here, partner dev manager. Anika and Miguel are the experts on the technical billing side. We saw your email about new SKUs, so today is basically make sure it’s compatible with Cloud Marketplace and Cloud Commerce.

sections.section_path: 2026 01 16 Gcp Marketplace Onboarding And Billing Review
sections.heading: 2026 01 16 Gcp Marketplace Onboarding And Billing Review
sections.content:
[00:33] Chris Osei: Yep, and I’m Chris, program lead on our side for the marketplace refresh. I’ll keep us on agenda and capture action items.

[00:41] Anika Desai: Hi all. Anika, partner engineering. I can talk through entitlement, procurement IDs, and the typical “gotchas” we see when SaaS vendors wire up the onboarding.

[00:50] Miguel Alvarez: Miguel here. Cloud Commerce metering / billing integrations. Happy to go deep on dimensions, aggregation, rounding, and what reviewers will look for.

[01:01] Stephanie Nguyen: Great. Quick context: we’re replacing legacy listings. We now have Hosted API usage-based, Dedicated capacity, and Private deployment. We want the marketplace SKUs to map cleanly to our internal billing meters. The primary issues we want to avoid are dimension mismatches and the buyer gets invoiced for something weird.

[01:20] Miguel Alvarez: Yeah. The big thing is consistency. Dimension names and IDs in the offer need to match what you’re sending in metering events. And be careful if you’re changing them later—customers don’t like it and it can break reporting.

[01:35] Cole Summers: That’s exactly what we’re trying to nail. Let me outline what we were thinking and you can tell us what’s realistic. For Hosted, we meter “tokens generated” and “input tokens” internally, but we can expose it as “tokens” total if that’s simpler. We also have embeddings measured as “embedding units” (basically per 1K tokens equivalent). For Dedicated, we have reserved GPU capacity, which internally is monthly commit + overage. Private is more of a platform fee plus support tier.

[02:05] Miguel Alvarez: Okay. So in Cloud Marketplace, you can do usage-based dimensions and you can do subscription pricing models, and you can also do committed-use style constructs depending on the product type. Most SaaS partners keep it simple: one or a small number of usage dimensions, like “1K tokens” or “1M tokens”, and then for a base subscription you do a seat or a flat monthly fee.

[02:29] Nadia Rahman: Quick question on granularity. If we do “1K tokens” as the unit, do you see partners reporting fractional quantities? Like 123.456 units? Or is it recommended to round?

[02:41] Miguel Alvarez: You can send decimal quantities, but you should document how you compute it and be consistent. The most common pattern is you aggregate per hour or per day and send integer quantities. But for token meters, lots of folks send decimals, just be explicit. Rounding differences between your UI and the invoice is where support tickets come from.

[03:02] Ben Carter: On the onboarding side, we have this subscription -> entitlement -> Redwood org provisioning. One issue we see on AWS is entitlements sometimes take a few minutes to show up. Is that also a thing on GCP?

[03:14] Anika Desai: Yep. It’s not usually super long, but there can be propagation delay. The UX expectation is you handle “pending” gracefully. Like, don’t show a scary error that says “you are not entitled.” Instead say “we’re still syncing your subscription, retry in a few minutes” and maybe a refresh button.

sections.section_path: 2026 01 16 Gcp Marketplace Onboarding And Billing Review
sections.heading: 2026 01 16 Gcp Marketplace Onboarding And Billing Review
sections.content:
[20:40] Anika Desai: Typically you’ll have a partner test project and a test buyer project. You procure your own product as a test buyer. Then you verify that your integration receives the entitlement. If you’re using the Cloud Commerce Partner API, you can query entitlements. If you’re using webhooks, ensure those are wired. Since you’re doing a console-based claim flow, you can also validate by retrieving entitlement status from your backend.

[21:08] Cole Summers: We’re using the partner API and a sync job, plus on-demand verify endpoint. Webhook we considered but didn’t want to rely solely on it.

[21:19] Miguel Alvarez: That’s fine. Webhook can be flaky if not retried. Polling plus retry is okay, just mind quotas.

[21:30] Nadia Rahman: For quotas, do you have ballpark? Like requests per minute? We’re not huge but we want to be safe.

[21:38] Miguel Alvarez: It depends on the project and API. I’ll send the doc. But generally, if you do a sync every 5 minutes and on-demand for onboarding, you’re fine.

[21:53] Stephanie Nguyen: Great.
[21:55] (pause)

[21:56] Ben Carter: A small UX question: when entitlement is not found, do you recommend we show “wait 10 minutes” or “wait 2 minutes”? We don’t want to over-promise.

[22:06] Anika Desai: I’d say “a few minutes” and allow retry. And show a timestamp “last checked at” to reassure them you’re doing something.

[22:18] Ben Carter: Nice idea.

[22:20] Chris Osei: Another edge case: procurement might buy in a different Google identity than the engineer uses (like billing@company.com). That means auto-detect entitlements won’t work.

[22:31] Anika Desai: Exactly. That’s why inputting entitlement ID is helpful, or a separate “admin invites user” workflow.

[22:41] Stephanie Nguyen: We’ll make sure docs call that out.

[22:45] Miguel Alvarez: On billing, one more thing: if you’re doing token usage, define what “token” means. Different models count differently. You should base it on what you count internally, but documentation should say it’s per model tokenizer.

[23:01] Cole Summers: Good point. Our API already reports token usage per request in the response metadata. We can use that as source of truth.

[23:10] Nadia Rahman: And we can expose daily usage summaries in console to match marketplace billing.

[23:15] Miguel Alvarez: That’s helpful for customer trust.

[23:19] Stephanie Nguyen: Okay. Let’s talk about dimension naming and plan structure. It sounds like recommended is:

- Hosted plan with usage dimensions (tokens, embeddings)
- Dedicated plan as subscription, possibly with an overage usage dimension
- Private plan as subscription
- Compliance add-on as bundle plans (Hosted+Compliance etc)

Is that fair?
[23:44] Priya Shah: Yes.

[23:46] Miguel Alvarez: Yes, that would be a clean structure.

[23:49] Cole Summers: For Dedicated overage, would we meter tokens or something else? Because customers might still care about tokens, not GPU hours.

[23:59] Miguel Alvarez: If the overage is “extra usage beyond included”, tokens is okay. If it’s “extra capacity”, maybe hours. But tokens is more straightforward given your product.

[24:12] Cole Summers: Great. We’ll think through included vs overage.

sections.section_path: 2026 01 16 Gcp Marketplace Onboarding And Billing Review
sections.heading: 2026 01 16 Gcp Marketplace Onboarding And Billing Review
sections.content:
[24:16] Chris Osei: I want to make sure we leave with concrete outputs. Cole will send a proposed mapping table and example payloads. Anika and Miguel will send docs and constraints. Ben will share screenshots/wireframes.

[24:31] Stephanie Nguyen: One question: in GCP marketplace, do customers expect to get credits / trial? We offer free credits on our website; does marketplace support that?

[24:41] Priya Shah: Marketplace trials exist in some contexts but not universally. Many partners handle trials outside marketplace or do a low-cost starter plan. If you want a trial, we can discuss, but it may complicate approval.

[24:56] Stephanie Nguyen: We’ll keep it simple for now.

[24:59] Ben Carter: Another thing: we have a dedicated onboarding docs page. Is it okay to link external docs from the listing?

[25:07] Priya Shah: Yes, you can link to documentation. Just make sure it’s stable URLs.

[25:12] Chris Osei: We’re finalizing vanity redirects for marketplace. Okay.

[25:16] (minor audio glitch)

[25:18] Nadia Rahman: Can we ask about time window for metering submissions? Like can we send usage events delayed by a day?

[25:26] Miguel Alvarez: There is a window; don’t send extremely late. A few hours delay is okay. A day is sometimes okay but not ideal. Send as close to real time as possible. Again, I’ll send guidance.

[25:43] Nadia Rahman: Got it.

[25:45] Cole Summers: For retry logic, if API errors, we retry with exponential backoff. If it fails for a long time, we queue. We can cap backlog.

[25:54] Miguel Alvarez: That’s fine. But make sure you don’t exceed the allowed backfill window.

[26:02] Stephanie Nguyen: Okay.

[26:04] Priya Shah: Any other questions from Redwood before we wrap?

[26:09] Stephanie Nguyen: I have one more: procurement question. Some buyers will ask “does buying through marketplace change the support terms / SLAs?” We have dedicated support tiers. Do you see any constraints on what we can say?

[26:23] Priya Shah: You can state support terms clearly. Just avoid promising things you can’t deliver. If there’s a premium SLA, you can make it a plan or an add-on, but it should be consistent.

[26:37] Ben Carter: We’ll align with our support team.

[26:40] Chris Osei: Okay. Let’s do a quick recap and next steps.

[26:45] Chris Osei: Recap:

- Dimension strategy: keep Hosted usage-based with a small set of dimensions (tokens, embeddings), use subscription plans for Dedicated/Private, consider bundled plans for compliance add-ons.
- Use stable IDs, don’t key logic off display names.
- Handle entitlement propagation delays with friendly UI + retry.
- Implement idempotency for metering events and alert on 4xx errors.
- Run staging test: subscribe -> entitlement -> org link -> API key -> sample traffic -> verify metering -> cancellation/plan change.

[27:21] Stephanie Nguyen: And action items: Cole will send draft mapping + payload examples, Ben will send UX screens, Anika/Miguel will send docs on quotas/rounding/validation.

[27:33] Anika Desai: Yep.

[27:35] Miguel Alvarez: Yep, I’ll send the metering validation checklist and rounding recommendations.

sections.section_path: 2026 01 16 Gcp Marketplace Onboarding And Billing Review
sections.heading: 2026 01 16 Gcp Marketplace Onboarding And Billing Review
sections.content:
[06:55] Miguel Alvarez: Dedicated capacity tends to fit better as subscription / contract. Usage metering for “gpu hours” works, but you need to align it with what you’re actually providing. If it’s truly reserved, then a monthly subscription fee is clearer. If there’s burst/overage, you can meter overage separately.

[07:16] Nadia Rahman: We can do either. Internally we track reserved pool size and then tokens anyway, but the contract is the key. If you recommend subscription for reserved, then our metering is mostly for overage.

[07:29] Priya Shah: From a procurement standpoint, enterprise buyers usually prefer a predictable subscription line item. Then usage-based Hosted is more PLG.

[07:41] Stephanie Nguyen: That matches what we’re seeing. One thing we’re worried about: we want three clear “paths” in the listing—Hosted, Dedicated, Private. But under the hood GCP constructs are not always “three products.” It’s one listing with plans, right?

[07:57] Priya Shah: Exactly. You typically have one product listing and multiple plans. You can describe the three modes in the copy, but technically it’s one product with pricing plans.

[08:12] Ben Carter: On the onboarding, would you expect different landing pages for different plans? Like, if someone buys Private, they shouldn’t be dropped into “create API key and call the hosted endpoint” because their next step is networking and deployment.

[08:26] Anika Desai: That’s a good point. Ideally yes: after entitlement, route them to the appropriate next steps. But you can also have a general landing page that asks “what did you purchase?” or reads the plan from the entitlement.

[08:43] Cole Summers: Reading the plan from entitlement is doable if the entitlement includes plan name. We just need to be careful with plan rename.

[08:52] Miguel Alvarez: Plan rename is okay if you keep the underlying plan ID stable. Don’t key logic off display name.

[09:01] Chris Osei: Noted. We’ll key off ID.

[09:05] Stephanie Nguyen: Let’s talk about reviewer expectations on the metering payload. Miguel, can you share what they check?

[09:14] Miguel Alvarez: Sure. They’ll check: (1) you’re using the correct API endpoints, (2) the consumerId or entitlement is valid, (3) the dimension is a valid one configured in your offer, (4) the quantity is non-negative and within reason, (5) timestamps are sane (not future by a day), (6) idempotency—you don’t double bill on retry.

[09:40] Nadia Rahman: On idempotency: we have an internal “usage_event_id” and we can keep a ledger. If we retry, we send the same event id. Is that a pattern you like to see?

[09:52] Miguel Alvarez: Yes. Exactly. Store the request ID and mark it as sent. Most of the “billing mismatch” issues are duplicate sends during outages.

[10:05] Ben Carter: Do you have any advice on how to validate end-to-end that metering is going to show up for the customer? Like, in AWS we can see it in the buyer account pretty quickly.

sections.section_path: 2026 01 16 Gcp Marketplace Onboarding And Billing Review
sections.heading: 2026 01 16 Gcp Marketplace Onboarding And Billing Review
sections.content:
[10:15] Miguel Alvarez: On GCP, you can see metering records in the partner console and via reports, but it’s not always instant. For testing, you want to confirm your API calls succeed and then use the console to verify the usage events are recorded. Anika can share the checklist.

[10:33] Anika Desai: Yeah, I can send a link. There’s a “test buyer” flow too. You procure with a test account, then you validate that entitlement is created and your backend can resolve it.

[10:47] Stephanie Nguyen: Great. Another question: dimension naming constraints. We saw some limitations around character length and allowed characters.

[10:56] Miguel Alvarez: Keep it short, alphanumeric plus underscore usually. Avoid spaces. If you have to include a version, don’t. Better to keep the same dimension and change the price model rather than changing the dimension name.

[11:13] Cole Summers: That’s helpful. We were going to do “hosted_tokens_1k” rather than “hosted_input_tokens_1k” and “hosted_output_tokens_1k” to keep it one dimension. We can still show the breakdown in our console for observability, but bill as total tokens.

[11:32] Miguel Alvarez: That’s a good compromise.

[11:35] Stephanie Nguyen: And embeddings we can keep separate.

[11:38] Miguel Alvarez: Yes.

[11:40] Chris Osei: I want to make sure we cover onboarding UX expectations. Ben, can you describe what we’re building and get GCP feedback?

[11:49] Ben Carter: Sure. So in our console, when you click “Get started”, there will be a “Purchased via marketplace?” path. If they choose GCP marketplace, we ask them to sign in. Then we try to auto-detect entitlements tied to that user, and if we can’t, we allow them to paste an entitlement ID. If entitlement is found, we show “link to existing org” or “create new org.” After that, we prompt them to create first API key for Hosted, or if the plan is Dedicated/Private, we route to request provisioning steps.

[12:24] Anika Desai: That’s pretty aligned with what we like to see. Two things: (1) make it very clear what to do if they’re not the person who purchased. Sometimes procurement buys and engineering uses. So include instructions like “ask the billing admin to invite you” or “forward this entitlement ID.” (2) include a retry experience for pending entitlements.

[12:50] Ben Carter: Yep. We have an error state “Entitlement not found” that currently suggests contacting support. We can change that to “may take a few minutes” and include refresh.

[13:02] Priya Shah: Also include support SLA information and the right support channel for marketplace customers. It doesn’t have to be complex, but the listing should say how to get help.

[13:12] Stephanie Nguyen: We’ll incorporate that into listing FAQs. On testing: we need a clear test plan. Chris, we have some draft steps; can we align with GCP?

sections.section_path: 2026 01 16 Gcp Marketplace Onboarding And Billing Review
sections.heading: 2026 01 16 Gcp Marketplace Onboarding And Billing Review
sections.content:
[13:22] Chris Osei: Yeah. Proposed test checklist:
1) Subscribe to plan in GCP Marketplace using test buyer
2) Verify entitlement exists (via API/console)
3) In Redwood console, run entitlement verification and link/create org
4) Generate an API key
5) Send a small set of inference requests (chat/text and embeddings)
6) Verify metering calls succeed and appear under correct dimension
7) Cancel subscription and verify access behavior (grace period?)
8) Re-subscribe / plan change and verify entitlements update
9) Negative tests: wrong entitlement, cross-org linking, delayed propagation

[14:03] Miguel Alvarez: That’s good. On cancellation: define your policy. Some partners cut off immediately, some allow a grace period. But it needs to match your listing terms and how you interpret the entitlement state.

[14:18] Cole Summers: Our default is to stop accepting billable traffic if entitlement is inactive, but we may allow a short grace if the cancellation is accidental. For marketplace we probably keep it strict.

[14:31] Anika Desai: During review, they’ll test cancel and see if your UI reflects it. If there’s a grace, document it.

[14:40] Nadia Rahman: On entitlement state changes, how quickly do we see “active -> cancelled”? That’s a potential race.

[14:49] Anika Desai: It’s usually quick, but again, you should poll or have a scheduled sync. Don’t assume immediate.

[15:00] Ben Carter: We have a sync job that runs every few minutes and on-demand verification. We can tighten it during onboarding.

[15:08] Miguel Alvarez: Just be careful with rate limits. If you have everyone spamming “verify entitlement” you might hit quotas. But for normal scale it’s okay.

[15:19] Stephanie Nguyen: One more thing: our SKUs include compliance add-ons (like extended audit log retention, compliance pack). Is it common to have add-ons as separate dimensions or separate plans?

[15:34] Priya Shah: It depends. If it’s truly an add-on, separate plan can be complicated. Some do “bundle plans” (base + add-on). Others handle add-ons off-marketplace. If you want it procured via marketplace, bundling plans is usually easiest.

[15:54] Miguel Alvarez: If you do it as a usage dimension, that’s weird for a monthly compliance pack. Better as subscription line item. But you can create a plan called “Hosted + Compliance” and so on.

[16:09] Cole Summers: That increases plan combinatorics. We were trying to keep it minimal.

[16:14] Stephanie Nguyen: For enterprise procurement, it might be okay. We can do a small number: Hosted, Hosted+Compliance, Dedicated, Dedicated+Compliance, Private. Something like that.

[16:26] Priya Shah: Exactly. Keep it manageable.

[16:29] Chris Osei: Let’s capture that as an open decision: add-ons as bundles vs separate plans.

[16:35] Ben Carter: If it’s bundled, onboarding can still read plan ID and show the right “features enabled” banner.

[16:42] Anika Desai: Yep.

[16:44] Miguel Alvarez: For dimensions, fewer is better. If you have too many, it’s harder to validate.

[16:52] Nadia Rahman: Another metering nuance: we do streaming responses. Tokens get generated over time. We aggregate at end of request. That means we may emit one usage record per request or per batch. Is that okay?

sections.section_path: 2026 01 16 Gcp Marketplace Onboarding And Billing Review
sections.heading: 2026 01 16 Gcp Marketplace Onboarding And Billing Review
sections.content:
[17:07] Miguel Alvarez: That’s okay. The marketplace doesn’t care if you batch, as long as it’s accurate and you can explain your aggregation. Many partners aggregate per hour to reduce volume.

[17:19] Cole Summers: We can aggregate per hour per org per dimension. That’s probably a good default.

[17:26] Miguel Alvarez: Yes.

[17:28] Stephanie Nguyen: Any pitfalls with multi-region? Our hosted API runs in multiple regions. If a GCP marketplace buyer uses us in EU, does billing care?

[17:39] Priya Shah: Billing doesn’t care, but listing and security docs might. If you claim data residency, make sure it’s accurate. The marketplace reviewers may look at your data handling statements.

[17:52] Chris Osei: We’re preparing a security packet; we’ll align wording.

[17:57] Anika Desai: From onboarding side, if you route them to a region selection, ensure it’s clear. Some customers think marketplace implies region-specific. It doesn’t necessarily.

[18:10] Ben Carter: We plan to ask region at org creation and default to the closest region, but allow override.

[18:18] Stephanie Nguyen: Great.
[18:20] (brief crosstalk)

[18:22] Stephanie Nguyen: Miguel, can we ask about “dimension mismatch” issues you’ve seen? We had one on AWS where our internal meter name didn’t match the marketplace dimension and we billed wrong. We’re trying to prevent it.

[18:37] Miguel Alvarez: Yeah, common. It’s usually one of: using display name instead of dimension ID, or typos, or changing the offer and not updating code. The best practice: keep a single source config file for mapping, version it, and add automated tests that validate the dimension list against what’s configured in marketplace.

[18:57] Cole Summers: We have a billing catalog config in code. We can add a test that asserts “these dimensions are the only allowed ones.” But we can’t programmatically query the marketplace config easily.

[19:10] Miguel Alvarez: You can still do a manual gate before launch: export the dimension list and compare. And once stable, don’t change often.

[19:21] Nadia Rahman: We also emit telemetry events in our pipeline. We can alert on unknown dimension errors.

[19:28] Miguel Alvarez: Perfect. Set alerts on 4xx responses from metering API.

[19:35] Chris Osei: Okay. Let’s do a quick pass on what GCP needs for submission beyond billing: screenshots, support, security docs, etc. Priya?

[19:46] Priya Shah: You’ll need: final listing copy, pricing plans configured, support contact info, a privacy policy link, and security documentation depending on the category. For enterprise oriented products, we often see SOC 2 statements, encryption, retention, audit logging. You don’t need to paste the whole report, but your claims must be accurate.

[20:10] Stephanie Nguyen: Understood. We’ll provide a marketplace security overview and pointers to evidence under NDA.

[20:18] Anika Desai: Reviewers like diagrams. Even a simple data flow diagram helps.

[20:23] Ben Carter: We have a diagram showing subscription -> entitlement -> Redwood control plane -> inference runtime. We’ll use it.

[20:31] Chris Osei: Back to testing. Anika, you mentioned a test buyer flow. Can you outline quickly? Just so we know if we need special accounts.

sections.section_path: 2026 01 16 Gcp Marketplace Onboarding And Billing Review
sections.heading: 2026 01 16 Gcp Marketplace Onboarding And Billing Review
sections.content:
[03:32] Stephanie Nguyen: That’s helpful. We’ve got an entitlement verification endpoint and a sync job; we can make sure the UI does the “pending” messaging.

[03:41] Priya Shah: Also important: the marketplace reviewers will click through the onboarding. If they hit a dead end, that’s friction during review. Provide a support link and clear instructions.

[03:53] Chris Osei: Got it. Maybe we jump into identifiers. Anika, can you talk about what we should store and what we can expect to receive? We’ve seen “consumer ID” in docs but there are like multiple names for it.

[04:07] Anika Desai: Yeah. So, you’ll have a procurement account / buyer account. When a customer subscribes, there’s an entitlement created. Depending on your integration, you’ll get a consumerId and entitlement name or resource. Your system should treat that as the source of truth for “is this customer subscribed” and also for mapping metering events to the right buyer.

[04:30] Cole Summers: For metering, we need a stable key to associate usage to the marketplace customer. We also have our internal “org_id”. So our thought was: marketplace entitlement maps to Redwood org, and then that org has one or more projects / API keys. Usage is aggregated at org level and then billed.

[04:49] Miguel Alvarez: That’s typical. Just ensure you don’t mix multiple entitlements into a single org without clear logic. If a customer buys two subscriptions, you need to decide whether that’s two entitlements attached to one org or two orgs. Reviewers will look for correct allocation.

[05:06] Ben Carter: We have an edge case: existing Redwood customers may subscribe later through marketplace for procurement reasons. So they want to link the marketplace subscription to an already-existing org.

[05:17] Anika Desai: That’s also common. UX expectation: you allow linking to an existing account. But ensure authentication is done. And avoid a scenario where someone can claim an entitlement that isn’t theirs.

[05:31] Stephanie Nguyen: Right. We require sign-in, then they paste an entitlement or we detect via login? We were thinking detect via a “claim token” page in our console.

[05:42] Anika Desai: Either works. Most partners do a redirect back with parameters, or they ask the user to input the entitlement ID. Redirect flows are nicer but more work. For review, either is acceptable as long as it’s documented.

[06:00] Chris Osei: For this phase we’re doing a marketplace-specific entrypoint in our console. It will prompt for “GCP marketplace subscription” and then run entitlement verification.

[06:10] Miguel Alvarez: That’s fine. On billing: I want to zoom in on the dimension list. Can you share what you propose?

[06:18] Cole Summers: We don’t have final IDs yet, but draft is something like:

- Hosted: “hosted_tokens_1k” and “hosted_embeddings_1k”
- Rerank: “rerank_requests_1k” (maybe)
- Dedicated: “dedicated_gpu_hour” or “dedicated_capacity_unit”
- Private: “private_platform_month”
- Add-ons: “compliance_pack_month”, “extended_audit_log_retention_month”

The big question is whether “Dedicated” should be a usage dimension or a subscription SKU.

[27:40] Priya Shah: And once you’ve done the staging test, we can do a short follow-up to review results and any issues.

[27:48] Stephanie Nguyen: Perfect. Thanks everyone.
[27:51] (call continues with scheduling chatter)

[28:00] Chris Osei: I’ll send the notes and propose a follow-up next week.

[28:05] Priya Shah: Great.
[28:07] Meeting ended (recording continued briefly)
[53:58] (end of recording)

sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Triage checklist (Support/CS) > 7) Mitigation options you can offer immediately (tier-dependent)
sections.content:
7) Mitigation options you can offer immediately (tier-dependent)

These are customer-facing actions CS/Support may propose, with SRE confirmation where possible:

- Temporarily reduce max context / max output tokens (if within acceptable product behavior).
- Temporarily shift traffic to the contracted primary route only (avoid experimental routes).
- Enable/disable streaming based on their client constraints (note: streaming affects perceived latency but should not invalidate throughput).
- If the customer has multi-deployment setup: fail over to a secondary deployment (Premium: may be Redwood-assisted).

Do not promise failover across regions unless the tier/contract explicitly includes it.

sections.section_path: 20280503 Region Fallback Priority Ops Inventory
sections.heading: 20280503 Region Fallback Priority Ops Inventory
sections.content:
- Patient clinical records (PHI) must remain in-region (EU) for EU patients.
- Operational metadata (service-level telemetry that does not include patient-identifiers) can be replicated to US for analytics if pseudonymized and access controlled.
- Backups of PHI: acceptable to store in US if encrypted with customer-managed keys and access is restricted to named personnel only — otherwise must stay in EU.

2) Failover order and cross-region replication:

- Preferred failover hierarchy: EU primary -> EU warm standby -> US emergency failover.
- Cross-region failover to US is permitted only for declared emergency windows (max 4 hours), must be pre-approved in runbook.
- Target RPO 15 minutes for active datasets; RTO target 30 minutes for critical APIs.

3) Logs & telemetry:

- Logs do contain limited PII (hashed patient IDs and occasional email addresses).
- We expect redaction at ingest for any free-text fields that might include PHI; hashed IDs are acceptable if the hash keys are kept on-region.
- Retention: default operational logs 90 days; audit logs 3 years. Long-term archival to our secure archive is possible after 90 days (encrypted, on-region if PHI).

4) Backups & snapshots:

- Daily incremental snapshots; weekly full snapshots.
- Immutable weekly snapshots for 90 days for critical datasets. Cross-region incremental copies only for analytics (non-PHI) or encrypted/full-access restricted backups with CMK.

5) Key management and attestations:

- Prefer CMK (KMS) for PHI datasets. We will require proof of key rotation logs and monthly HSM audit extracts if HSM used.

6) Audit evidence:

- SOC 2 Type II report, access log exports (filtered to our account), key rotation logs, and one sample sanitized query/log bundle showing redaction.

Attachments: PHI_handling_requirements.pdf (internal control summary).

Availability: Tom and I are available Tue/Wed next week 10:00–12:00 ET for the technical deep-dive. If you can send an invite with a short agenda, we’ll confirm.

Thanks,
Elena

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Known issues (Support-facing)
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Known issues (Support-facing)
sections.content:
Known issues (Support-facing)

1) **Retry-After header missing on some overload responses**

- Symptom: Customer receives 429/503 overload payload but no Retry-After.
- Workaround: Recommend exponential backoff with jitter as above.
- Action: Escalate if reproducible; include route + correlation IDs.

2) **Fallback model not triggering as expected**

- Symptom: Customer has configured fallback but still sees repeated 503 without failover.
- Workaround: Customer can temporarily specify an alternate model/region explicitly (if acceptable) while we investigate.
- Action: Escalate; include tenant ID, configured fallback policy (what they intended), and correlation IDs.

3) **Customer interprets 503 as “platform outage”**

- Guidance: Use the approved response language; direct them to Retry-After and backoff guidance.

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Common customer questions + approved responses > “Can you increase my limits?”
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Common customer questions + approved responses > “Can you increase my limits?”
sections.content:
“Can you increase my limits?”

Guidance:

- Confirm whether they are hitting **429** (likely limit-related) vs **503** (regional/model saturation).
- If 429 is persistent at normal traffic levels, route to CS for capacity/tier discussion.
- If 503 is persistent, treat as reliability issue and escalate to Eng.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Common failure modes and quick routing hints
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Common failure modes and quick routing hints
sections.content:
Common failure modes and quick routing hints

- **Customer sees lower throughput than Redwood reports:** often a measurement mismatch (streaming token accounting, end-to-end latency vs throughput, counting input tokens). Engage Observability if persistent.
- **Throughput drops with GPU pegged:** suspect contention, node health, thermal throttling, network bottleneck; page Infra.
- **Throughput drops with low utilization:** suspect admission control limiting, customer throttling, or workload shift to longer contexts; page SRE; ask customer for concurrency/workload details.
- **Regional capacity constraint / failover behavior:** check tier failover posture; page Infra and SRE; do not promise cross-region without tier/contract confirmation.

---

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > What is the Dedicated Throughput SLO (customer-facing summary)
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > What is the Dedicated Throughput SLO (customer-facing summary)
sections.content:
What is the Dedicated Throughput SLO (customer-facing summary)

Dedicated Throughput SLO guarantees a **minimum sustained throughput floor** for an eligible Dedicated deployment under defined conditions.

**High-level definition (internal summary):**

- Metric: throughput measured as **billable output tokens per second**, computed per deployment, aggregated over a rolling window.
- Scope: Dedicated deployments only (not Hosted API, not eval/sandbox deployments).
- Eligibility: model/version and configuration must be within the customer’s contracted Dedicated configuration (e.g., pinned model family/version, supported max context, supported shape).

**Common non-eligibility / exclusions (not exhaustive):**

- Customer-side throttling or client concurrency limits causing underutilization.
- Customer workload violating sizing assumptions (e.g., contexts above configured limit, unsupported parameter combinations).
- Warm-up periods after scale-from-zero or cold start (tier-dependent; see “Warm pool / startup” below).
- Incidents due to customer networking/VPC misconfig in Private connectivity paths (if applicable).

When in doubt, treat as potentially eligible, start the triage, and engage SRE.

---

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Service credits / compensation (internal guidance) > Approval path (default)
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Service credits / compensation (internal guidance) > Approval path (default)
sections.content:
Approval path (default)

1) CS/Support compiles incident details and SRE confirmation.
2) SRE provides breach window + summary.
3) Product Dedicated confirms entitlement interpretation (tier/exclusions).
4) Finance (Laura Bennett / delegate) validates policy compliance and amount.
5) Legal (Sofia Mendes / delegate) reviews if there is contract ambiguity or if a non-standard remedy is proposed.
6) CS communicates outcome to customer.

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > How to interpret and use correlation IDs > How Support should use them internally
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > How to interpret and use correlation IDs > How Support should use them internally
sections.content:
How Support should use them internally

- Paste the ID(s) into the internal log search / tracing tool.
- Capture:
  - the **error.code**
  - the **route** (e.g., `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/responses`, embeddings endpoint)
  - the **region** (requested + served)
  - whether **Retry-After** was present and its value

If Support cannot access dashboards/tracing, escalate with the IDs and all details in the escalation template below.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Severity levels (Support/CS view)
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Severity levels (Support/CS view)
sections.content:
Severity levels (Support/CS view)

Use these severities to standardize response; SRE may map to their incident severities.

**SEV-1 (Critical, likely customer-impacting breach)**

- Premium tier customer reports sustained throughput below floor OR SRE burn-rate alert is firing.
- Clear production impact (e.g., queue buildup, timeouts, user-visible latency spikes).
- Immediate paging required.

**SEV-2 (High, likely degradation / at-risk of breach)**

- Throughput is below expected but not yet confirmed as an SLO breach.
- Customer impact is moderate OR limited to a subset of traffic/routes.
- Paging may be required depending on tier and duration.

**SEV-3 (Moderate, investigation / metrics discrepancy)**

- Conflicting metrics (customer vs Redwood dashboards), short-lived dips, or suspected measurement artifacts.
- No clear production impact.

---

Service credits / compensation (internal guidance)

**Important:** Do not commit to a credit amount in writing until approvals are complete.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Customer communications guide > Communication principles
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Customer communications guide > Communication principles
sections.content:
Customer communications guide

Communication principles

- Use a single owner for customer updates (CS/Support), even if multiple engineering teams are engaged.
- Acknowledge impact quickly; avoid speculating on root cause.
- Provide time-bound next update (“next update in 30 minutes”).
- For Premium accounts, default to more frequent updates and written summaries.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Evidence and logging requirements
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Evidence and logging requirements
sections.content:
Evidence and logging requirements

For any SEV-1/SEV-2 and any credit review, capture:

- Customer ticket link
- Incident link (if created)
- Dashboard links (throughput vs floor, saturation, errors)
- Request IDs / traces used for debugging
- Summary of customer-side traffic confirmation
- Timeline of mitigations and when throughput stabilized

---

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Warm pool / startup considerations
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Warm pool / startup considerations
sections.content:
Warm pool / startup considerations

Some tiers include warm pool guarantees (or faster recovery expectations). During triage, identify if the customer is within a warm-up window:

- Did the deployment recently scale from zero?
- Was there a recent model reload, config change, or node replacement?
- Did traffic resume after prolonged inactivity?

If warm-up is suspected, note it explicitly in the customer thread and ask SRE to confirm whether the event is excluded by policy.

---

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Triage checklist (Support/CS) > 5) Check if this is a metrics discrepancy
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Triage checklist (Support/CS) > 5) Check if this is a metrics discrepancy
sections.content:
5) Check if this is a metrics discrepancy

If customer numbers differ from Redwood:

- Ask what they are measuring (wall-clock end-to-end, tokens counted, streaming vs non-streaming).
- Request a single representative request ID and a 10–20 minute sample window.

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Common customer questions + approved responses > “Is Redwood down?”
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Common customer questions + approved responses > “Is Redwood down?”
sections.content:
Common customer questions + approved responses

“Is Redwood down?”

Approved response:
“Not necessarily. These errors indicate Redwood is protecting service reliability during temporary saturation in a specific region/model. We reject early with clear retry guidance to avoid timeouts and degraded performance. Please follow the Retry-After header and exponential backoff. If the issue persists beyond a short window, share correlation IDs and we’ll investigate.”

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Paging and escalation triggers (when to page SRE / Infra) > Engage Observability (not a page; async unless SEV-1)
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Paging and escalation triggers (when to page SRE / Infra) > Engage Observability (not a page; async unless SEV-1)
sections.content:
Engage Observability (not a page; async unless SEV-1)

- Throughput dashboards disagree with billing/export numbers.
- Recent metric changes (e.g., streaming token accounting) suspected.
- Missing labels (deployment_id, model, region) prevents accurate attribution.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Appendix: Minimal internal handoff note (for paging)
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Appendix: Minimal internal handoff note (for paging)
sections.content:
Appendix: Minimal internal handoff note (for paging)

When paging SRE/Infra, include:

- “Dedicated Throughput SLO: suspected/confirmed”
- Deployment ID
- Tier + region
- Time window and whether ongoing
- Customer-confirmed load/concurrency (if available)
- Dashboard link
- Any correlated symptoms (timeouts, 5xx, queue depth)

This reduces back-and-forth and speeds mitigation.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Purpose
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Purpose
sections.content:
Purpose

This playbook defines the end-to-end process for handling Dedicated **Throughput SLO** misses or suspected misses. It is designed for Customer Success (CS) and Support to:

- Triage quickly and consistently.
- Engage the correct on-call teams (SRE / Infra / Observability) at the right time.
- Communicate clearly with customers, including status updates and written summaries.
- Route service-credit / compensation requests through the correct approval path.

This page is **restricted** because it includes internal paging triggers and credit approval guidance.

---

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Retry & backoff guidance (what we should recommend) > Streaming-specific guidance
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Retry & backoff guidance (what we should recommend) > Streaming-specific guidance
sections.content:
Streaming-specific guidance

Streaming workloads can worsen overload if clients open many concurrent streams.

- Recommend **lower streaming concurrency** during peak periods.
- If the customer can tolerate it, recommend **shorter outputs** (reduce `max_tokens`) and/or **shorter prompts**.
- If a stream fails mid-response with an overload error on reconnect attempts, advise them to back off and resume with a bounded number of attempts.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Roles and ownership during an SLO event
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Roles and ownership during an SLO event
sections.content:
Roles and ownership during an SLO event

**Support/CS (Incident Driver for customer comms)**

- Owns the customer thread, updates, and expectation management.
- Owns the case record: timeline, impact, and customer confirmations.
- Initiates escalation and ensures correct teams are engaged.

**SRE On-Call (Technical Incident Lead)**

- Confirms whether the SLO is breached per the canonical evaluator.
- Drives mitigation and coordinates cross-functional response.
- Provides internal/external technical summary for comms.

**Infra/Fleet On-Call (Capacity / shape / provisioning owner)**

- Addresses capacity constraints, noisy-neighbor isolation issues, node failures, and shape-level performance anomalies.

**Observability (as-needed)**

- Validates metric correctness (e.g., streaming accounting anomalies), dashboard discrepancies, missing tags.

**Product Dedicated (as-needed)**

- Confirms entitlement interpretation (tier rules, burst policy, failover posture).
- Aligns on customer-facing messaging for edge cases.

**Finance/FP&A + Legal (as-needed for credits/comp)**

- Approves service credits above policy thresholds and any non-standard compensation.

---

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > When to escalate to Engineering (Eng Oncall / SRE)
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > When to escalate to Engineering (Eng Oncall / SRE)
sections.content:
When to escalate to Engineering (Eng Oncall / SRE)

Escalate immediately if any of the following are true:

- **Enterprise customer** reporting sustained overload errors impacting production.
- Overload errors persist for **>15 minutes** with correct backoff behavior.
- **No Retry-After** observed on multiple responses for the same route/region/model.
- Suspected **misclassification** (e.g., 500s that should be 429/503 overload, or overload codes returned with 200/stream interruptions).
- **Fallback routing configured** but not activating.
- Customer reports sharp regression (new errors) coincident with a canary/rollout and provides IDs.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Triage checklist (Support/CS) > 4) Check the Dedicated Throughput dashboard for that deployment
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Triage checklist (Support/CS) > 4) Check the Dedicated Throughput dashboard for that deployment
sections.content:
4) Check the Dedicated Throughput dashboard for that deployment

Look for:

- Rolling-window throughput vs committed floor
- Error rate/timeout correlation
- GPU saturation, queue depth, admission control shedding
- Recent routing pool changes or failovers

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > How to recognize overload-protection responses > Common HTTP statuses
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > How to recognize overload-protection responses > Common HTTP statuses
sections.content:
How to recognize overload-protection responses

Common HTTP statuses

- **429 Too Many Requests**
  - Used for admission controls such as per-tenant concurrency caps, token buckets, or tier limits.
  - Usually safe to retry with backoff if Retry-After is provided.

- **503 Service Unavailable**
  - Used when the platform is overloaded at the regional/model level (breaker open) or actively shedding load to protect SLOs.
  - Usually safe to retry with backoff and/or reduce load. May persist until capacity recovers.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Triage checklist (Support/CS) > 2) Confirm the customer is driving enough load
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Triage checklist (Support/CS) > 2) Confirm the customer is driving enough load
sections.content:
2) Confirm the customer is driving enough load

Ask:

- Current request concurrency
- Any client-side rate limiting (explicit QPS cap, worker pool limit)
- Any recent application deploy or traffic change

If the customer is under-driving load, throughput may be low without being an SLO failure.

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Error payload: what customers see
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Error payload: what customers see
sections.content:
Error payload: what customers see

Overload errors are additive and JSON-compatible with existing response parsing.

Typical shape (example):

- `error.type`: `overload_error` (or `rate_limit_error` in some cases)
- `error.code`: stable machine code
- `error.message`: human-readable
- `error.request_id`: mirrors `x-redwood-request-id` where available
- `error.correlation_id`: mirrors `x-redwood-correlation-id` where available

Example snippet (illustrative only):
{
  "error": {
    "type": "overload_error",
    "code": "BREAKER_OPEN",
    "message": "The service is temporarily overloaded. Please retry after the specified delay.",
    "request_id": "req_01J9...",
    "correlation_id": "corr_01J9..."
  }
}

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Purpose
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Purpose
sections.content:
Purpose

This page helps Support/CS respond to customer reports of new “overload protection” errors (circuit breakers + load shedding) on Redwood Hosted API.

Goals:

- Explain what the customer is seeing (stable semantics vs ambiguous timeouts/5xx).
- Provide canonical retry/backoff guidance to prevent retry storms.
- Show how to interpret correlation IDs so Engineering can quickly trace requests.
- Define escalation criteria and the minimum information to collect.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Paging and escalation triggers (when to page SRE / Infra) > Page Infra/Fleet On-Call when any of the following is true (often in parallel)
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Paging and escalation triggers (when to page SRE / Infra) > Page Infra/Fleet On-Call when any of the following is true (often in parallel)
sections.content:
Page Infra/Fleet On-Call when any of the following is true (often in parallel)

- GPU/node health signals indicate failures, evictions, ECC errors, or repeated container restarts.
- Saturation: GPU utilization pinned while throughput drops (suspected contention, thermal throttling, network bottleneck).
- Capacity: the deployment appears mapped to the wrong pool/shape or lacks the expected headroom.
- Region-wide capacity constraint impacting Dedicated pools.

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Canonical mapping: status → meaning → what we tell customers
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Canonical mapping: status → meaning → what we tell customers
sections.content:
Canonical mapping: status → meaning → what we tell customers

Use this table to drive consistent customer guidance.

| HTTP | Typical meaning | What Support should say | Customer action |
|------|------------------|--------------------------|-----------------|
| 429 | Admission control / rate limiting / tier cap hit | “Your request was rejected to protect system stability. This is not a model failure; it indicates you are sending requests faster than the current allowed rate/concurrency.” | Respect Retry-After; implement exponential backoff + jitter; reduce concurrency; consider batching; if persistent, discuss tier/capacity options. |
| 503 | Regional/model breaker open or load shedding | “Redwood is temporarily overloaded in the requested region/model. We are rejecting early to avoid timeouts and protect overall reliability.” | Respect Retry-After; backoff + jitter; optionally route to another region/model if configured; reduce max_tokens/streaming concurrency; retry with bounded attempts. |

Notes:

- If the customer reports **timeouts** with no JSON error, treat as a separate issue (possible client/network or upstream timeouts) and escalate based on impact.
- If the customer gets **5xx** without the overload payload, collect details; it may be an unrelated incident.

sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Customer communications guide > Target update cadence (recommended)
sections.content:
Target update cadence (recommended)

- SEV-1: initial response within 15 minutes; updates every 30 minutes until stable.
- SEV-2: initial response within 1 hour; updates every 2–4 hours until stable.
- SEV-3: initial response within 1 business day; updates daily or as material changes occur.

sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Triage checklist (Support/CS) > 8) Open an incident record (internal) if SEV-1/SEV-2
sections.content:

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > How to recognize overload-protection responses > Expected headers (may vary by route)
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > How to recognize overload-protection responses > Expected headers (may vary by route)
sections.content:
Expected headers (may vary by route)

- **Retry-After**: integer seconds is preferred (e.g., `Retry-After: 2`).
- **x-redwood-request-id**: unique ID for a single request attempt.
- **x-redwood-correlation-id**: groups related attempts across services (gateway → routing → runtime). Some clients/logs only show one of these; either is helpful.

If the response is 429/503 *and* includes a Redwood overload error code in the JSON body, treat it as overload protection.

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Retry & backoff guidance (what we should recommend) > Recommended algorithm (support-approved)
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Retry & backoff guidance (what we should recommend) > Recommended algorithm (support-approved)
sections.content:
Recommended algorithm (support-approved)

If `Retry-After` is present:

- Sleep `Retry-After` seconds, then retry.

If `Retry-After` is missing:

- Backoff schedule suggestion: 0.5s, 1s, 2s, 4s, then stop (max 4 retries), each with ±20–40% jitter.

Bounds:

- Maximum total retry time budget: **~10–20 seconds** for interactive apps, **~60 seconds** for batch jobs.
- Maximum concurrent retries: keep to a small fraction of steady-state concurrency (e.g., 10–20%).

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > What changed (customer-facing)
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > What changed (customer-facing)
sections.content:
What changed (customer-facing)

When the platform is saturated (GPU capacity, scheduler backlog, downstream dependency brownout), Redwood may reject requests *early* and predictably rather than allowing them to time out or generate random 5xx.

Customers may now see:

- **429** responses for admission / quota / per-tenant caps.
- **503** responses when a regional/model circuit breaker is open or the system is actively shedding load.

These responses:

- Include stable **error codes** and a machine-readable JSON payload.
- Typically include a **Retry-After** header to indicate safe retry timing.
- Include Redwood request/correlation IDs for tracing.

sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Retry & backoff guidance (what we should recommend) > Golden rules
sections.content:
Retry & backoff guidance (what we should recommend)

Golden rules

- **Always respect Retry-After** when provided.
- **Use exponential backoff with jitter**; do not retry immediately.
- **Cap retries** to avoid amplifying overload.
- **Reduce concurrency** rather than increasing it during overload.
- Prefer **idempotency keys** for safe retries on non-streaming requests.

sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > SLOs (targets) > General notes
sections.content:
SLOs (targets)

General notes

- SLOs are evaluated over a **rolling 28-day window**.
- Unless specified, targets apply per region (e.g., us-east, eu-west).
- We define both **p95 and p99** latency objectives for enterprise; best-effort uses p95 as primary.

sections.section_path: Policy Engine Failover Extensions Draft
sections.heading: Policy Engine Failover Extensions Draft
sections.content:
- Decision must include:
  - decision_type (NO_OP | FAILOVER | PARTIAL_SHIFT | ROLLBACK | HOLD)
  - chosen_reason (canonical enum)
  - evidence: ordered list of signals used, with values, freshness, and thresholds.
  - rejected_candidates: (optional) top 1–3 alternatives and why they were not selected.

Proposed changes to policy engine
A) New predicates / functions
1) region_health(region, signal_type) -> {status, value, confidence, freshness_seconds}

- Wrapper that pulls normalized data from payload and enforces freshness calculations.

2) is_authoritative_reachability_down(region) -> bool

- True only if:
  - reachability.status == down
  - confidence >= configured_min_confidence (default 0.9)
  - freshness_seconds <= reachability_max_staleness (default 30s)

3) burn_rate_exceeded(region, metric, window, threshold) -> bool

- Works for errors_5xx_burn and tail_latency_burn.
- Window must be one of approved windows (e.g., 1m/5m/30m) to avoid configuration drift.

4) capacity_hard_gate(region) -> bool

- True if headroom below threshold AND capacity signal confidence is high.
- Intended to prevent shifting into an already overloaded region.

5) corroborated(primary_signal, secondary_signal) -> bool

- Enforces ADR-042 “required corroboration signals” when configured.
- Example: if tail latency burn triggers, require either 5xx burn OR reachability degraded/down OR control plane degraded.

6) hold_down_active(last_flip_at, min_hold_down_seconds) -> bool

- If true, policy engine returns HOLD unless reachability down is authoritative.

7) flip_budget_ok(tenant_id, route_id, max_flips_per_hour) -> bool

- Input includes a precomputed counter from controller/state store (policy engine does not store state).

8) blast_radius_ok(tenant_tier, requested_action) -> bool

- Enforces “can’t shift more than X% traffic for tier Y without approval”.
- For Hosted, blast radius is route-scoped; for Dedicated, pool-scoped.

B) Deterministic evaluation mode (required)

- Add an “evaluation_mode” field:
  - recommend: compute decision + evidence; do not mark as executable
  - enforce: compute decision; include explicit requested_action(s)
- Engine must produce identical decision_type and evidence in both modes (action packaging differs).

C) Signal hierarchy evaluation (ADR-042)
Priority order (proposed canonical order for v1):
1) Reachability DOWN (authoritative) => FAILOVER (unless no healthy fallback)
2) Errors (5xx) fast burn (high severity) => FAILOVER or PARTIAL_SHIFT depending on blast radius and capacity
3) Tail latency burn (p99/p95) => PARTIAL_SHIFT first; escalate to FAILOVER if corroborated and sustained
4) Capacity exhaustion / hard gate => HOLD + load shed (controller action), avoid shifting into constrained region
5) Control plane degradation => HOLD (do not flip rapidly; prevent oscillation)

Notes:

- “No healthy fallback” means every eligible fallback region fails capacity_hard_gate OR reachability is down OR stale beyond threshold.
- If no healthy fallback, decision should be HOLD and include “degrade_allowed=true” hint (controller can activate load shedding / retry-after).

D) Policy language / config schema additions
Add new fields (names tentative):

- failover:
  - enabled: boolean
  - eligible_regions: [us-east, eu-west, ...]
  - signal_requirements:
    - primary_trigger: enum
    - corroboration: [enum]
    - min_confidence: float
    - max_staleness_seconds: int
  - dampening:
    - min_hold_down_seconds: int
    - require_sustain_seconds: int (for non-reachability triggers)
  - safety:
    - require_approval: boolean (default true for prod initially)
    - max_flips_per_hour: int
    - max_traffic_shift_percent: int
    - rollback:
      - auto_rollback_enabled: boolean
      - rollback_after_seconds: int
      - rollback_require_healthy_primary_seconds: int

E) Output schema
Decision output (single object, JSON):
