sections.section_path: Burst Capacity Retro Notes
sections.heading: Burst Capacity Retro Notes
sections.content:
- Symptom: customer asked why burst line item didn’t match dashboard usage; we found ~1.8–2.3% overcount in a specific retry pattern.
- Root cause: metering event emitted pre-idempotency; retried requests emitted duplicate usage increments.
- Fix: idempotency keys + reconciliation checks.
- Ref: GitHub:redwood/pr-24108, Jira:SUP-28488

D) Noisy neighbor scare (tail latency increase for a non-burst tenant)

- Symptom: p95/p99 latency increase for a non-burst tenant correlated with another tenant’s burst window.
- What we learned: even if pool isolation is “logical,” shared control-plane/routing and some shared fleet components can cause tail amplification under saturation.
- Mitigation used: reduced global cap + increased cooldown for bursting tenant + forced routing fallback for that tenant for 30 min.
- Ref: Jira:SUP-28455

E) Support confusion: 429s when burst cap reached (expected but poorly messaged)

- We returned 429/overload when both baseline+burst caps were reached; some customers expected queuing instead.
- For GA we need crisp guidance: recommended retry/backoff strategy and what will/won’t queue.
- Ref: Jira:SUP-28503

Guardrails that were too strict (beta feedback)
1) Cooldown windows were overly punitive for spiky-but-legit workloads

- Current behavior: once a tenant hits max burst ratio, cooldown kicks in even if they drop below quickly.
- Effect: denial bursts after short spikes; customers perceive “flaky burst.”
- Proposal: cooldown should be based on sustained saturation (e.g., N seconds over threshold) or make cooldown proportional to burst duration, not a flat window.

2) Max burst ratio default (x1.5) was too conservative for “weekly batch” customers

- Several beta tenants expected x2–x3 for short windows (10–30 min) and were willing to pay.
- But we must pair higher ratios with stronger fairness + fleet safety + SLO gates.

3) Admission determinism vs latency tradeoff

- We enforced determinism by evaluating multiple signals synchronously; in some cases this added controller latency and increased timeouts.
- Suggestion: determinism requirement should be: “same inputs => same decision” but inputs can be snapshot-based (cached) within a bounded TTL.

Guardrails that were too lax (or missing)
1) Retry amplification guard

- When customers got denials, some clients retried immediately with high concurrency.
- We need an explicit “retry-after” / backoff hint tied to denial reason codes, and optionally server-side throttling at gateway.

2) Alerting gaps for “telemetry freshness” and “admission controller dependency health”

- We lacked a strong, paging-quality indicator for telemetry freshness degradation (it showed in graphs but didn’t page until customers complained).
- Admission controller dependency p99 did not have an error-budget aligned alert.

3) Fairness under mixed priority tiers needs stronger anti-starvation proofs

- We introduced priority tiers late in beta; we didn’t run enough multi-tenant stress tests for gold/silver combos.
- Need explicit starvation bound (e.g., min guaranteed tokens) and test harness enforcement.

4) Config propagation / console staleness

- One customer ticket: burst limit updated but Console showed stale value for too long.
- Root cause likely caching/prop delay; not a safety issue but it undermines trust.
- Ref: Jira:SUP-28541

Key metrics from beta (rough, from dashboards)

sections.section_path: Pr 18458 Smart Routing Fallback When Breaker Open
sections.heading: Pr 18458 Smart Routing Fallback When Breaker Open
sections.content:
Elena Popov (author): Default is max 1 fallback attempt per request. There’s an internal config to allow 2 only for the (region hop -> model hop) path, but I kept it disabled by default and added a hard cap + test. Added explicit checks: Dedicated/Private never route into Hosted, and Hosted never routes into Dedicated.

Ravi Menon (review): Loop prevention looks good. One concern: you’re using requested_model as a label value in metrics. That can be high cardinality. Please bucket by model family or a normalized name.

Elena Popov (author): Good catch. Updated metrics to use requested_model_family (derived from the catalog) and route_group (chat/embeddings/rerank), and removed raw model IDs. Added a metrics test to enforce label set.

Peter Holtz (embedded SRE, review): What’s the trigger mapping? We should only fallback on overload-derived classifications, not generic 503s from downstream. Also ensure correlation ID is preserved for support.

Elena Popov (author): Added overload_mapping.ts and tests. We only fallback on explicit overload reasons (breaker_open, shed, capacity_unavailable) coming from gateway/runtime classification. Generic downstream 503/500 doesn’t trigger fallback. Correlation ID is preserved; added integration test asserting x-redwood-correlation-id is unchanged.

Rafael Mendes (SRE lead, review): Please add a guard against fallback storms: if the fallback target is also overloaded, we should not keep trying. Make sure we return the overload error and include a stable internal reason for dashboards.

Elena Popov (author): Implemented: if fallback attempt returns overload again, we stop (bounded) and return the overload classification. We emit fallback_exhausted with result=overload and include internal reason in routing decision logs (not as a metric label).

Jordan Lee (policy engine, review): Policy selection should be tenant-aware and route-aware. Ensure we validate that the fallback target is in the allowlist; no implicit compatibility.

Elena Popov (author): Done. Fallback targets must be explicitly configured via policy for the tenant + route selector; we also require compatibility check against catalog (same modality + context window constraints). No implicit model swaps.

Mina Haddad (review): Approved after last changes.
Ravi Menon (review): Approved.
Peter Holtz (review): Approved.

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Signal flow (normative) > Runtime → telemetry → routing/gateway (aggregated)
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Signal flow (normative) > Runtime → telemetry → routing/gateway (aggregated)
sections.content:
Runtime → telemetry → routing/gateway (aggregated)

Runtime exports saturation metrics at pool/cluster granularity:

- scheduler_queue_depth (gauge)
- scheduler_backlog_ms (gauge)
- token_throughput_utilization (0..1)
- kv_cache_pressure (0..1)
- memory_pressure_proxy (0..1)

A telemetry aggregation layer produces:

- per-region/per-model “saturation state” (e.g., normal / elevated / critical)
- smoothed utilization signals (EMA or rolling windows)
- recommended admission modifiers (e.g., suggested shed percent)

Gateway and routing consume **aggregated** signals; they should not consume high-cardinality per-node metrics.

Sup 48377 Canary Traffic Split Not Matching Config

Source type: jira
Document ID: dsid_94f568e4161d4d78b0db60af2b611746
Release: v1.0.0
Benchmark: EnterpriseRAG-Bench synthetic upstream data
Hosted canary rollout: traffic split in us-east not matching Console config (canary receiving ~25% when set to 10%)

Issue summary
Customer reports that the canary cohort is receiving substantially more traffic than configured for a Hosted route rollout. Console shows canary set to 10% (after being reduced from 25%), but observed canary traffic remains ~22–27% in us-east.

Impact

- Customer sees increased cost/latency regression exposure compared to intended 10% canary.
- Customer is a beta design partner; they are using canary rollouts to validate a new quantization profile.

Customer report (via Support)

- Route: /v1/chat/completions (Hosted)
- Workspace/tenant: northstar-prod
- Rollout name/id (from customer screenshot): rll_9f3c2d3a
- Baseline: llama-3.1-70b-instruct v2025-04-03
- Canary: llama-3.1-70b-instruct v2025-04-16 (q8_0)
- Traffic schedule:
  - Step 1: 1% (ok)
  - Step 2: 5% (ok)
  - Step 3: 25% (ok)
  - Step 4: reduced to 10% (intended rollback in step) — mismatch started here

Environment

- prod, region: us-east
- Customer notes: eu-west appears closer to expected (not fully confirmed), but the majority of their traffic is us-east.

Evidence / reproduction
Customer provided:
1) Request logs showing response header X-Redwood-Rollout-Cohort=canary for ~1/4 of requests while Console shows 10%.
2) A sample of request IDs from a 10-minute window (2025-04-18 16:05–16:15 UTC) where cohort assignment was canary unexpectedly.

Support verification
Pulled routing decision logs in us-east for tenant northstar-prod and rollout rll_9f3c2d3a:

- router_decision fields observed:
  - rollout_id=rll_9f3c2d3a
  - configured_canary_percent=25 (unexpected)
  - console_step_target_percent=10 (expected)
  - cohort=canary
- Log example (redacted):
  - ts=2025-04-18T16:11:03Z request_id=req_01HV... tenant=northstar-prod route=/v1/chat/completions region=us-east rollout_id=rll_9f3c2d3a configured_canary_percent=25 hash_bucket=17 cohort=canary

Initial hypothesis
Smart Routing in us-east is using a stale rollout config (still at 25%) after a step change to 10% was applied in Console/control plane.

Immediate mitigation

- If confirmed stale config on a subset of router pods, restart/roll router deployment in us-east OR force a full config resync.
- Customer can also pause rollout to 0% canary as a safety measure (but report indicates Console changes are not reflecting, so may not be sufficient without router refresh).

Requested from customer

- Exact time they changed from 25% -> 10%
- Whether they use a consistent cohort key (e.g., user_id) vs relying on request_id (for sanity; not expected to cause systematic 2.5x increase, but helpful)

Internal notes
This resembles the beta incident in #incidents where a watch stream drop caused rollout config updates not to propagate to a subset of router pods in us-east. See related incident and upcoming router watchdog/resync change.

Next actions

- (Eng) Verify config watch health + last-applied rollout version on us-east router pods.
- (SRE) Check for watch lag / dropped stream in us-east around 15:40–16:00 UTC.
- (Support) Provide customer with mitigation steps and expected timeline.

sections.section_path: Sup 28451 Invoice Tokens Do Not Match Usage Api
sections.heading: Sup 28451 Invoice Tokens Do Not Match Usage Api
sections.content:
Sup 28451 Invoice Tokens Do Not Match Usage Api

Source type: jira
Document ID: dsid_d04dea2d736445c3af6934b900a12ef9
Release: v1.0.0
Benchmark: EnterpriseRAG-Bench synthetic upstream data
Invoice token counts do not match Usage API export (Acme AI) — suspected duplicate metering on streaming retry/fallback

Customer: Acme AI
Issue summary

- Acme AI reports February invoice tokens are higher than their Usage API export totals for the same billing period.
- They are summing Usage API daily exports by model and region and comparing to the invoice line items.

Impact

- Potential overcharge claim / invoice dispute.
- Risk: RevRec confidence + customer trust.

Billing period / artifacts

- Invoice: INV-2026-02-ACME (Feb 2026 usage)
- Customer comparison window: 2026-01-01 00:00:00 UTC through 2026-01-31 23:59:59 UTC (per invoice)
- Customer export method: /v1/usage?start_date=2026-01-01&end_date=2026-01-31 (aggregated by day)

Observed discrepancy (initial)

- Invoice total billed tokens: 9,842,110
- Usage API export total tokens: 9,521,774
- Delta: +320,336 tokens on invoice (+3.36%)
- Delta concentrated in streaming chat completions on rw-llama-70b-instruct (us-east) between 2026-01-18 and 2026-01-24.

Hypotheses
1) Duplicate billing ledger writes on server-side retry/fallback for streaming requests (same customer request counted twice).
2) Usage API export is de-duping by request_id while billing ledger is not (or uses different idempotency key).
3) Late-arriving events / backfills included in invoice but missing from Usage API due to export freshness window.
4) Token counting mismatch between OpenAI-compatible endpoints vs native endpoints (less likely for this specific window).

Investigation notes (what we checked)

- Compared billing_ledger_v1 aggregates vs usage_events_v1 aggregates for the same account_id, model, region, and day.
- Sampled 25 request_ids from the highest-delta day (2026-01-21) and traced request lifecycle in request logs.
- Looked for patterns: streaming disconnects, 5xx on first attempt, fallback routing to a compatible variant, and subsequent successful retry.

Findings

- Confirmed duplicate ledger rows for a subset of streaming requests that experienced a server-side retry/fallback.
- Pattern:
  - First attempt returns partial stream then terminates (upstream timeout / capacity blip).
  - Gateway triggers internal retry to a compatible backend.
  - Billing hook emitted two chargeable usage records (same customer idempotency key missing/empty on first attempt) and both were ingested into billing_ledger_v1.
  - Usage API export (customer-facing) is sourced from usage_events_v1 where we dedupe on (account_id, request_id, event_sequence) and therefore only shows one.
- This explains invoice > usage export.

Evidence (redacted)

- Example request_id: req_01HNX9V8T1Q2A3B4C5D6E7F8
  - usage_events_v1: 1 record, total_tokens=3,412
  - billing_ledger_v1: 2 records, total_tokens=3,412 and total_tokens=3,412 (duplicate)
  - gateway log: "stream_retry=true" and "fallback_route=rw-llama-70b-instruct@v2026-01-15 -> rw-llama-70b-instruct@v2026-01-15" (same model, different backend instance)

Customer communication needs

- Provide a clear explanation: discrepancy is a metering bug on retry/fallback for streaming, not a difference in tokenization rules.
- Provide corrected totals for the disputed period and proposed remediation (credit vs re-issue) per Finance/Legal policy.

Proposed remediation

- Engineering: ship fix to ensure billing hook idempotency for streaming retry/fallback (prevent duplicate ledger entries) + add regression tests.
- Finance: issue credit for confirmed overbilled tokens for Jan usage (applied on next invoice), avoid retroactive re-issue unless required.

Next steps / owners

sections.content:
Investigation notes (internal)

Hypothesis: us-east protected-route capacity protection enabled for Proxima allowlisted accounts; per-route/per-tier admission control is active and may be gating bursts more aggressively than intended for this customer’s contractual traffic shape.

Checks performed:

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Purpose
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Purpose
sections.content:
Purpose

This document defines **per-route SLOs and error budget policy** for Redwood Inference’s **Hosted API** as it relates to **hot-route capacity protection** (tier-aware quotas, priority routing, and controlled shedding).

The intent is to:

- Explicitly define **enterprise vs best-effort** expectations for the highest-traffic routes.
- Make overload behavior **measurable and supportable** (clear SLIs + dashboards + alerts).
- Align alerting to overload protection so we page on **enterprise degradation**, not expected best-effort shedding.

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Error budgets > Budget stop-the-line triggers
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Error budgets > Budget stop-the-line triggers
sections.content:
Budget stop-the-line triggers

For enterprise protected routes, any of the following triggers a “stop the line” review in the weekly reliability sync (or async in #eng-sre if urgent):

- Availability error budget burn ≥ **50%** in 7 days
- p99 latency SLO violated for ≥ **2 hours** in a day (sustained)
- Overload shedding observed for enterprise traffic (non-zero sustained) outside planned game day / load test windows

sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Internal-only: where to look (for Support with access)

- Incident channels: #eng-oncall, #incidents (look for breaker announcements).

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Definitions > Route tiers
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Definitions > Route tiers
sections.content:
Definitions

Route tiers

We classify requests into one of the following tiers at the gateway/policy engine:

- **Enterprise (Protected):** SLA-bearing tenants and allowlisted enterprise accounts for protected routes. These requests receive priority admission and are protected during fleet pressure.
- **Best-effort:** all other traffic. Best-effort may be throttled earlier and more aggressively to preserve fleet health and enterprise budgets.

- Otherwise, advise them to implement client-side fallback only if they can validate output compatibility and safety.

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Definitions > Overload / throttling semantics
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Definitions > Overload / throttling semantics
sections.content:
Overload / throttling semantics

Requests may be rejected with HTTP **429** for:

- **Quota/rate limit enforcement** (tenant policy)
- **Overload shedding/admission control** (fleet protection)

We distinguish causes via standardized reason code headers/payloads (see Support doc for exact fields). For SLO accounting, we treat quota-throttled and overload-shed requests differently by tier (see SLI rules below).

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Error budgets > Error budget policy (what we do when we burn)
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Error budgets > Error budget policy (what we do when we burn)
sections.content:
Error budget policy (what we do when we burn)

**Enterprise (Protected) routes**

- If burn is elevated, the default stance is **protect SLOs over throughput**.
- Allowed mitigations (in priority order):
  1) Tighten best-effort admission control thresholds (shed earlier)
  2) Temporarily reduce best-effort burst allowances
  3) Increase enterprise reserved capacity / pool weights (if available)
  4) Enable guarded fallback policies where contractually allowed
  5) As last resort: temporary enterprise throttling with exec/on-call approval and proactive comms

**Best-effort routes**

- Best-effort can be shed under pressure; we do not page purely on best-effort 429 shedding.
- If best-effort availability drops due to 5xx (not 429 overload-shed), we investigate as a normal reliability regression.

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Error budgets > Error budget calculation
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Error budgets > Error budget calculation
sections.content:
Error budgets

Error budget calculation

For an SLO target **T** over a 28-day window:

- Error budget = **1 − T**

Examples:

- 99.95% availability ⇒ 0.05% error budget (≈ 21.6 minutes of downtime equivalent over 28 days)
- 99.5% availability ⇒ 0.5% error budget

We track budgets separately per:

- route
- region
- tier

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Operational guidance > How to interpret 429s for SLOs
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Operational guidance > How to interpret 429s for SLOs
sections.content:
Operational guidance

How to interpret 429s for SLOs

- **Enterprise 429 overload-shed:** treat as incident-worthy and investigate capacity signals, admission thresholds, route budgets, and pool weights.
- **Best-effort 429 overload-shed:** expected under pressure; use this to validate the protection is working (enterprise should remain stable).
- **Quota 429 (any tier):** not an SLO failure; route to Support/Solutions for policy adjustment if needed.

sections.section_path: Sup 864999 Sliced Ingest Priority Class Throttle Config
sections.heading: Sup 864999 Sliced Ingest Priority Class Throttle Config
sections.content:
Sup 864999 Sliced Ingest Priority Class Throttle Config

Source type: jira
Document ID: dsid_5f3a672da4974781a5577b0f3d4993e9
Release: v1.0.0
Benchmark: EnterpriseRAG-Bench synthetic upstream data
Sustained 429s during sliced ingest with priority class mismatch after dedicated pool migration

Issue summary:
Customer reports sustained 429 responses across a set of sliced ingest workers after migrating ingestion to a Dedicated pool. The traffic mix is: low-latency chat calls (priority=high) and large multi-part embedding uploads (priority=background). After the migration, background uploads are intermittently exhausting burst credits at the per-route layer and causing opaque 429s for high-priority short calls during peak windows.

Impact:

- ~30% of short chat requests returned 429 between 09:00-11:30 PDT on 2026-03-10 for Streamly AI.
- Customer reports user-facing errors and retry amplification in their orchestrator.
- Business impact: partial degradation of their real-time features during peak ingest windows.

Environment:

- Dedicated pool: dp-132-usw
- Region: us-west
- Ingest coordinator version: 2026.02.3
- Rate-limiter service version: 1.14.0-canary

Observed behaviour:

- Persistent 429s reported by customer for short-lived chat requests coincident with high concurrency uploads.
- Throttle headers (when present) show per-route-window exhaustion; some requests show no X-RateLimit headers (opaque 429).

Expected behaviour:

- High-priority interactive calls should be isolated into a small burst pool and not experience 429s while background uploads borrow burst credit from a separate pool (or be rate-limited gracefully).

Customer asks:

- Why are small chat calls getting 429s when their load is relatively small?
- How to configure priority classes and burst pools for dedicated pools to prevent this?

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Canonical mapping: status → meaning → what we tell customers
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Canonical mapping: status → meaning → what we tell customers
sections.content:
Canonical mapping: status → meaning → what we tell customers

Use this table to drive consistent customer guidance.

| HTTP | Typical meaning | What Support should say | Customer action |
|------|------------------|--------------------------|-----------------|
| 429 | Admission control / rate limiting / tier cap hit | “Your request was rejected to protect system stability. This is not a model failure; it indicates you are sending requests faster than the current allowed rate/concurrency.” | Respect Retry-After; implement exponential backoff + jitter; reduce concurrency; consider batching; if persistent, discuss tier/capacity options. |
| 503 | Regional/model breaker open or load shedding | “Redwood is temporarily overloaded in the requested region/model. We are rejecting early to avoid timeouts and protect overall reliability.” | Respect Retry-After; backoff + jitter; optionally route to another region/model if configured; reduce max_tokens/streaming concurrency; retry with bounded attempts. |

Notes:

- If the customer reports **timeouts** with no JSON error, treat as a separate issue (possible client/network or upstream timeouts) and escalate based on impact.
- If the customer gets **5xx** without the overload payload, collect details; it may be an unrelated incident.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Common failure modes and quick routing hints
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Common failure modes and quick routing hints
sections.content:
Common failure modes and quick routing hints

- **Customer sees lower throughput than Redwood reports:** often a measurement mismatch (streaming token accounting, end-to-end latency vs throughput, counting input tokens). Engage Observability if persistent.
- **Throughput drops with GPU pegged:** suspect contention, node health, thermal throttling, network bottleneck; page Infra.
- **Throughput drops with low utilization:** suspect admission control limiting, customer throttling, or workload shift to longer contexts; page SRE; ask customer for concurrency/workload details.
- **Regional capacity constraint / failover behavior:** check tier failover posture; page Infra and SRE; do not promise cross-region without tier/contract confirmation.

---

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Error payload: what customers see
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Error payload: what customers see
sections.content:
Error payload: what customers see

Overload errors are additive and JSON-compatible with existing response parsing.

Typical shape (example):

- `error.type`: `overload_error` (or `rate_limit_error` in some cases)
- `error.code`: stable machine code
- `error.message`: human-readable
- `error.request_id`: mirrors `x-redwood-request-id` where available
- `error.correlation_id`: mirrors `x-redwood-correlation-id` where available

Example snippet (illustrative only):
{
  "error": {
    "type": "overload_error",
    "code": "BREAKER_OPEN",
    "message": "The service is temporarily overloaded. Please retry after the specified delay.",
    "request_id": "req_01J9...",
    "correlation_id": "corr_01J9..."
  }
}

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Quick triage checklist (Support)
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Quick triage checklist (Support)
sections.content:
Quick triage checklist (Support)

1) Confirm this is an overload-protection response (see “How to recognize” below).
2) Verify the customer is following recommended retry/backoff (or advise them to change).
3) Collect required debug info (IDs, time window, region/model, response headers).
4) Determine if this is expected transient overload vs a bug/misconfig (missing Retry-After, incorrect status mapping, fallback not triggering).
5) Escalate to Eng Oncall when criteria are met (see “When to escalate”).

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Known issues (Support-facing)
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Known issues (Support-facing)
sections.content:
Known issues (Support-facing)

1) **Retry-After header missing on some overload responses**

- Symptom: Customer receives 429/503 overload payload but no Retry-After.
- Workaround: Recommend exponential backoff with jitter as above.
- Action: Escalate if reproducible; include route + correlation IDs.

2) **Fallback model not triggering as expected**

- Symptom: Customer has configured fallback but still sees repeated 503 without failover.
- Workaround: Customer can temporarily specify an alternate model/region explicitly (if acceptable) while we investigate.
- Action: Escalate; include tenant ID, configured fallback policy (what they intended), and correlation IDs.

3) **Customer interprets 503 as “platform outage”**

- Guidance: Use the approved response language; direct them to Retry-After and backoff guidance.

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Purpose
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Purpose
sections.content:
Purpose

This page helps Support/CS respond to customer reports of new “overload protection” errors (circuit breakers + load shedding) on Redwood Hosted API.

Goals:

- Explain what the customer is seeing (stable semantics vs ambiguous timeouts/5xx).
- Provide canonical retry/backoff guidance to prevent retry storms.
- Show how to interpret correlation IDs so Engineering can quickly trace requests.
- Define escalation criteria and the minimum information to collect.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > What is the Dedicated Throughput SLO (customer-facing summary)
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > What is the Dedicated Throughput SLO (customer-facing summary)
sections.content:
What is the Dedicated Throughput SLO (customer-facing summary)

Dedicated Throughput SLO guarantees a **minimum sustained throughput floor** for an eligible Dedicated deployment under defined conditions.

**High-level definition (internal summary):**

- Metric: throughput measured as **billable output tokens per second**, computed per deployment, aggregated over a rolling window.
- Scope: Dedicated deployments only (not Hosted API, not eval/sandbox deployments).
- Eligibility: model/version and configuration must be within the customer’s contracted Dedicated configuration (e.g., pinned model family/version, supported max context, supported shape).

**Common non-eligibility / exclusions (not exhaustive):**

- Customer-side throttling or client concurrency limits causing underutilization.
- Customer workload violating sizing assumptions (e.g., contexts above configured limit, unsupported parameter combinations).
- Warm-up periods after scale-from-zero or cold start (tier-dependent; see “Warm pool / startup” below).
- Incidents due to customer networking/VPC misconfig in Private connectivity paths (if applicable).

When in doubt, treat as potentially eligible, start the triage, and engage SRE.

---

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > How to recognize overload-protection responses > Common HTTP statuses
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > How to recognize overload-protection responses > Common HTTP statuses
sections.content:
How to recognize overload-protection responses

Common HTTP statuses

- **429 Too Many Requests**
  - Used for admission controls such as per-tenant concurrency caps, token buckets, or tier limits.
  - Usually safe to retry with backoff if Retry-After is provided.

- **503 Service Unavailable**
  - Used when the platform is overloaded at the regional/model level (breaker open) or actively shedding load to protect SLOs.
  - Usually safe to retry with backoff and/or reduce load. May persist until capacity recovers.

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Revision history
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Revision history
sections.content:
Revision history

- 2025-11-10: Initial publication for overload error rollout (Support readiness).
- 2025-12-05: Updated retry guidance; clarified correlation IDs and escalation thresholds.

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > When to escalate to Engineering (Eng Oncall / SRE)
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > When to escalate to Engineering (Eng Oncall / SRE)
sections.content:
When to escalate to Engineering (Eng Oncall / SRE)

Escalate immediately if any of the following are true:

- **Enterprise customer** reporting sustained overload errors impacting production.
- Overload errors persist for **>15 minutes** with correct backoff behavior.
- **No Retry-After** observed on multiple responses for the same route/region/model.
- Suspected **misclassification** (e.g., 500s that should be 429/503 overload, or overload codes returned with 200/stream interruptions).
- **Fallback routing configured** but not activating.
- Customer reports sharp regression (new errors) coincident with a canary/rollout and provides IDs.

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > How to recognize overload-protection responses > Expected headers (may vary by route)
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > How to recognize overload-protection responses > Expected headers (may vary by route)
sections.content:
Expected headers (may vary by route)

- **Retry-After**: integer seconds is preferred (e.g., `Retry-After: 2`).
- **x-redwood-request-id**: unique ID for a single request attempt.
- **x-redwood-correlation-id**: groups related attempts across services (gateway → routing → runtime). Some clients/logs only show one of these; either is helpful.

If the response is 429/503 *and* includes a Redwood overload error code in the JSON body, treat it as overload protection.

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Retry & backoff guidance (what we should recommend) > Recommended algorithm (support-approved)
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Retry & backoff guidance (what we should recommend) > Recommended algorithm (support-approved)
sections.content:
Recommended algorithm (support-approved)

If `Retry-After` is present:

- Sleep `Retry-After` seconds, then retry.

If `Retry-After` is missing:

- Backoff schedule suggestion: 0.5s, 1s, 2s, 4s, then stop (max 4 retries), each with ±20–40% jitter.

Bounds:

- Maximum total retry time budget: **~10–20 seconds** for interactive apps, **~60 seconds** for batch jobs.
- Maximum concurrent retries: keep to a small fraction of steady-state concurrency (e.g., 10–20%).

G. Measurement system and authoritative records

**Approved clause (standard):**
“Fees are based on Redwood’s measurement systems and usage records. Redwood will provide usage reporting via invoice detail, Console, or usage export/API. In the event of conflict, the invoice and supporting usage report for the billing period will control, subject to Customer’s dispute rights.”

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Alerting (paging + ticketing) > Enterprise availability burn alerts (recommended)
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Alerting (paging + ticketing) > Enterprise availability burn alerts (recommended)
sections.content:
Enterprise availability burn alerts (recommended)

For each protected route x region:

- **Page (Sev2):** 28d SLO burn rate with multi-window thresholds
  - Fast burn: 5m and 1h windows > **14x** budget burn
  - Slow burn: 30m and 6h windows > **6x** budget burn
- **Ticket:** 2h and 1d windows > **2x** burn

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Severity levels (Support/CS view)
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Severity levels (Support/CS view)
sections.content:
Severity levels (Support/CS view)

Use these severities to standardize response; SRE may map to their incident severities.

**SEV-1 (Critical, likely customer-impacting breach)**

- Premium tier customer reports sustained throughput below floor OR SRE burn-rate alert is firing.
- Clear production impact (e.g., queue buildup, timeouts, user-visible latency spikes).
- Immediate paging required.

**SEV-2 (High, likely degradation / at-risk of breach)**

- Throughput is below expected but not yet confirmed as an SLO breach.
- Customer impact is moderate OR limited to a subset of traffic/routes.
- Paging may be required depending on tier and duration.

**SEV-3 (Moderate, investigation / metrics discrepancy)**

- Conflicting metrics (customer vs Redwood dashboards), short-lived dips, or suspected measurement artifacts.
- No clear production impact.

sections.section_path: Sliced Ingest 429S Dedicated Pool Priority Class Debug Notes
sections.heading: Sliced Ingest 429S Dedicated Pool Priority Class Debug Notes
sections.content:
- A burst-pool weight recalculation occurs on route attach to a dedicated pool.
- Under high fanout (multipart chunk completion callbacks + interactive requests), an attach sequence can read stale bucket state and allow background borrow to temporarily draw from the interactive pool’s credits.
- Separately, when the edge proxy is under callback-related backpressure, it can return 429 before the normal header-enrichment path runs, producing opaque 429s.

Mitigations applied / tested (new since ticket)
Temporary customer-facing workaround (still valid)

- Stagger background multipart uploads and add jitter to the flush window.
- Reduce background upload concurrency (Streamly tested <= 6 workers) during peak interactive usage.

Config change (applied on 2026-03-12 call)

- On dp-132-usw we reserved burst capacity explicitly for interactive routes.
- Updated reservation target: reserve 30% (previous internal suggestion was 20%) of interactive burst credits exclusively for priority=high routes.
- Also separated the route groups so callbacks cannot share the same per-route window as interactive endpoints.

Patch status (updated)

- Rate-limiter fix was originally tracked as “target 1.14.1”.
- As of 2026-03-19: fix is in 1.14.1-rc2 and deployed to canary in us-west dedicated pools (including dp-132-usw) for validation.
- Early results: eliminates the negative token deltas we were seeing during attach bursts; interactive 429 rate decreased materially during the flush window.

Results from customer validation (new)

- 2026-03-12 (trial during scheduled flush):
  - Interactive error rate improved; remaining 429s clustered around callback spikes.
  - Customer confirmed jitter reduced the “all-at-once” failure mode.
- 2026-03-20 (post 1.14.1-rc2 canary + reserved burst config still in place):
  - No sustained 429s for /v1/chat during the 09:00–10:00 window.
  - A few 429s remain on background /v1/embed chunk callbacks (expected; acceptable if retried with backoff).

Open questions / TODO

- Edge proxy: ensure X-RateLimit headers are emitted even under backpressure for 429s originating from rate-limiter.
- Confirm whether signed URL callback endpoints should be assigned their own priority class (e.g., “callback-low”) distinct from generic background.
- Add a regression test: attach burst + high fanout + two priority classes should never allow cross-pool borrow that depletes interactive tokens.

Recommended next steps (updated plan)
1) Keep the reserved interactive burst split (30%) for dedicated pools with mixed interactive + bulk ingest traffic.
2) Promote rate-limiter 1.14.1 from rc to stable after 48h canary observation (watch: rlim.route.tokens.available deltas, interactive 429 rate, attach timing).
3) Edge proxy change: always populate rate-limit headers (or at least a stable error code) for 429s; avoid “opaque 429”.
4) Update the support playbook page with explicit guidance for signed URL callback fanout (jitter + concurrency caps + route separation).
5) Schedule a controlled load test with Streamly AI for 3 consecutive peak windows and collect traces + request IDs for closure criteria.

Notes / timeline crumbs (for internal use)

- 2026-03-10: incident window; strong correlation with cron flush.
- 2026-03-11: Eng suspected weight inversion / attach sequence sensitivity.
- 2026-03-12: customer call; implemented burst reservation + client-side jitter.
- 2026-03-19: 1.14.1-rc2 canary deployed to us-west dedicated.
- 2026-03-20: customer reports no sustained interactive 429s during flush.

Closure criteria (for SUP-864999)

sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > How to interpret and use correlation IDs > Where customers can find them

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Retry & backoff guidance (what we should recommend) > Golden rules
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Retry & backoff guidance (what we should recommend) > Golden rules
sections.content:
Retry & backoff guidance (what we should recommend)

Golden rules

- **Always respect Retry-After** when provided.
- **Use exponential backoff with jitter**; do not retry immediately.
- **Cap retries** to avoid amplifying overload.
- **Reduce concurrency** rather than increasing it during overload.
- Prefer **idempotency keys** for safe retries on non-streaming requests.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Definition > Canonical SLI and SLO > Canonical throughput metric (SLI)
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Definition > Canonical SLI and SLO > Canonical throughput metric (SLI)
sections.content:
Canonical SLI and SLO

Canonical throughput metric (SLI)

**SLI name:** Dedicated Throughput Floor Attainment
**SLI definition (per deployment):**
For each `deployment_id`, compute the fraction of eligible 5-minute windows in which the **observed output token rate** meets or exceeds the committed floor.

A 5-minute window is considered **good** if:

- `observed_tps(deployment_id, window) >= committed_tps(deployment_id) * 1.00`

A window is **bad** if:

- `observed_tps(deployment_id, window) < committed_tps(deployment_id) * 1.00`

**Why tokens/sec:** Token throughput is the most stable cross-model, cross-request indicator for generation routes and aligns with customer-perceived capacity for streaming/chat.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Definition > Burn-rate alerting > Paging vs ticketing
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Definition > Burn-rate alerting > Paging vs ticketing
sections.content:
Paging vs ticketing

**Paging alerts (customer-impacting / requires oncall response):**

- **Fast burn:** burn rate >= **14x** over **1h** AND burn rate >= **6x** over **6h**
  - Interpretation: likely to exhaust error budget within ~2.1 days if sustained.

**Ticket alerts (investigate during business hours):**

- **Slow burn:** burn rate >= **3x** over **24h**
  - Interpretation: will exhaust error budget within ~10 days if sustained.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Paging and escalation triggers (when to page SRE / Infra) > Page SRE On-Call immediately when any of the following is true
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Paging and escalation triggers (when to page SRE / Infra) > Page SRE On-Call immediately when any of the following is true
sections.content:
Paging and escalation triggers (when to page SRE / Infra)

Page SRE On-Call immediately when any of the following is true

- Premium tier customer: reported throughput below committed floor for **>10 minutes**, AND they confirm they are not client-throttled.
- Any tier: a Dedicated Throughput SLO **burn-rate alert** is firing for the deployment.
- Any tier: repeated or escalating customer timeouts/5xx correlated with throughput drop.
- Any tier: throughput drop correlates with recent Redwood changes (rollout, routing, driver/runtime update).

Which IDs to ask for

2) `x-redwood-request-id` (single request attempt)
3) Timestamp + region + model + route if IDs are not available

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Summary
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Summary
sections.content:
Summary

This ADR defines how the production performance canary computes baselines and evaluates regressions for per-model serving performance (primarily p95 latency and tokens/sec). It documents:

- Baseline computation approach (rolling vs fixed) and when each is used.
- Regression thresholds (warning vs paging) and how they are applied.
- Minimum sample sizes and confidence requirements to avoid noisy alerts.
- Anti-flap / dedupe logic to prevent alert storms during drift, telemetry delays, or small-sample variance.

Clause library (approved language)

Use the below clauses as starting points. Do not materially alter without Legal review.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Context / Problem
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Context / Problem
sections.content:
Context / Problem

Redwood’s serving runtime changes frequently (kernel selection updates, scheduler heuristics, model config changes, GPU fleet changes, and staged rollouts). We need an always-on canary that:

- Detects real p95 latency regressions and throughput drops early.
- Produces actionable signals for attribution (kernel vs scheduler vs infra).
- Avoids paging on expected variance and baseline drift (e.g., slow fleet mix changes or regional differences).

The key design tension is baseline choice:

- A **fixed baseline** is stable and easy to reason about during rollouts, but can become stale as hardware/driver stacks and workloads evolve.
- A **rolling baseline** adapts over time, but can drift (masking regressions) or create false positives if drift is misinterpreted as regression.

- “Spin up many parallel retries to get through.”

sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Warm pool / startup considerations

Warm pool / startup considerations

Some tiers include warm pool guarantees (or faster recovery expectations). During triage, identify if the customer is within a warm-up window:

- Did the deployment recently scale from zero?
- Was there a recent model reload, config change, or node replacement?
- Did traffic resume after prolonged inactivity?

If warm-up is suspected, note it explicitly in the customer thread and ask SRE to confirm whether the event is excluded by policy.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Definition > Measurement semantics > Streaming token accounting
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Definition > Measurement semantics > Streaming token accounting
sections.content:
Streaming token accounting

For streaming responses:

- Output tokens are counted when emitted by the runtime, attributed to the originating request.
- We de-duplicate token counters to avoid double counting caused by stream chunk retries.

Operational note: streaming accounting semantics were corrected in **PR-19422** (“Fix throughput metric double counting streaming”). Any backfills or comparisons across that boundary must annotate the change.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Purpose
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Purpose
sections.content:
Purpose

This playbook defines the end-to-end process for handling Dedicated **Throughput SLO** misses or suspected misses. It is designed for Customer Success (CS) and Support to:

- Triage quickly and consistently.
- Engage the correct on-call teams (SRE / Infra / Observability) at the right time.
- Communicate clearly with customers, including status updates and written summaries.
- Route service-credit / compensation requests through the correct approval path.

This page is **restricted** because it includes internal paging triggers and credit approval guidance.

---

sections.heading: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Drafting guidance (what to include in usage-based terms) > Required building blocks
sections.content:
Drafting guidance (what to include in usage-based terms)

Required building blocks

For any Order Form/SOW with usage-based fees, include:
1) Usage unit definition (tokens, embeddings units, requests, GPU-seconds if applicable)
2) Billing measurement and reporting source (invoice + usage report)
3) Caching and retries treatment (at least at a high level)
4) Dispute window + audit mechanics (reasonable; avoids open-ended re-billing risk)
5) Credits/refunds policy (when available; how applied)
6) Change management notice (especially if customer requests strict metering invariants)

3) “Caching must always reduce price.”

**Position:** Caching may reduce billed tokens depending on eligibility and product policy.
**Response:** Use caching clause; avoid hard commitments. If needed for the deal, define a limited-term promotional adjustment with Finance sign-off.

**Exhibit X — Usage Definitions (Example)**

- “Billed Tokens” means the token quantity reported by Redwood for billing, which may account for caching adjustments and promotional inclusions, as reflected in Redwood’s usage report.
- “Idempotency Key” means a unique identifier provided by Customer to allow safe retries without duplicate logical charges.
- “Cache Hit” means a request (or portion thereof) served from Redwood-managed cache, which may be reported as cached usage and may be billed differently as reflected in the usage report.

sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Roles and ownership during an SLO event
sections.content:
Roles and ownership during an SLO event

**Support/CS (Incident Driver for customer comms)**

- Owns the customer thread, updates, and expectation management.
- Owns the case record: timeline, impact, and customer confirmations.
- Initiates escalation and ensures correct teams are engaged.

**SRE On-Call (Technical Incident Lead)**

- Confirms whether the SLO is breached per the canonical evaluator.
- Drives mitigation and coordinates cross-functional response.
- Provides internal/external technical summary for comms.

**Infra/Fleet On-Call (Capacity / shape / provisioning owner)**

- Addresses capacity constraints, noisy-neighbor isolation issues, node failures, and shape-level performance anomalies.

**Observability (as-needed)**

- Validates metric correctness (e.g., streaming accounting anomalies), dashboard discrepancies, missing tags.

**Product Dedicated (as-needed)**

- Confirms entitlement interpretation (tier rules, burst policy, failover posture).
- Aligns on customer-facing messaging for edge cases.

**Finance/FP&A + Legal (as-needed for credits/comp)**

- Approves service credits above policy thresholds and any non-standard compensation.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Decision
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Decision
sections.content:
Decision

We adopt a **hybrid baseline strategy**:

1) **Primary baseline = Fixed, versioned baseline per (model, model_version, runtime_build, kernel_set_id, hardware_sku) with optional region override**

- Baselines are generated from controlled canary runs (prod-like load) and stored as immutable artifacts.
- Baselines are explicitly tied to the runtime build and kernel selection identifiers so comparisons remain meaningful.
- This is the baseline used for rollout gating and for paging.

2) **Secondary baseline = Rolling “health baseline” used for drift monitoring and threshold calibration (not for paging)**

- We compute a rolling reference from recent stable periods (default: last 7 days) to detect slow environmental drift and to inform recalibration.
- Rolling baseline is not used to auto-suppress a fixed-baseline regression; it is used as a triage and tuning signal.

3) **Baseline freeze rules**

- During a runtime rollout (canary/gradual), the baseline used for alerts is **frozen** to the most recent fixed baseline for the currently active runtime build on that ring.
- If an incident is declared for a perf regression, baseline updates are **paused** for affected keys until incident closure.

4) **Threshold evaluation requires minimum sample size + sustained breach + hysteresis**

- Alerts require both a minimum number of canary requests and sustained breach across multiple evaluation windows.
- Alert clear conditions are stricter than trigger conditions (hysteresis) to reduce flapping.

sections.heading: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Internal operational guardrails (contracting) > Backfills and corrections
sections.content:
Backfills and corrections

If Redwood discovers a metering bug:

- Default approach is **forward-looking fixes** with audit trail.
- Retroactive invoice changes require Finance + Legal approval.

sections.section_path: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Definitions (approved internal meanings) > 1) “Token”
sections.heading: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Definitions (approved internal meanings) > 1) “Token”
sections.content:
1) “Token”

**Token** means a discrete unit of text as processed by the applicable model’s tokenization scheme. Tokenization is model-dependent.

Important internal positions:

- Token counts are **model-specific** and may differ between models and versions.
- For chat-style endpoints, token counts may include system/developer messages, tool call payloads, and structured output formatting as applicable.
- We support (and prefer to contract around) **billed tokens** as the invoicing unit, rather than raw “input + output tokens,” because billed tokens reflects caching/discounting rules.

Recommended terminology:

- **Input Tokens / Prompt Tokens**: tokens attributable to the request context provided by the customer.
- **Output Tokens / Completion Tokens**: tokens generated by the model in response.
- **Billed Tokens**: the token quantity used for billing after applying billing rules (e.g., caching adjustments, promotional discounts, free-tier inclusion), as shown on the invoice and/or usage reports.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Implementation Notes / Requirements
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Implementation Notes / Requirements
sections.content:
Implementation Notes / Requirements

1. Baseline artifacts must be stored in an access-controlled, versioned store with auditability (who/when created).
2. Canary config must support per-model overrides:
   - thresholds by severity
   - whether region-specific keys are enabled
   - “top model” flag affecting paging eligibility
3. Alert payloads must include:
   - observed value, baseline value, percent change
   - sample counts and token counts
   - runtime_build_id, kernel_set_id, hardware_sku, region
   - links to dashboards, traces, and runbook
4. Changes to default thresholds must go through an ADR update or SRE-approved change request.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Decision Drivers
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Decision Drivers
sections.content:
Decision Drivers

1. **Low noise / high trust**: warnings should be useful; pages should be rare and high-confidence.
2. **Fast detection**: detect regressions within ~10–30 minutes for top models in covered regions.
3. **Attribution**: baseline keys must align to dimensions needed for root cause (runtime build, kernel tags, SKU).
4. **Operational simplicity**: SRE/on-call should have a predictable interpretation of “regression vs baseline,” including during ongoing rollouts.
5. **Guardrails against drift and telemetry issues**: avoid alert storms caused by baseline drift, delayed metric ingestion, and label cardinality errors.

sections.section_path: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Purpose
sections.heading: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Purpose
sections.content:
Purpose

This playbook provides Redwood Inference’s approved legal guidance and clause library for **usage-based pricing** across Redwood API (Hosted) and related packaging. It is designed to:

- Ensure **consistent definitions** (tokens, requests, cache hits, retries) across MSAs, Order Forms, pricing pages, and Sales communications.
- Reduce **invoice disputes** by aligning contract language with metering behavior.
- Support **revenue recognition (RevRec)** and audit readiness by defining authoritative sources, dispute windows, and credit/refund mechanics.

This page is **restricted** because it contains clause language and internal positions.

sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Paging and escalation triggers (when to page SRE / Infra) > Engage Observability (not a page; async unless SEV-1)
sections.content:
Engage Observability (not a page; async unless SEV-1)

- Throughput dashboards disagree with billing/export numbers.
- Recent metric changes (e.g., streaming token accounting) suspected.
- Missing labels (deployment_id, model, region) prevents accurate attribution.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Baseline Keys (What defines “like-for-like”)
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Baseline Keys (What defines “like-for-like”)
sections.content:
Baseline Keys (What defines “like-for-like”)

Baseline artifacts and regression evaluation are keyed by the following dimensions:

**Required baseline key fields (v1):**

- model_id (canonical model identifier)
- model_version (registry version / hash)
- runtime_build_id (serving runtime build tag)
- kernel_set_id (kernel selection/version identifier)
- hardware_sku (e.g., H100-80GB, A100-80GB)

**Optional fields (only when variance requires it):**

- region (enabled for regions with materially different fleet/network characteristics)
- capacity_tier (hosted vs dedicated pools) when pools differ materially

Notes:

- We do NOT key baselines by customer, endpoint, or prompt content (privacy + cardinality constraints).
- Scheduler configuration flags that materially change behavior must be reflected either in runtime_build_id or an explicit scheduler_profile tag (introduced only if needed; kept off by default to control cardinality).

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Baseline Computation > Rolling health baseline (calibration only)
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Baseline Computation > Rolling health baseline (calibration only)
sections.content:
Rolling health baseline (calibration only)

- Window: trailing 7 days, excluding periods marked as “rollout” or “incident.”
- Aggregation: daily aggregates with robust statistics (median-of-daily-p95) to reduce sensitivity to short spikes.
- Purpose:
  - detect slow drift (e.g., fleet changes) that may warrant generating a new fixed baseline
  - suggest region/SKU overrides when variance is consistently higher

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Alternatives Considered > A) Pure rolling baseline (always updated)
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Alternatives Considered > A) Pure rolling baseline (always updated)
sections.content:
Alternatives Considered

A) Pure rolling baseline (always updated)

Pros:

- Adapts to drift without explicit re-baselining.

Cons:

- Risk of masking slow regressions (baseline chases the regression).
- Hard to use for rollout gating (“moving goalposts”).
- Susceptible to alert storms if rolling logic is impacted by label bugs or ingestion gaps.

Decision: Rejected for paging/gating. Allowed only as a secondary calibration signal.

sections.section_path: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Definitions (approved internal meanings) > 5) “Retry”
sections.heading: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Definitions (approved internal meanings) > 5) “Retry”
sections.content:
5) “Retry”

Retry can occur on:

- **Client side** (customer’s SDK/app retries)
- **Server side** (Redwood retries/fallback routing to preserve availability)

Internal positions:

- We aim to bill **once per logical request** where retries are transparently handled under the same idempotency key.
- If the customer does not use idempotency keys and submits duplicate requests, those may be billable.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Customer communications guide > Communication principles
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Customer communications guide > Communication principles
sections.content:
Customer communications guide

Communication principles

- Use a single owner for customer updates (CS/Support), even if multiple engineering teams are engaged.
- Acknowledge impact quickly; avoid speculating on root cause.
- Provide time-bound next update (“next update in 30 minutes”).
- For Premium accounts, default to more frequent updates and written summaries.

sections.section_path: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Deal desk checklist (for usage-based terms)
sections.heading: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Deal desk checklist (for usage-based terms)
sections.content:
Deal desk checklist (for usage-based terms)

Before sending paper:
1) Confirm the usage unit(s) match the product packaging (tokens vs requests vs embeddings)
2) Confirm “billed tokens” language is used where available
3) Ensure retries/idempotency clause is included if customer is retrying or using streaming
4) Confirm dispute window is 30 days (or approved exception)
5) Confirm credits policy matches Finance policy and RevRec requirements
6) Link to usage reporting source and avoid promises of exact parity with other providers

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Appendix A: Example Per-Model Overrides (illustrative)
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Appendix A: Example Per-Model Overrides (illustrative)
sections.content:
Appendix A: Example Per-Model Overrides (illustrative)

- Top model (customer-critical): paging at +15% p95 E2E, -12% tokens/sec, stricter min token count.
- High-variance model: warning only, wider thresholds (+15% / -10%), region-specific baseline enabled.
- New kernel rollout candidate: temporary tighter warning (+8%) during rollout ring, but paging remains at default until validated.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Regression Definition > Core comparison method (v1)
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Regression Definition > Core comparison method (v1)
sections.content:
Core comparison method (v1)

For each metric M and key K in each evaluation window W:

- Compute observed metric value O(K, W).
- Fetch baseline value B(K) and baseline variability estimates when available.
- Compute percent change: Δ = (O - B) / B.

We use percent change thresholds with guardrails (min samples + sustained breach). Percent thresholds are chosen because:

- Different models have different absolute latencies.
- p95 is the primary SLO-relevant tail metric.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Open Questions (tracked outside ADR)
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Open Questions (tracked outside ADR)
sections.content:
Open Questions (tracked outside ADR)

- Whether to introduce a scheduler_profile tag in baseline keys (cardinality vs attribution benefit).
- Whether to page on runtime-only p95 for certain enterprise-dedicated pools (when E2E has additional network variance).
- Whether to incorporate a lightweight statistical test (e.g., bootstrap CI on p95) for models with unusually high variance.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Minimum Sample Sizes and Windowing > Minimum samples (per key K, per window)
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Minimum Sample Sizes and Windowing > Minimum samples (per key K, per window)
sections.content:
Minimum samples (per key K, per window)

- **Latency metrics**: minimum **200 successful canary requests** per window.
- **Tokens/sec**: minimum **200 successful canary requests** per window AND minimum **50,000 total generated tokens** per window.

If sample requirements are not met:

- No alert state change is allowed (prevents flapping in low-coverage periods).
- Dashboard panels display “insufficient sample” annotation.

Rationale:

- Tail latency (p95/p99) is unreliable with very small N.
- Tokens/sec needs sufficient token volume to smooth per-request variance.

Caching may reduce compute performed by Redwood. Contract language must avoid obligating Redwood to charge based on compute cost; instead, define how caching affects billed tokens.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Definition > Exclusions (non-counted windows/requests) > Request-level exclusions
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Definition > Exclusions (non-counted windows/requests) > Request-level exclusions
sections.content:
Request-level exclusions

The following requests are excluded from both numerator and denominator:

- **Customer-side throttling or pacing** that prevents the deployment from being demand-saturated while measuring throughput (e.g., the customer sends traffic well below the committed floor and attempts to interpret low throughput as non-compliance).
- **Client disconnects / cancellations** before generation completes (where Redwood terminates work early).
- **Invalid requests** or requests that violate documented limits (e.g., context > supported max for the purchased shape, unsupported model version).
- **Customer-enforced caps** that materially reduce achievable throughput, including:
  - Very low `max_tokens` combined with high request overhead patterns (evaluated case-by-case; see “edge-case review” below)
  - Customer-set concurrency limits below recommended saturation settings

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Consequences > Negative / Tradeoffs
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Consequences > Negative / Tradeoffs
sections.content:
Negative / Tradeoffs

- Requires baseline artifact generation whenever major runtime/kernel changes land for covered models/SKUs.
- Some true regressions may be detected slightly later due to sustained-breach requirements.
- Optional region/tier overrides add complexity when enabled.

sections.section_path: Sup 28463 Double Charged For Retries
sections.heading: Sup 28463 Double Charged For Retries
sections.content:
Sup 28463 Double Charged For Retries

Source type: jira
Document ID: dsid_2f1f0358b85148f19d38f619891bfb15
Release: v1.0.0
Benchmark: EnterpriseRAG-Bench synthetic upstream data
Acme AI reports being double-charged tokens on retry/fallback path (streaming) in Hosted API

Issue summary:
Acme AI reports that token usage on invoice preview is higher than their own aggregation of the Usage API for the same time window. They believe they are being billed twice when (a) their client retries after timeouts/5xx and/or (b) Redwood performs a server-side fallback retry during streaming.

Impact:

- Customer-reported overcharge risk and trust hit; potential credit request.
- Meter integrity risk: duplicate usage events on retry/fallback path may skew billing, pricing experiments, and gross margin model.

Customer evidence (from Support):

- Spike in billed tokens on 2026-02-06 around 19:00–21:00 UTC.
- Correlates to elevated 502/timeout errors and client retry behavior.
- Requests primarily via OpenAI-compatible /v1/chat/completions with stream=true.

Environment:

- Prod, region us-east
- Models: llama-3.1-70b primary, fallback variant enabled by routing policy

Suspected failure mode:
Usage event dedupe/idempotency for streaming retry/fallback path is insufficient. When an initial attempt emits partial tokens and then triggers an internal retry/fallback (or when the gateway retries before completion), both attempts may be marked billable and included in the billing aggregation, resulting in double-counting for a single logical client request.

Initial triage links:

- Slack: sources/slack/support/1770083321-customer-reporting-double-charged-retries.json
- Related Eng work: pr-27463 (retry double-count fix), perf-canary metering scenarios (pr-912)

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Rollout Guidance
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Rollout Guidance
sections.content:
Rollout Guidance

- Phase 1 (single region): warnings only, tune per-model overrides until noise is acceptable.
- Phase 2: enable paging only for top models with proven low variance and stable baselines.
- Phase 3: integrate gating with release engineering once paging signal is trusted (warning can gate early as “soft fail,” paging as “hard fail”).

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Definition > Measurement semantics > Observed throughput calculation (tokens/sec)
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Definition > Measurement semantics > Observed throughput calculation (tokens/sec)
sections.content:
Observed throughput calculation (tokens/sec)

For each deployment and 5-minute window:

- `observed_tps = eligible_output_tokens / eligible_generation_wall_time_seconds`

Where:

- **eligible_output_tokens** counts output tokens generated for eligible requests whose generation occurs within the window.
- **eligible_generation_wall_time_seconds** is the sum of per-request generation durations for eligible requests, measured at Redwood’s gateway/runtime boundary.

Notes:

- We use **wall time spent generating** rather than total window duration to avoid penalizing low-utilization periods.
- This SLO measures our ability to serve when the customer is asking for capacity, not whether the customer sends enough traffic to saturate the deployment.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Alternatives Considered > C) Per-region baselines always on
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Alternatives Considered > C) Per-region baselines always on
sections.content:
C) Per-region baselines always on

Pros:

- Reduces false positives due to cross-region fleet differences.

Cons:

- Baseline explosion (more artifacts and config), operational overhead.

Decision: Region is optional and only enabled for models/regions where observed variance requires it.

sections.section_path: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Clause library (approved language) > H. Dispute window (recommended default)
sections.heading: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Clause library (approved language) > H. Dispute window (recommended default)
sections.content:
H. Dispute window (recommended default)

**Approved clause (standard):**
“Customer must notify Redwood in writing of any good-faith dispute regarding an invoice within thirty (30) days of the invoice date, describing the basis for the dispute in reasonable detail. If Customer does not dispute an invoice within this period, the invoice will be deemed accepted.”

**Fallback positions:**

- 45 days: acceptable for larger enterprise if requested.
- 60+ days: requires CFO (Laura Bennett) approval due to RevRec and cash collection risk.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Default Thresholds (v1) > Runtime-only attribution signals (non-paging by default)
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Default Thresholds (v1) > Runtime-only attribution signals (non-paging by default)
sections.content:
Runtime-only attribution signals (non-paging by default)

These are emitted to dashboards and included in alert payloads, but do not page unless explicitly enabled for a model:

- Queueing time p95 +25% (suggests scheduler/fleet saturation)
- Prefill p95 +15% (suggests kernel/model config regressions)
- Decode p95 +15% (suggests kernel/model config regressions)

Rationale:

- Paging should be driven by end-to-end customer-impact proxy (E2E p95 and tokens/sec).
- Breakdown metrics improve triage but are often noisier and more sensitive to load mix.

sections.section_path: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Clause library (approved language) > I. Credits and refunds (usage-based)
sections.heading: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Clause library (approved language) > I. Credits and refunds (usage-based)
sections.content:
I. Credits and refunds (usage-based)

**Approved clause (standard):**
“Credits, if any, are applied to future invoices unless otherwise required by law. Except as expressly provided in the Agreement, fees are non-refundable.”

**Optional add-on (when SLA credits apply):**
“Service credits are Customer’s sole and exclusive remedy for any failure to meet a service level, and will be calculated and applied as described in the applicable SLA.”

sections.section_path: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Clause library (approved language) > E. Caching treatment
sections.heading: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Clause library (approved language) > E. Caching treatment
sections.content:
E. Caching treatment

**Approved clause (standard):**
“Redwood may employ caching and other optimization techniques. Usage reports may distinguish cached and non-cached usage. Redwood may apply billing adjustments (including reduced billed tokens) for eligible cached content as described in Redwood documentation. Optimization techniques may change over time.”

**Alternative clause (customer requests explicit fairness statement):**
“Redwood will not charge more than once for the same logical request submitted with the same idempotency key, and may reduce charges when caching is applied, as reflected in the usage report.”

sections.section_path: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Definitions (approved internal meanings) > 2) “Request”
sections.heading: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Definitions (approved internal meanings) > 2) “Request”
sections.content:
2) “Request”

A **Request** is an API call that is accepted by Redwood’s service and results in an attempt to process the call (including streaming requests). Do not tie “request” to “successful response” unless Product/Finance explicitly approves.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Consequences > Positive
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Consequences > Positive
sections.content:
Consequences

Positive

- Stable, versioned baselines support rollout gates and high-confidence paging.
- Rolling health baseline provides drift visibility without undermining safety.
- Anti-flap controls reduce alert noise and prevent incident-bot storms.

sections.section_path: 20260828 Crucible Inference Sitrep
sections.heading: 20260828 Crucible Inference Sitrep
sections.content:
Root cause: A recently deployed autoscaler policy update combined with a rare kernel failure on a single GPU instance produced cascading queue pressure; autoscaler oscillation and a lag in instance replacement led to transient 5xxs and reduced throughput. The failing instance also intermittently returned degraded kernel performance which amplified tail latency.

What we did:

- Emergency capacity bump and routing to fallback model variant on 2026-08-28 at 08:28 PDT — immediate tail-latency improved and throughput returned to baseline within ~12 minutes.
- Drained and reprovisioned the failing instance; patched the kernel path in the affected image and rolled a hotfix to prevent identical failures.
- Reverted the autoscaler policy update and introduced a short cool-down to prevent oscillation.

Impact:

- Customer observed peak 5xx rate of 8% and throughput drop to ~60% of baseline for a ~10-minute window. No customer data exfiltration.

Next steps / action items: 
1) We will publish a short postmortem to the customer by EOD with the timeline and mitigations (Hannah + Stephanie).
2) Engineering (Marcus) to harden autoscaler policy testing and add a canary step for autoscaler changes.
3) Product to add a routing knob for immediate cross-model fallback triggered by SLA breach (Marcus + Product).
4) Finance to confirm priority-burst billing terms for this incident (Laura).

Attachments: postmortem-draft.md, kpi_before_after.png

Thanks everyone for the quick triage. Julia — we are sending a tailored postmortem and are happy to run a joint technical review next week if you'd like.

— Marcus Lin
Principal Engineer, Serving Runtime

sections.section_path: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Clause library (approved language) > F. Retries and idempotency
sections.heading: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Clause library (approved language) > F. Retries and idempotency
sections.content:
F. Retries and idempotency

**Approved clause (standard):**
“Customer is responsible for implementing idempotency keys for retryable requests. Redwood will use commercially reasonable efforts to avoid duplicate billing for server-side retries performed under the same logical request identifier. Customer-submitted duplicate requests may be billable.”

**Negotiation notes:**

- Do not guarantee “no double billing ever.” Instead: “commercially reasonable efforts” + dispute process.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Alternatives Considered > B) Pure fixed baseline (never updated unless manual)
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Alternatives Considered > B) Pure fixed baseline (never updated unless manual)
sections.content:
B) Pure fixed baseline (never updated unless manual)

Pros:

- Extremely stable; easy to reason about.

Cons:

- Becomes stale as fleet/hardware/driver changes accumulate; increases false positives over time.
- Forces frequent manual work to remain relevant.

Decision: Rejected as the only strategy. Adopted as primary baseline with explicit regeneration workflows.

sections.content:
A. Usage unit (Tokens) — baseline clause

**Approved clause (standard):**
“Usage is measured in tokens processed by the applicable model. A token is a unit of text determined by the model’s tokenization scheme. Fees are calculated based on the number of billed tokens reported by Redwood for the applicable billing period. Token counts may vary by model and model version.”

**Negotiation notes:**

- If customer requests a fixed tokenization algorithm, respond that tokenization is model-dependent and tied to the model provider’s implementation.
- If customer requests billing purely on input+output tokens, steer to “billed tokens” and point to reporting transparency.

Sean Gallagher: root cause candidate: us-east routers running old version, using IP fallback and route-only seed => canary assignment biased.

Aisha Bello: config patch has landed. Observed canary pct in us-east is dropping: 0.22 -> 0.11 over last 2m.

Elena Popov: confirming propagation complete on all us-east POPs. should converge to ~0 within a few mins.

Rafael Mendes: good containment. Next action: get us-east routers to 1.38.3 ASAP.

Emily Zhao: I can kick a redeploy for us-east only. Need release channel sign-off since we’re mid-beta.

Sean Gallagher: do it. This is safety-related.

Hannah Rivera: meanwhile I’ll pause the orchestrator step timer? If Console is still counting soak at 10% but us-east is effectively 0, it may confuse auto-stop logic.

Vikram Singh: more logs from us-east show `cohort_key_present=false` a lot. Northstar doesn’t send x-rw-user-key consistently; they rely on our default. Our default should use `x-request-id` but it looks like 1.38.2 uses IP first. That’s the skew.

Ravi Menon: yep 1.38.3 changed fallback precedence: `x-rw-user-key` > `x-rw-session-id` > `request_id` (stable for retries) > last resort IP. Also fixes hash seed to include tenant+route.

Aisha Bello: metrics update: us-east canary pct now 0.01 (effectively off). us-west and eu-central remain ~0.10.

Rafael Mendes: ok. once redeploy done, we can remove region override and go back to intended 10% globally.

Sean Gallagher: careful: remove override after confirming cohorting logs show expected hash inputs and observed split matches.

Mina Haddad: +1. Let’s verify on one POP first.

Emily Zhao: us-east now on 1.38.3 across the fleet.

```

cohort_key_source=header:x-rw-user-key

Looks good.

Elena Popov: I can revert the override now.

Sean Gallagher: do it, but watch for a few minutes. also note we might still see variance if they don’t send stable user key and request_ids are random per request (not per user). That’s ok though; expected distribution still correct.

sections.section_path: Postmortem Perf Canary False Positive Alert Storm > What happened (symptoms)
sections.heading: Postmortem Perf Canary False Positive Alert Storm > What happened (symptoms)
sections.content:
What happened (symptoms)

The canary’s regression evaluator compared observed p95 latency/tokens-sec against per-model baselines. After model expansion:

- Many evaluations used **fallback baseline values** because the baseline lookup key did not match (baseline existed under a different dimension set).
- Metric series were fragmented by high-cardinality labels; the regression evaluator saw many “small-N” series and oscillated between “enough samples” and “not enough samples” depending on which series was queried.
- Alert rules did not consistently enforce **minimum sample size across the same grouping** used by the evaluator, which allowed small, noisy slices to trip thresholds.
- incident-bot dedupe keys lacked stable identifiers for (model, version, region, sku, runtime_build), so the same underlying symptom created repeated threads/pages.
