sections.section_path: Cross Role Tool Access Governance And Self Service Handbook 2027
sections.heading: Cross Role Tool Access Governance And Self Service Handbook 2027
sections.content:
- Emergency access (e.g., incident mitigation) uses the Fast-Track Exception flow:
  1) Requester files an incident-tagged access request with justification and incident ID.
  2) On-call approver (manager or designated incident commander) may grant a 4-hour temporary token via the Access Portal.
  3) Security must be notified within 1 hour and will follow up to convert to a formal exception or revoke.
- All emergency grants are logged and retroactively reviewed as part of the incident postmortem.

7) Deprovisioning and Offboarding

- Standard offboarding timeline:
  - Day 0: account disabled for interactive access within 4 hours of HR offboarding signal.
  - Day 1: short-lived API tokens invalidated; persistent service accounts rotated if necessary.
  - Day 7: cloud console roles removed; scheduled backup of any outstanding owner responsibilities.
- Manager responsibility: reassign ownership before final removal.
- Audit: people-ops runs weekly deprovisioning reports, security runs monthly verification.

8) Periodic Access Reviews

- Quarterly review for all high-risk roles.
- Biannual review for medium-risk.
- Annual review for low-risk.
- Review process: automated report produced by Access Portal -> owner validates or initiates deprovisioning -> people-ops enforces changes within 7 business days.

9) Tool Onboarding Checklist (for Tool Owners)

1. Identify required roles and map to least-privilege sets.
2. Document roles in the Role Catalog section of the owner page.
3. Define which roles are self-service vs require approval.
4. Provide an onboarding runbook with contact points and SLOs.
5. Register tool owner and escalation email in the Access Portal.
6. Provide a test account and verification steps for the access flow.

10) Technical Integration Patterns

- Recommended: integrate tool with SSO and SCIM for group sync.
- Fallback: if SCIM unavailable, implement an API-based provisioning endpoint with scoped tokens and change tracking.
- Example access request payload (JSON):

{
  "requester": "user@redwood.com",
  "tool": "grafana-prod",
  "role": "viewer",
  "justification": "Oncall rotation",
  "expires_at": "2026-02-28T23:59:00Z"
}

- Example CLI (Access Portal CLI):

$ rwd-access request --tool grafana-prod --role viewer --justification "oncall"

11) Monitoring, Auditing and KPIs

- KPIs to track: time-to-provision (median), percent self-service, number of active exceptions, time-to-deprovision after offboard.
- Reporting cadence: weekly provisioning dashboard, monthly audit exports (CSV) to security vault.
- Audit checks: verify no more than 5% of production-admin grants are older than 30 days without re-approval.

12) De-Escalation and Dispute Resolution

- If a manager or user disputes a grant or removal, escalate to people-ops with the ticket ID. People-ops will convene: manager, tool owner, and security to adjudicate within 5 business days.

13) Sample Runbook: Granting Prod-Read Access (Manager-Approved)

1. Manager submits request in Access Portal with business justification.
2. Portal routes to tool owner notification and manager approval.
3. On approval, provisioning job runs (SCIM or API).
4. Access granted; audit log written; notification sent to requester and manager.
5. After 90 days, system creates a renewal task for the manager.

14) Implementation Roadmap (next 18 months)

- Q2 2026: Complete SCIM integrations for top 10 tools.
- Q3 2026: Launch delegated team-admin roles for large product groups.
- Q4 2026: Build exception analytics dashboard and automatic expiration nudges.

sections.heading: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Clause library (approved language) > H. Dispute window (recommended default)

H. Dispute window (recommended default)

**Approved clause (standard):**
“Customer must notify Redwood in writing of any good-faith dispute regarding an invoice within thirty (30) days of the invoice date, describing the basis for the dispute in reasonable detail. If Customer does not dispute an invoice within this period, the invoice will be deemed accepted.”

sections.section_path: Key Management Standard Kms Integrations > Policy summary (MUST/SHOULD) > Observability controls
sections.heading: Key Management Standard Kms Integrations > Policy summary (MUST/SHOULD) > Observability controls
sections.content:
Observability controls

- MUST emit standard metrics and trace spans for every KMS operation.
- MUST map provider-specific errors to the canonical Redwood KMS error taxonomy.
- SHOULD provide dashboards and alerts (or explicitly document why the integration is low-risk/no alerting needed).

sections.section_path: Key Management Standard Kms Integrations > Scope > In scope
sections.heading: Key Management Standard Kms Integrations > Scope > In scope
sections.content:
Scope

In scope

- Any code path that calls a cloud KMS/HSM or on-prem KMS interface for: encrypt, decrypt, generate data key, re-encrypt, describe key, list key versions, or grant/permission operations.
- Control-plane and data-plane components.
- Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.

sections.section_path: Key Management Standard Kms Integrations > Timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, and caching > Circuit breaker / degrade mode
sections.heading: Key Management Standard Kms Integrations > Timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, and caching > Circuit breaker / degrade mode
sections.content:
Circuit breaker / degrade mode

Where KMS failure can cause cascading outages:

- MUST implement circuit breaker behavior and document the degrade policy.
- MUST define what happens when the circuit is open (examples):
  - Fail closed with clear errors and backpressure (default for cryptographic strictness)
  - Limited fail open only if data confidentiality/integrity is not reduced (rare; requires Security approval)
- MUST have SRE-reviewed alerting for circuit open events.

sections.section_path: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Internal operational guardrails (contracting) > Month-end close and late-arriving events
sections.heading: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Internal operational guardrails (contracting) > Month-end close and late-arriving events
sections.content:
Internal operational guardrails (contracting)

Month-end close and late-arriving events

Finance operates a month-end close process with a usage data freeze window and controlled backfills.

- Contract language should not obligate real-time corrections for late events.
- Use the dispute clause and reconciliation process to handle exceptions.

sections.section_path: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Redlines: common asks and recommended responses > 4) “Dispute window must be 90 days.”
sections.heading: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Redlines: common asks and recommended responses > 4) “Dispute window must be 90 days.”
sections.content:
4) “Dispute window must be 90 days.”

**Position:** Generally no.
**Response:** Offer 45 days; if deal size justifies, escalate to CFO/GC with RevRec impact assessment.

sections.section_path: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Scope
sections.heading: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Scope
sections.content:
Scope

Applies to:

- Hosted API usage-based charges (tokens/requests/embeddings units)
- Metered add-ons where usage events are the basis of invoicing
- Dedicated and Private agreements only where they incorporate usage-based overages or burst (primary Dedicated meter definitions live elsewhere)

Out of scope:

- Full MSA templates (see Legal templates repository)
- Export-controlled or regulated country-specific addenda (escalate to Legal)

sections.section_path: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Escalation path (when to pull in Legal/Finance/Engineering) > Escalate to GC (Michael Grant)
sections.heading: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Escalation path (when to pull in Legal/Finance/Engineering) > Escalate to GC (Michael Grant)
sections.content:
Escalate to GC (Michael Grant)

- Any language that constrains Redwood’s ability to modify measurement systems
- Any customer request for regulatory/compliance commitments tied to billing logs
- Any threat of litigation or formal audit request

sections.section_path: Key Management Standard Kms Integrations > Required reviews for new KMS call sites > Evidence to attach to the PR / design review
sections.heading: Key Management Standard Kms Integrations > Required reviews for new KMS call sites > Evidence to attach to the PR / design review
sections.content:
Evidence to attach to the PR / design review

- Link to the call site inventory entry (service + operation + key ID class)
- IAM policy diff (or Terraform module usage) demonstrating least privilege
- Observability screenshots/links (dashboards, metric names) or validation logs from staging
- Failure-mode test plan or test results (timeouts, throttling, AccessDenied, key disabled)
- Rotation readiness statement (how dual-read and rollback are handled)

sections.section_path: Key Management Standard Kms Integrations > Owner and change management
sections.heading: Key Management Standard Kms Integrations > Owner and change management
sections.content:
Owner and change management

- Owner: Security Engineering
- Changes to this standard require Security + SRE review and are announced in #eng-security and #eng-sre.

---
Appendix: Quick guidance for common pitfalls

- **AccessDenied in Private deployments**: almost always mis-scoped principal/key policy/region mismatch. Ensure preflight validation checks are enabled and run.
- **Throttle spikes**: confirm retry jitter is enabled and that request concurrency has backpressure. Do not “solve” throttling by increasing retries.
- **InvalidCiphertext during rotation**: treat as potential key/version mismatch; verify dual-read settings and that ciphertext metadata includes the correct key reference.

sections.section_path: Key Management Standard Kms Integrations > Incident handling and operational expectations > Required artifacts
sections.heading: Key Management Standard Kms Integrations > Incident handling and operational expectations > Required artifacts
sections.content:
Incident handling and operational expectations

Required artifacts

- A runbook or runbook section describing:
  - Symptoms, dashboards, and log queries
  - Common root causes (AccessDenied, throttling, timeout spikes, wrong key ID)
  - Mitigation steps and safe stopgaps
  - Escalation path to Security + Platform
- Link the runbook to on-call rotations and ensure it is discoverable.

sections.section_path: Key Management Standard Kms Integrations > Policy summary (MUST/SHOULD) > Security controls
sections.heading: Key Management Standard Kms Integrations > Policy summary (MUST/SHOULD) > Security controls
sections.content:
Security controls

- MUST use envelope encryption for application data at rest when using KMS (DEKs for data; KEKs for wrapping).
- MUST scope IAM to least privilege for the specific key(s), operations, and environment.
- MUST separate runtime decrypt/encrypt permissions from rotation/admin permissions (separate roles/principals) for Dedicated/Private unless explicitly infeasible.
- MUST emit audit-relevant logs for key/rotation configuration changes (cutovers, key ID changes, policy toggles).
- MUST not log plaintext, DEKs, or wrapped key material.
- SHOULD use KMS/HSM-backed keys for regulated workloads (customer requirement-dependent).

sections.section_path: Company Horizon Quay Ai Infrastructure
sections.heading: Company Horizon Quay Ai Infrastructure
sections.content:
- Profile: Horizon Quay is a global maritime logistics SaaS (port ops + scheduling). Heavy real-time chat+assistant for ops centers; embeddings for manifest search; reranking for ETA predictions.
- Capacity ask: Reserved pool sized for 8 sustained A100-equivalent GPUs per primary region (NA + EU). Expected steady-state: ~350–600 RPS for short payload chat (avg token window 256). Burst to ~1k RPS during shift changes.
- Performance targets: P95 text-gen latency <= 80ms, P99 <= 220ms for chat on dedicated pool; throughput guarantees of 500 RPS sustained per region.
- SLA position (customer asks): 99.95% uptime across dedicated pools; 30% credit at 99.9–99.95; 50% credit below 99.9; request for monthly credit cap and cumulative measurement window.
- Redwood counterproposals discussed: baseline 99.95 SLA with quarterly reconciliation; credit schedule tiered: 99.9–99.95 = 10% service credit, 99.5–99.9 = 30%, <99.5 = 60% (proposal to legal). Redwood wants max cap at 6 months' fee.
- Maintenance windows: customer requires predictable maintenance windows not during shift-change windows (06:00–09:00 UTC). Proposed weekly 02:00–04:00 region-local maintenance with 72h advance notice; emergency maintenance with 48h notice and rolling failover.
- Support / escalation: Horizon Quay requires 24/7 hotline for Sev1 with 15-minute acknowledgement, 2-hour remediate SLA target for critical infrastructure, 4-hour for Sev2. Redwood proposes 15min ack, 1h initial response, remediation time objective to be defined per incident severity in SOW.
- Throughput guarantees & reserved GPU planning: plan includes capacity buffer for 1.5x expected steady-state; autoscaling burst into shared pool allowed with pre-authorized fallback; need explicit routing policy for latency-first vs cost-first (customer wants latency-first for ops-critical calls).
- Security/compliance: customer requires SOC2 Type II report, KMS integration for customer-managed keys, audit logs retained 12 months, option for EU-only residency for EU traffic.
- POC summary (3 weeks):
  * Week 0: onboarding, network peering, SSO test (SAML).
  * Week 1: model import + inference validation, baseline latency/throughput profiling.
  * Week 2: load testing to 1.2x forecast, KV/prefix cache tuning, batch tuning.
  * Week 3: SLA stress scenarios, failover drill, cost/perf report and recommended reserved sizing.
- POC status: onboarding complete; peering and SSO in staging done; load tests scheduled 2026-03-15. Initial latency targets met on small-scale tests; sustained throughput test pending.
- Procurement notes: finance wants committed capacity discount tiers and an option to convert to Dedicated Reserved on annual renewal. Legal flagged service credit language and liability cap.
- Quote history: pricing deck sent 2026-02-28 (drive link). Redwood gave two sizing options: 8x reserved (latency-priority) and 12x with burst (cost amortized). Horizon Quay prefers 8x + autoscale to shared.
- Direct quotes from stakeholders: "We cannot accept blackouts during port shift windows — any maintenance must be out of peak or have a clear failover plan." — Head of Ops.
- Next steps (concrete): Redwood to produce SLA redline + SOW by 2026-03-17; schedule legal review call 2026-03-22; run scheduled load test 2026-03-15; finalize forecasted ARR and draft PO template after pricing revision.
- Internal AE reminders: capture agreed uptime measurement buckets, document monthly reporting cadence, confirm escrow/backup plan for on-prem fallbacks.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Purpose
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Purpose
sections.content:
Purpose

This playbook defines the end-to-end process for handling Dedicated **Throughput SLO** misses or suspected misses. It is designed for Customer Success (CS) and Support to:

- Triage quickly and consistently.
- Engage the correct on-call teams (SRE / Infra / Observability) at the right time.
- Communicate clearly with customers, including status updates and written summaries.
- Route service-credit / compensation requests through the correct approval path.

This page is **restricted** because it includes internal paging triggers and credit approval guidance.

---

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Common failure modes and quick routing hints
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Common failure modes and quick routing hints
sections.content:
Common failure modes and quick routing hints

- **Customer sees lower throughput than Redwood reports:** often a measurement mismatch (streaming token accounting, end-to-end latency vs throughput, counting input tokens). Engage Observability if persistent.
- **Throughput drops with GPU pegged:** suspect contention, node health, thermal throttling, network bottleneck; page Infra.
- **Throughput drops with low utilization:** suspect admission control limiting, customer throttling, or workload shift to longer contexts; page SRE; ask customer for concurrency/workload details.
- **Regional capacity constraint / failover behavior:** check tier failover posture; page Infra and SRE; do not promise cross-region without tier/contract confirmation.

---

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Warm pool / startup considerations
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Warm pool / startup considerations
sections.content:
Warm pool / startup considerations

Some tiers include warm pool guarantees (or faster recovery expectations). During triage, identify if the customer is within a warm-up window:

- Did the deployment recently scale from zero?
- Was there a recent model reload, config change, or node replacement?
- Did traffic resume after prolonged inactivity?

If warm-up is suspected, note it explicitly in the customer thread and ask SRE to confirm whether the event is excluded by policy.

---

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Roles and ownership during an SLO event
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Roles and ownership during an SLO event
sections.content:
Roles and ownership during an SLO event

**Support/CS (Incident Driver for customer comms)**

- Owns the customer thread, updates, and expectation management.
- Owns the case record: timeline, impact, and customer confirmations.
- Initiates escalation and ensures correct teams are engaged.

**SRE On-Call (Technical Incident Lead)**

- Confirms whether the SLO is breached per the canonical evaluator.
- Drives mitigation and coordinates cross-functional response.
- Provides internal/external technical summary for comms.

**Infra/Fleet On-Call (Capacity / shape / provisioning owner)**

- Addresses capacity constraints, noisy-neighbor isolation issues, node failures, and shape-level performance anomalies.

**Observability (as-needed)**

- Validates metric correctness (e.g., streaming accounting anomalies), dashboard discrepancies, missing tags.

**Product Dedicated (as-needed)**

- Confirms entitlement interpretation (tier rules, burst policy, failover posture).
- Aligns on customer-facing messaging for edge cases.

**Finance/FP&A + Legal (as-needed for credits/comp)**

- Approves service credits above policy thresholds and any non-standard compensation.

---

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Evidence and logging requirements
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Evidence and logging requirements
sections.content:
Evidence and logging requirements

For any SEV-1/SEV-2 and any credit review, capture:

- Customer ticket link
- Incident link (if created)
- Dashboard links (throughput vs floor, saturation, errors)
- Request IDs / traces used for debugging
- Summary of customer-side traffic confirmation
- Timeline of mitigations and when throughput stabilized

---

sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Customer communications guide > Target update cadence (recommended)
sections.content:
Target update cadence (recommended)

- SEV-1: initial response within 15 minutes; updates every 30 minutes until stable.
- SEV-2: initial response within 1 hour; updates every 2–4 hours until stable.
- SEV-3: initial response within 1 business day; updates daily or as material changes occur.

sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Triage checklist (Support/CS) > 5) Check if this is a metrics discrepancy

5) Check if this is a metrics discrepancy

If customer numbers differ from Redwood:

- Ask what they are measuring (wall-clock end-to-end, tokens counted, streaming vs non-streaming).
- Request a single representative request ID and a 10–20 minute sample window.

sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Triage checklist (Support/CS) > 2) Confirm the customer is driving enough load

Ask:

- Current request concurrency
- Any client-side rate limiting (explicit QPS cap, worker pool limit)

- For Premium accounts, default to more frequent updates and written summaries.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Service credits / compensation (internal guidance) > Which tiers are typically credit-eligible?

sections.content:
Which tiers are typically credit-eligible?

- **Premium:** written throughput commitment; credit review is standard for confirmed breaches.
- **Plus:** may be eligible depending on contract addenda; treat as “review required.”
- **Standard:** generally best-effort; credit requests require Product + Finance approval.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Service credits / compensation (internal guidance) > Approval path (default)
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Service credits / compensation (internal guidance) > Approval path (default)
sections.content:
Approval path (default)

1) CS/Support compiles incident details and SRE confirmation.
2) SRE provides breach window + summary.
3) Product Dedicated confirms entitlement interpretation (tier/exclusions).
4) Finance (Laura Bennett / delegate) validates policy compliance and amount.
5) Legal (Sofia Mendes / delegate) reviews if there is contract ambiguity or if a non-standard remedy is proposed.
6) CS communicates outcome to customer.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > What is the Dedicated Throughput SLO (customer-facing summary)
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > What is the Dedicated Throughput SLO (customer-facing summary)
sections.content:
What is the Dedicated Throughput SLO (customer-facing summary)

Dedicated Throughput SLO guarantees a **minimum sustained throughput floor** for an eligible Dedicated deployment under defined conditions.

**High-level definition (internal summary):**

- Metric: throughput measured as **billable output tokens per second**, computed per deployment, aggregated over a rolling window.
- Scope: Dedicated deployments only (not Hosted API, not eval/sandbox deployments).
- Eligibility: model/version and configuration must be within the customer’s contracted Dedicated configuration (e.g., pinned model family/version, supported max context, supported shape).

**Common non-eligibility / exclusions (not exhaustive):**

- Customer-side throttling or client concurrency limits causing underutilization.
- Customer workload violating sizing assumptions (e.g., contexts above configured limit, unsupported parameter combinations).
- Warm-up periods after scale-from-zero or cold start (tier-dependent; see “Warm pool / startup” below).
- Incidents due to customer networking/VPC misconfig in Private connectivity paths (if applicable).

When in doubt, treat as potentially eligible, start the triage, and engage SRE.

7) Mitigation options you can offer immediately (tier-dependent)

These are customer-facing actions CS/Support may propose, with SRE confirmation where possible:

- Temporarily reduce max context / max output tokens (if within acceptable product behavior).
- Temporarily shift traffic to the contracted primary route only (avoid experimental routes).
- Enable/disable streaming based on their client constraints (note: streaming affects perceived latency but should not invalidate throughput).
- If the customer has multi-deployment setup: fail over to a secondary deployment (Premium: may be Redwood-assisted).

Severity levels (Support/CS view)

Use these severities to standardize response; SRE may map to their incident severities.

**SEV-1 (Critical, likely customer-impacting breach)**

- Premium tier customer reports sustained throughput below floor OR SRE burn-rate alert is firing.
- Clear production impact (e.g., queue buildup, timeouts, user-visible latency spikes).
- Immediate paging required.

**SEV-2 (High, likely degradation / at-risk of breach)**

- Throughput is below expected but not yet confirmed as an SLO breach.
- Customer impact is moderate OR limited to a subset of traffic/routes.
- Paging may be required depending on tier and duration.

**SEV-3 (Moderate, investigation / metrics discrepancy)**

- Conflicting metrics (customer vs Redwood dashboards), short-lived dips, or suspected measurement artifacts.
- No clear production impact.

sections.section_path: Eng 776543 Kvcache Ghost Refcount Decay Rolling Heal Playbook
sections.heading: Eng 776543 Kvcache Ghost Refcount Decay Rolling Heal Playbook
sections.content:
Summary: During a capacity surge on 2025-11-08 we observed a slow but persistent memory growth on several serving nodes which culminated in degraded tail latency and two short-lived OOMs. Investigation showed a new class of 'ghost' entries in the KV prefix cache: entries whose refcount had decayed below zero (underflow) due to an interaction between async compaction, prefetch migration, and a recent refcount optimization. These ghost entries never surfaced as normal cache misses and therefore were not collected by the existing eviction heuristics, leading to gradual slab exhaustion on hot shards. This ticket captures detection heuristics, an emergency snapshot sanitization runbook, a staged rolling-heal design (scheduled drains + isolated snapshot rewrite), telemetry improvements, and a rollout/verification plan.
Memory growth first seen 2025-11-06, customer latency degradation at p95/p99 experienced across dedicated and hosted clusters on 2025-11-08. Two nodes hit transient OOMs and auto-recovered (restarts). No persistent data loss; customer requests were served with fallbacks but experienced elevated errors and higher per-token latency. Estimated affected capacity 8% of serving fleet during surge window.
Concurrency bug: an optimization in the refcount update path batched decrement operations to reduce atomic ops. Under a race where async compaction rewrites slab bitmaps concurrently with prefetch migrators moving KV records across buckets, the batched decrement could be applied twice for the same logical record. This produced negative refcounts and left entries in an invisible 'ghost' state that bypassed eviction score updates. Compaction also left behind partial tombstone metadata which confused the slab reclaim heuristics.
A1: Emergency snapshot sanitization script - implement and run a conservative scanner to detect negative refcounts and mark entries for reclamation. Owner: Marcus Li. Due: 2025-11-18.
A2: Prefetch/refcount critical section rewrite - ensure decrement operations are idempotent and move batched application under compaction locks. Owner: Priya Nair. Due: 2025-11-22.
A3: Scheduled rolling-heal plan - implement scheduled small drains (10-15min) per shard during off-peak for 2 weeks to allow safe slab rewrite without customer-impacting restarts. Owner: SRE Team (lead: Daniel Kim). Due: 2025-11-26.
A4: Eviction heuristics patch - add ghost-detection heuristic: treat entries with refcount < 0 or missing eviction timestamp as high-priority reclamation candidates. Owner: Elena Garcia. Due: 2025-12-02.
A5: Telemetry expansion - emit refcount histograms, negative-refcount counter, slab-fragmentation gauge, and open traces when a snapshot sanitization runs. Owner: Observability (lead: Omar Hassan). Due: 2025-11-20.
A6: End-to-end test harness - add a fault-injection test that simulates compaction/prefetch races and validates snapshot sanitizer removes ghosts without losing live entries. Owner: QA (lead: Mei Chen). Due: 2025-12-05.
A7: Post-rollout review and automation - automate periodic snapshot sanitization in maintenance windows and add alerting when negative-refcount rate > 0 over 10m. Owner: Marcus Li. Due: 2025-12-12.
A8: Documentation - update runbooks and run the incident playbook with SRE for on-call run-through. Owner: SRE runbooks (lead: Priya Nair). Due: 2025-11-30.
Add metric: kvcache.refcount.negative.count (counter) - increment every time sanitizer detects a negative refcount
Add gauge: kvcache.slab.fragmentation_pct (percent) - updated on compaction completion
Add histogram: kvcache.eviction.latency_ms - measure time from detection -> reclaimed
Trace: attach sanitizer-run-id to traces and correlate with allocation spikes (link to dashboard)

sections.heading: Eng 776543 Kvcache Ghost Refcount Decay Rolling Heal Playbook
sections.content:
Alert: create kvcache_negative_refcount_rate > 0 for 10m -> P1 alert to oncall
Stage 0 (canary): run snapshot sanitization in read-only mode against one non-production fleet to validate detection (no reclamation). Owner: Marcus Li. Window: 2025-11-18 02:00-04:00 UTC.
Stage 1 (pilot): run sanitizer in reclamation mode on 5% of low-traffic shards with automated validation and crash-safe checkpoints. Monitor memory, latency, errors. Rollback if p99 latency increases > 15% or error rate > 2x baseline. Window: 2025-11-19.
Stage 2 (gradual): start scheduled rolling-heal drains: drain 3% of shards every 30m during off-peak, run sanitization, and bring back. Target fleet complete in 72h. Abort conditions: OOMs, persistent error spikes, or eviction backlog growth. Owner: SRE.
Stage 3 (global): deploy refcount idempotency and eviction heuristic patches with canary traffic gating then full roll. Tie to runtime-1.21 release and monitor for 7 days.
Post-sanitization memory regression test against replayed workload for 48h
No new negative-refcount increments in metrics for 72h after full rollout
p50/p95/p99 latency at or below pre-incident baseline within 2% for 7 days
Run the fault-injection harness in CI and require green before merging patches

sections.heading: Int 738205 Wifi Bridge Nat Source Rewrite Breaks Vpn Policy
sections.content:
Int 738205 Wifi Bridge Nat Source Rewrite Breaks Vpn Policy

Source type: jira
Document ID: dsid_e728a420a02a4ddcb125e6adb09d211e
Release: v1.0.0
Benchmark: EnterpriseRAG-Bench synthetic upstream data
Office edge bridge in NAT mode rewriting source IPs and causing VPN policy routing failures and SSO timeouts

Issue summary: After a recent office CAB change at the SoMa satellite office we started seeing a sustained increase in VPN session failures and SSO timeouts for users on the office Wi‑Fi. Impact: ~12-18% of users at SoMa experience intermittent 403/SSO timeouts or are unable to reach internal services that normally resolve via VPN private IPs. Service impact is localized to the office LAN and affects employees using company Wi‑Fi and a subset of developer services behind policy-based routing. Initial hypothesis: an intermediate bridge/AP that was re-provisioned to 'NAT' mode is rewriting source addresses causing VPN policy lookup to fail, triggering mis-routed traffic and SSO token validation errors.
1) Connect a laptop to SoMa corporate Wi‑Fi (ssid: Redwood-Corp).
2) Establish Redwood VPN (WireGuard client) and authenticate via SSO (Okta).
3) Attempt to curl an internal service at 10.11.20.5: expect success; observed: connection resets or 403 responses.
4) Observe device local IP (e.g., 192.168.50.34) and the outbound NATed IP as seen by internal services (packets show 10.100.200.1 source after NAT rewrite).
Clients on office Wi‑Fi see internal service requests fail intermittently. Packet captures from service frontends show source IPs mapped to 10.100.200.0/24 (bridge appliance SNAT pool) instead of clients' VPN-assigned 10.8.0.0/16 addresses. Okta SSO validation rejects token assertions when source IP does not match expected corporate ranges, causing auth flows to fail.
Traffic from VPN clients should preserve VPN-assigned source addresses. Office bridge should be in passthrough mode for tunneled traffic so policy-based routing at the gateway can correctly match flows and SSO sees expected IP ranges.
2026-03-10T09:22:13Z firewall[gw-usw-1]: policy_lookup: src=10.8.12.45 dst=10.11.20.5 matched=internal-web-cluster action=allow
2026-03-10T09:22:13Z app-fw[web-01]: tcpdump: in.ether src=10.100.200.14:52344 > 10.11.20.5:443 SYN
2026-03-10T09:23:01Z okta-proxy[auth-01]: token_validation: ip_mismatch user=jared@example.com expected_range=10.8.0.0/16 seen_ip=10.100.200.14

- Confirmed bridge device model: Ubiquiti UBB‑Edge v2 (serial: UB-1212). Reprovisioning on 2026-03-09 set its WAN mode to 'Gateway (NAT)' instead of 'Bridge'.
- tcpdump on web-01 shows multiple connections with SNATed sources 10.100.200.0/24. When testing from a home client via remote VPN this does not occur; home clients preserve 10.8.x source addresses.
- ip rule list on gw-usw-1 shows policy routing keyed on src network 10.8.0.0/16. Because SNAT rewrote source to 10.100.200.x the kernel falls back to default route and packets get dropped or mis-routed to edge ACLs.
- Quick check: ssh to bridge admin UI -> Network -> NAT Mode = Enabled. CLI 'iptables -t nat -L -n' shows POSTROUTING MASQUERADE for bridge LAN range.
- Hypothesis validated by temporary change: disabled NAT on bridge -> source IPs preserved -> internal service connectivity restored and SSO token validations succeed.

sections.section_path: Pr 96123 Chat V1 Param Normalizer Role Alias Stop Dedupe Stream Backpressure
sections.heading: Pr 96123 Chat V1 Param Normalizer Role Alias Stop Dedupe Stream Backpressure
sections.content:
Motivation: Close a set of subtle incompatibilities between our /v1/chat.completions adapter and OpenAI's behavior that have been causing developer friction in streaming function-call flows and stop/logprobs handling. This PR implements a compact 'parameter normalizer' layer and a streaming framing/backpressure handshake to make the adapter tolerant of real-world clients and OpenAI-style payloads. Summary of changes: - Parameter normalizer: unify and sanitize incoming params (max_tokens, temperature, top_p, n, presence_penalty) and map them to our internal API consistently; accept both string and numeric encodings, preserve explicit nulls, and prefer client-provided values for edge cases. - Role aliasing: accept and normalize role names coming from clients ("assistant", "system", "user", "tool", and legacy aliases like "ai" or "bot"); ensure role is preserved in both final and streaming envelopes. - Stop sequence deduplication: support stop as string or array; expand single-string stops into an array; dedupe overlapping sequences (e.g. ["

", "


"]) and maintain order stability to match OpenAI semantics. - Sparse logprobs: add an opt-in sparse_logprobs mode that mirrors OpenAI's sparse token-level logprob structure when requested; keep heavy-weight computation behind an explicit flag to avoid perf regressions. - Streaming framing & backpressure: introduce a light handshake in the stream start (sent as first SSE/delta) that communicates our token framing and heartbeat expectations; implement backpressure signaling for HTTP/2 clients to avoid partial JSON objects when a client pauses mid-stream. - Function-call streaming support: improve chunking for function_call.name/arguments so that streaming deltas assemble deterministically into valid JSON payloads even across reconnects; final chunk action inserts a stable end-of-function marker to make reconstruction robust. - Response envelope parity: normalize streaming deltas to include a minimal structured 'choice' envelope (id, index, finish_reason) so downstream OpenAI-compat consumers don't need ad-hoc heuristics. - Tests & docs: add unit and integration tests for the normalizer, streaming handshake scenarios, and a new example in the docs showing a robust client reconnection strategy. Checklist: - [x] Parameter mapping implemented and unit-tested - [x] Streaming handshake and backpressure implemented with integration tests - [x] Role aliasing covered by parser tests - [x] Stop dedupe logic covered and fuzz-tested - [x] Sparse logprobs gating and tests - [x] Docs updated (compatibility section + example client) - [x] Runtime perf smoke tests run on canary cluster Notable design decisions: - We intentionally do not try to replicate obscure historical OpenAI quirks; instead the normalizer applies conservative, well-documented rules and exposes a strict compatibility flag for customers who really need historical behavior. - The streaming handshake is opt-out via a client header (X-Redwood-Compat: openai-v1) to avoid breaking existing non-OpenAI clients. - Sparse logprobs are computed on-demand and annotated in the response metadata to allow downstream billing/observability. Related: ENG-4321 (parameter normalization epic), SUP-2107 (customer-reported toolcall truncation).
Samir: Can you clarify how explicit null values are treated vs missing keys? There was a customer case where max_tokens=null meant 'use default' rather than '0'.
Author (Evelyn): Normalizer treats explicit null as 'unset' and falls back to model defaults; added a unit test for that scenario.

Cross-role Tool Access Governance and Self-Service Handbook

Summary:

This handbook defines the governance model, operational runbook, and self-service flows for granting, reviewing, and revoking access to Redwood’s internal tools across roles and teams. It is intended for people-ops, engineering managers, security reviewers, and tool maintainers. The goal is to make tool access predictable, auditable, and fast while minimizing over-permissioning.

Key Principles:

- Least privilege by default: users receive the minimum role required to do their job.
- Role-driven access: we prefer role-based assignments with ephemeral exceptions.
- Self-service first, manual oversight when necessary: automate safe, common grants.
- Clear ownership: every tool has an owner and an escalation path.
- Auditable lifecycle: provisioning, reviews and deprovisioning are tracked centrally.

1) Scope and Definitions

- Tool: any internal SaaS, self-hosted service, or repo that requires explicit credentials or permissions (examples: AWS consoles, Jira admin groups, prod Grafana, CI pipelines).
- Role: a named collection of permissions (e.g., developer-readonly, infra-operator).
- Access Request: a request submitted to the Access Portal for a role or tool-specific permission.
- Exception: temporary access outside standard roles; must have an expiration and approver.

2) Ownership and Responsibilities

- Tool Owner (team-specified): maintains the role catalog, documents required permissions, defines safe self-service gates, and responds to escalations.
- People Ops: owns onboarding/offboarding orchestration, periodic review cadence, and highest-level policy.
- Security: defines acceptable exception policies, approves high-risk tools, and performs audits.
- Manager (requester approver): verifies business need and ties access to role/mission.

3) Access Model (high level)

- Role Catalog: canonical list of roles for common tools; stored in the Access Portal.
- Self-Service Roles: low-risk roles that can be assigned instantly (examples: docs-edit, ci-reader)
- Request-and-Approve Roles: medium-risk roles requiring manager approval (examples: staging-deploy, metrics-writer)
- Manual Approval Roles: high-risk roles requiring security review (examples: prod-admin, billing-admin)

4) Standard Provisioning Flow (Self-Service preferred)

1. User initiates request via Access Portal (or CLI).
2. For self-service roles: immediate grant recorded in audit log; user notified.
3. For manager-approval roles: manager receives approval email and must respond within 48 business hours; if approved, provisioning executes automatically.
4. For security-approval roles: security reviewer staged; expected SLA is 3 business days.
5. All grants include metadata: requester, approver, justification, expiration (if exception), and ticket ID.

5) Approval Matrix (sample)

| Tool Category | Example Tools | Typical Role Name | Approval Path | Max SLA for Approval | Expiration Policy |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| Low risk | Docs, Internal Wiki | docs-edit | Self-service | Instant | Persistent (attached to employment) |
| Medium risk | Staging CI, Dev DB | staging-deploy | Manager | 48 business hours | 90 days (auto-renew) |
| High risk | Production infra, Billing | prod-admin | Manager + Security | 3 business days | 7 days (explicit extension only) |

6) Exception and Emergency Access

sections.section_path: Cross Role Tool Access Governance And Self Service Handbook 2027
sections.heading: Cross Role Tool Access Governance And Self Service Handbook 2027
sections.content:
- Emergency access (e.g., incident mitigation) uses the Fast-Track Exception flow:
  1) Requester files an incident-tagged access request with justification and incident ID.
  2) On-call approver (manager or designated incident commander) may grant a 4-hour temporary token via the Access Portal.
  3) Security must be notified within 1 hour and will follow up to convert to a formal exception or revoke.
- All emergency grants are logged and retroactively reviewed as part of the incident postmortem.

7) Deprovisioning and Offboarding

- Standard offboarding timeline:
  - Day 0: account disabled for interactive access within 4 hours of HR offboarding signal.
  - Day 1: short-lived API tokens invalidated; persistent service accounts rotated if necessary.
  - Day 7: cloud console roles removed; scheduled backup of any outstanding owner responsibilities.
- Manager responsibility: reassign ownership before final removal.
- Audit: people-ops runs weekly deprovisioning reports, security runs monthly verification.

8) Periodic Access Reviews

- Quarterly review for all high-risk roles.
- Biannual review for medium-risk.
- Annual review for low-risk.
- Review process: automated report produced by Access Portal -> owner validates or initiates deprovisioning -> people-ops enforces changes within 7 business days.

9) Tool Onboarding Checklist (for Tool Owners)

1. Identify required roles and map to least-privilege sets.
2. Document roles in the Role Catalog section of the owner page.
3. Define which roles are self-service vs require approval.
4. Provide an onboarding runbook with contact points and SLOs.
5. Register tool owner and escalation email in the Access Portal.
6. Provide a test account and verification steps for the access flow.

10) Technical Integration Patterns

- Recommended: integrate tool with SSO and SCIM for group sync.
- Fallback: if SCIM unavailable, implement an API-based provisioning endpoint with scoped tokens and change tracking.
- Example access request payload (JSON):

{
  "requester": "user@redwood.com",
  "tool": "grafana-prod",
  "role": "viewer",
  "justification": "Oncall rotation",
  "expires_at": "2026-02-28T23:59:00Z"
}

- Example CLI (Access Portal CLI):

$ rwd-access request --tool grafana-prod --role viewer --justification "oncall"

11) Monitoring, Auditing and KPIs

- KPIs to track: time-to-provision (median), percent self-service, number of active exceptions, time-to-deprovision after offboard.
- Reporting cadence: weekly provisioning dashboard, monthly audit exports (CSV) to security vault.
- Audit checks: verify no more than 5% of production-admin grants are older than 30 days without re-approval.

12) De-Escalation and Dispute Resolution

- If a manager or user disputes a grant or removal, escalate to people-ops with the ticket ID. People-ops will convene: manager, tool owner, and security to adjudicate within 5 business days.

13) Sample Runbook: Granting Prod-Read Access (Manager-Approved)

1. Manager submits request in Access Portal with business justification.
2. Portal routes to tool owner notification and manager approval.
3. On approval, provisioning job runs (SCIM or API).
4. Access granted; audit log written; notification sent to requester and manager.
5. After 90 days, system creates a renewal task for the manager.

14) Implementation Roadmap (next 18 months)

- Q2 2026: Complete SCIM integrations for top 10 tools.
- Q3 2026: Launch delegated team-admin roles for large product groups.
- Q4 2026: Build exception analytics dashboard and automatic expiration nudges.

entitlements-and-purchase-pathways-playbook-2030
Overview
=======

Purpose: This playbook consolidates company-wide procedures for entitlements (access and permissions), change governance, data handling expectations, procurement and expense approvals, vendor lifecycle management, and travel approvals. It is intended for all Redwood employees and contractors who request or approve resources, commit changes to production, or manage third-party relationships.

Scope: Applies to hosted, dedicated, and private deployment teams, platform and infra teams, procurement interactions, people-ops travel arrangements, and any third party that will access Redwood systems or customer data.

Quick links: Access Portal (Okta + Access Request), VendorHub (procurement back-end), ExpenseFlow (employee expenses), Legal intake form, Security questionnaire (security.redwood.local).

Roles and responsibilities
--------------------------

- Requestor: person initiating an access, change, purchase, vendor relationship, or travel booking. Responsible for completeness and business justification.
- Manager/Approver: direct manager who validates business need and budget availability.
- Approving Officer (Finance/Procurement): validates procurement thresholds, tax, and vendor classification.
- Security Reviewer: evaluates data access risk and mandatory controls (SOC2, encryption, contract clauses).
- Legal Reviewer: reviews contract terms for vendor agreements above threshold or with custom IP/data terms.
- Proc Ops (Vendor Onboarding): completes supplier setup, obtains W-9/COI as applicable.

Principles
----------

- Least privilege: grant minimal entitlements required for the job and set automatic expiration where practical.
- Segregation of duties: approval and provisioning paths must not be owned by the same individual for medium/high risk requests.
- Evidence-first approvals: all approvals must be attached to the request in VendorHub or Access Portal.
- Risk proportionality: stricter controls for vendors with data access, privileged infra access, or requests above financial thresholds.

Access & permissions (entitlement lifecycle)
-------------------------------------------
1) Request process

- Use the Access Portal (accessible from the Redwood Console > Tools > Access Request).
- Provide: justification, target systems (service name and environment), requested role (exact RBAC role), duration, and manager approval.
- For long-lived roles (>90 days), supply quarterly business justification and add reviewer in Access Portal.

2) Approval matrix (summary)

- Day-to-day access to non-prod systems: manager approval.
- Prod read-only access: manager + security notification.
- Prod privileged/infra access (SSH, K8s-admin, DB write): manager + security + infra-owner approval.
- Emergency elevated access: break-glass procedure (see Runbook ID: RG-2026-breakglass).

3) Provisioning and deprovisioning

- Provisioning is automated via Okta + Terraform runbooks (Infra-IAC). On approval, provisioning SLA is 2 business days for standard requests, 8 hours for emergency sprints.
- Access expirations are enforced: default 30 days for contractor requests, 90 days for internal hires unless renewed.

4) Periodic review

- Quarterly access attestation: team owners must validate active entitlements and remove stale accounts. Failure to respond triggers automated revocation notices.

Change management
-----------------

Scope: Any modification to production services, infra provisioning, IAM policies, or customer-facing configuration.

Change categories and approval paths:

sections.content:
Purpose

This page is the single index for Redwood Inference’s prospect-facing **Security Evidence Pack** used during the Vertical ABM pilot (and reusable beyond) for regulated workloads (financial services, healthcare, and other compliance-driven buyers).

It describes:

- What artifacts are included (and what we do *not* share)
- How Sales/SEs request access for a prospect
- How Security/GRC shares evidence securely and tracks distribution
- Confidentiality rules and common “gotchas” (SOC 2 handling, retention/data boundary language)

This page is **restricted** because it references the internal sharing process and controlled artifacts.

---

C) Logging, auditability, and access controls

7) **Audit log sample (redacted) + field reference**

- Includes a redacted JSON sample of key audit log event types and a field glossary.
- Typical fields covered:
  - event_time, event_type

- Used during technical deep dives for regulated buyers.

sections.heading: Abm Pilot Security Evidence Pack Index > When to use this evidence pack
sections.content:
When to use this evidence pack

Use the evidence pack when a prospect:

- Requests “proof” beyond the Security FAQ (e.g., **SOC 2**, pen test attestation, encryption diagrams)
- Is moving into **security review**, **procurement**, **POC**, or **Private/Dedicated architecture** discussions
- Requires security documentation before allowing a technical pilot or data access

If the prospect only needs high-level posture statements, start with the **Regulated Workloads Security FAQ** and only escalate to evidence if requested.

- Treat all evidence pack artifacts as **Confidential / Controlled**.
- Do not modify controlled artifacts (SOC 2, formal statements). If you need a tailored statement, request it via GRC.
- Do not make absolute claims (e.g., “HIPAA certified”, “fully compliant with X”) unless explicitly approved in the Security FAQ.
- If a prospect requests a signed attestation, route to **Michael Grant (Legal)** and **Olga Petrov (GRC)**.

- Prospect requests full pen test report or vulnerability details

sections.section_path: Entitlements And Purchase Pathways Playbook 2030
sections.heading: Entitlements And Purchase Pathways Playbook 2030
sections.content:
- Initial intake: vendor submitted via VendorHub, 1 business day acknowledgement.
- Risk assessment: Security performs questionnaire review; expect 5-7 business days for standard vendors, 15-20 days for those handling Restricted data.
- Contracting: Legal drafts/negotiates terms; standard NDA/SOW templates for low-risk vendors. Time: 5–15 business days depending on terms.
- Procurement & finance: vendor setup (W-9/COI), tax classification, payment terms.

Minimum vendor requirements by risk tier:

- Low risk (no data access): PO, standard SOE, vendor contact, invoice cadence.
- Medium risk (limited data access): PO, signed DPA, security questionnaire, SOC2 Type II preferred.
- High risk (customer data or privileged infra access): PO, DPA, SOC2 Type II or penetration test report, system access plan, contractual breach notification clause, indemnity terms.

Offboarding and termination:

- Termination checklist: revoke credentials, recover assets, enforce data return/deletion, final invoice reconciliation, and a post-termination confirmation from vendor. Procurement must retain termination evidence for 7 years.

Travel policy (high level)
-------------------------

Booking: Use Travel Portal (linked from Redwood Console). Lowest reasonable fare policy applies for economy class. Business class requires exec-level pre-approval for travel over 8 hours.

Approvals: Manager approves travel requests in Travel Portal. International travel must include security and people-ops notification if travel is to high-risk countries listed by People Ops.

Per diems and expenses: See ExpenseFlow caps. Receipts required for all items >$25.

Safety and incident reporting:

- In case of an incident while traveling, contact People Ops emergency line and Security: security@redwood.com. All incidents must be reported within 24 hours.

Templates and forms (where to find)
----------------------------------

- Procurement intake form: VendorHub > New Request > Procurement Intake (use template 'Procurement-Intake-v2').
- Data Erasure Request: Redwood Console > Data Requests.
- Change request template: CRB ticket template in Jira (project: RED-CHANGES).
- Access request template: Access Portal (select role and environment).

Example procurement JSON payload (for VendorHub API)
{
  "requestor": "alice@example.com",
  "vendor": "Acme Analytics",
  "amount_usd": "7500",
  "justification": "Production observability for dedicated clusters",
  "budget_tag": "infra-monitoring",
  "required_by": "2027-02-15"
}
Appendix: enforcement and exceptions
-----------------------------------

- Exceptions: Managers may request a documented exception for short-lived needs; exceptions require a written business case and a compliance review.
- Enforcement: Repeated policy violations (e.g., unmanaged vendor engagements or expired privileged access) will be escalated to the employee's manager and may trigger procurement suspension or disciplinary review.

Contacts and ownership
----------------------

- Policy owner: Finance-Legal (policy owner contact: procurement@redwood.com).
- Security contact for vendor risk: security@redwood.com.
- People Ops travel & benefits: people-ops@redwood.com.

Revision history
----------------

- 2026-11-12: Initial draft published by Maya Chen.
- 2026-12-03: Updated procurement thresholds and added emergency change SLA (reviewed by Luis Alvarez and Priya Nair).

-------------------------------

sections.section_path: Entitlements And Purchase Pathways Playbook 2030
sections.heading: Entitlements And Purchase Pathways Playbook 2030
sections.content:
- Standard change: pre-approved, repeatable changes (e.g., routine OS patching via controlled pipeline). Requires change ticket and notification to SRE runbook subscribers.
- Normal change: requires Change Review Board (CRB) approval for higher impact (planned releases that affect SLAs). CRB meets twice weekly.
- Emergency change: immediate fixes that must follow the emergency roll-forward checklist and be retroactively documented in the change ticket.

Change windows and freezes:

- Quarterly freeze: last two business days of each quarter are freeze windows for major releases unless exception approved by CTO and SRE lead.
- High-risk releases: require canary rollout and 30% traffic validation for 24 hours before full rollout.

Change request minimum content (ticket):

1. Change owner and contact
2. Rollout and rollback plan with automation steps
3. Expected impact and post-deploy validation steps
4. Backout criteria and timeline
5. Stakeholder notification list

SLOs and audit

- All normal changes must have an associated ticket and be auditable for 12 months.
- Emergency changes must be documented within 48 hours.

Data management and classification
--------------------------------
Classification levels:

- Public: content intended for public consumption.
- Internal: operational information not intended for external distribution.
- Confidential: employee, business, or customer information that requires access controls.
- Restricted: regulated or highly sensitive data (PII, payment data, health data) that requires encryption at rest and in transit, strict access controls, and audit logging.

Handling rules (summary):

- Confidential & Restricted: store only in approved systems (Redwood Console vaults, encrypted S3 with KMS). No vendor transfer without security and legal sign-off.
- Data retention: default retention for logs is 90 days; for customer-facing telemetry retention follows contractual obligations.

Template Clauses (common redlines and recommended language)

3) Escrow/KMS: "For on-prem or model-hosting arrangements where customer datasets or model weights may be subject to e-discovery or regulatory requests, vendor must provide an escrow arrangement or KMS integration documented in Schedule 3."

- Confirm limitation of liability and insurance obligations.

Procurement: Legal Risk Triage & Escalation SOP
Overview
This Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) describes Redwood Inference's end-to-end triage for procurement items that require legal review or cross-functional escalation. The goal is to reduce cycle time, ensure appropriate risk controls for contracting and billing, and provide clear ownership and SLA targets for each review tier.

Scope

- Applies to all vendor engagements, SOWs, license purchases, hardware leases (including GPU reservations), SaaS subscriptions, and professional services agreements initiated via Procurement.
- Excludes low-value purchases that follow the corporate purchasing card (P-card) policy (see Finance policy: /confluence/finance-and-legal/procurement/p-card-guidelines).

Definitions
1) Low-risk procurement: Purchase value <$25k, no data access, vendor uses standard market terms, no cross-border data transfer.
2) Medium-risk procurement: $25k–$250k, includes limited data access (non-sensitive), or requires limited bespoke terms (payment schedules, warranty clarifications).
3) High-risk procurement: >$250k, access to customer data or models, on-prem or network connectivity required, escrow/KMS requirements, change to indemnity/limitation clauses, or vendor requested data residency exceptions.
4) Contracting Owner: Procurement lead assigned to the purchase.
5) Legal Triage Owner: Commercial counsel assigned to initial review.

Decision Matrix (quick reference)
| Value band | Data access | Special clauses requested | Initial path | SLA (initial review) | Escalation

| --- | --- | --- | --- | ---: | --- |

| <$25k | None | Standard T&C | Procurement approval | 2 business days | Procurement Manager
| <$25k | Non-sensitive | Minor clarifications | Procurement + Legal FYI | 3 business days | Legal (if changes requested)
| $25k–$250k | Non-sensitive | Payment / warranty edits | Legal triage | 5 business days | Senior Counsel
| >$250k or any sensitive data | Any | Any bespoke confidentiality / KMS / escrow | Legal + Security + Finance | 10 business days | GC + Head of Procurement + Security

Procedure (step-by-step)

sections.section_path: Procurement Legal Risk Escalation Sop 2026
sections.heading: Procurement Legal Risk Escalation Sop 2026
sections.content:
1. Procurement Request Intake
   a. Requestor opens a PR in the Procurement system (Jira/Workday) with required attachments: vendor quote, SOW, standard T&C, and vendor risk questionnaire.
   b. Procurement Owner tags the request with one of the risk bands and assigns Contracting Owner.
2. Automated Pre-checks (Procurement)
   a. Validate vendor is in the approved vendor list and has completed KYC.
   b. Run vendor risk scan (third-party risk tool) — attach report.
3. Legal Triage (Commercial Counsel)
   a. Counsel performs 3-screen review: (1) identify material exposures (indemnity, liability caps, warranty, IP, data access); (2) verify billing & rev-rec implications (see RevRec checklist below); (3) recommend standard redlines.
   b. Counsel applies template responses from the Clause Library for common items (data transfer addendum, limited indemnity, software license grant).
4. Cross-functional Review (when required)
   a. Security: Required for any network connectivity, data access, KMS/escrow, or on-prem deployments. Security lead must sign off within 3 business days of assignment.
   b. Finance: Required for contracts with atypical billing cadence, revenue-sharing, or subscription modifications; Finance must verify revenue recognition implications and billing trigger alignment.
   c. Product/Platform: Required for technical SOW accuracy and operational acceptance criteria for managed services.
5. Negotiation & Approval
   a. Procurement leads negotiations on non-legal commercial terms; legal negotiates legal language.
   b. For high-risk contracts, the final approval requires sign-off from Head of Procurement, Commercial Counsel, and Director of Finance.
6. Execution & Post-signature Controls
   a. Store executed contract in the contract repository (DocuSign + ContractDB) and tag with metadata (see Contract Metadata section).
   b. Trigger supplier onboarding checklists: finance onboarding (AP routing), security onboarding (vulnerability scan), and ops onboarding (service acceptance).

Contract Metadata (required fields stored in ContractDB)

- contract_id: unique Redwood identifier (e.g., RDW-CTR-2026-000123)
- vendor_legal_name
- purchasing_owner: "team/person"
- commercial_owner: "Procurement lead"
- legal_owner: "Commercial counsel"
- start_date / end_date / renewal_terms
- not_to_exceed_value / committed_spend_line_items
- billing_trigger: invoicing cadence and event that triggers rev-rec (see billing examples)
- data_classification_and_controls: none | non-sensitive | regulated | restricted
- kyc_status: complete | incomplete
- escrow_or_kms_required: yes | no
- confidentiality: internal | restricted | customer-only
- signed_copy_link: internal URL to storage

Revenue Recognition & Billing Checklist (Finance items to confirm before legal approval)

- Identify performance obligations and the billing trigger for each (e.g., access to API endpoints vs. delivery of physical hardware).
- Confirm whether contract changes the timing of revenue recognition (advance payments, non-refundable fees, milestone billing).
- Map invoicing cadence to subscription terms; attach billing examples: 
  Example 1: Monthly subscription — bill in arrears on 1st of following month; revenue recognized ratably over month.
  Example 2: Annual prepay — bill at execution; revenue recognized ratably over 12 months.
  Example 3: Hardware + installation SOW — hardware recognized at delivery; installation revenue recognized over acceptance period (SOW acceptance).

Service Level Targets for Reviews

- Procurement initial intake validation: 1 business day.
- Legal initial triage (see Decision Matrix): 2–10 business days depending on band.
- Security review when required: 3 business days.
- Complete negotiated contract to signature for medium-risk: target 15 business days; high-risk: target 30 business days.

Escalation Contacts

Page 2: Enablement guide (Console + API/SDK)

**Proposed title:** “Enable a quantization profile for a route”

**Required elements**

  1) Navigate to Route → Performance/Optimize → Quantization

sections.section_path: Quantization Profiles Customer Docs Plan > Product language and terminology
sections.heading: Quantization Profiles Customer Docs Plan > Product language and terminology
sections.content:
Product language and terminology

We need consistent, customer-friendly wording:

- **Quantization profile**: A versioned, Redwood-validated configuration for running a specific model variant using a specific quantization method/precision combination.
- **Profile library**: The set of published profiles per model variant. Customers choose a profile for a route.
- **Route-level enablement**: Profiles are enabled per route, not globally for all tenant traffic (v1).
- **Fallback**: If a request is incompatible (hardware/sequence length constraints) or profile application fails safe checks, Redwood serves using baseline precision for that request (or route) while emitting an event.

Avoid ambiguous language:

- Avoid saying “Redwood automatically picks the best profile.”
- Avoid “lossless” claims. Use “aims to preserve quality” and emphasize eval/monitoring.

sections.section_path: Quantization Profiles Customer Docs Plan > Open questions
sections.heading: Quantization Profiles Customer Docs Plan > Open questions
sections.content:
Open questions

1. **Alias semantics:** Will we expose “recommended/latest” aliases in v1 GA or only pinned profile IDs/versions? If aliases exist, we must document how we prevent silent changes (e.g., aliases only change on customer action vs Redwood updates).
2. **Customer-facing compatibility matrix:** What is the minimum viable matrix we can keep current without excessive operational load? (Proposal: publish for top 10 models + major GPU classes first.)
3. **What can we safely publish about quality thresholds?** We should align with Applied ML on whether to include specific numeric deltas or keep it as qualitative guidance.
4. **Request metadata surface:** What is the final customer-visible mechanism to confirm applied profile (headers, response fields, trace attribute)? This must be stable.

sections.content:
Audience and use cases

**Primary audiences**

- Software engineers and ML engineers integrating Redwood routes who want to reduce cost/token.
- Platform teams managing production change control (audit logs, RBAC, rollbacks).

**Customer use cases we need to support in docs**

1. Enable an approved quantization profile for a single route (hosted API).
2. Enable profile for a route with region/tier constraints (Dedicated + multi-region hosted).
3. Validate quality and latency before expanding traffic.
4. Diagnose output changes, elevated fallback rate, or latency regressions.
5. Roll back (route-level disable; global kill-switch is internal-only but mention its existence at a high level).

sections.section_path: Quantization Profiles Customer Docs Plan > Information architecture (public docs) > Page 4: Evaluation best practices
sections.heading: Quantization Profiles Customer Docs Plan > Information architecture (public docs) > Page 4: Evaluation best practices
sections.content:
Page 4: Evaluation best practices

**Proposed title:** “How to evaluate quality and latency before rollout”

**Customer-friendly guidance**

- Suggested evaluation approach:
  - Identify representative prompts (production samples + edge cases).
  - Run baseline vs profile-enabled comparisons.
  - Use A/B sampling (e.g., 1–5% traffic) with a rollback threshold.

- What to measure
  - Quality: task-specific metrics (pass@k, exact match, ranking metrics) + human review where appropriate.
  - Latency: p50/p95 decode latency and time-to-first-token.
  - Cost: cost/token and throughput.

- Rollout strategy
  1) Enable in staging on a non-critical route
  2) Canary in production (small % traffic)
  3) Expand gradually with monitoring

- Provide explicit “stop conditions”
  - Elevated fallback rate
  - Increased error rate
  - Statistically meaningful quality regression on a defined slice

**Note:** We cannot publish Redwood’s internal thresholds verbatim if they are considered sensitive, but we can publish recommended guardrails (e.g., “predefine acceptable deltas and require sign-off”). We will align with Selene Huang (quality guardrails) on what’s safe to disclose.

sections.section_path: Quantization Profiles Customer Docs Plan > Information architecture (public docs) > Page 5: Troubleshooting + rollback
sections.heading: Quantization Profiles Customer Docs Plan > Information architecture (public docs) > Page 5: Troubleshooting + rollback
sections.content:
Page 5: Troubleshooting + rollback

**Proposed title:** “Troubleshooting quantization profiles”

**Structure: symptom → likely cause → how to confirm → resolution**

Required symptoms:

- Console says profile is incompatible
  - Common causes: wrong model variant, unsupported GPU class, context length exceeds profile limit.
  - Resolution: choose another profile; reduce max tokens/context; use baseline.

- Output quality changed unexpectedly
  - Confirm: compare baseline vs profile, check whether fallback occurred (mixed behavior can look inconsistent).
  - Resolution: disable profile; run eval; contact support with request IDs.

- p95 latency increased
  - Confirm: look at per-route latency panels; check TTFT vs decode; check batching/caching changes.
  - Resolution: disable profile; adjust route concurrency/batching; consult Redwood support.

- Elevated fallback rate
  - Confirm: dashboard panel + route events.
  - Likely causes: requests exceed profile constraints; region/GPU mismatch; deployment drift.
  - Resolution: tighten route constraints; pick compatible profile; disable.

- 5xx errors after enabling
  - Confirm: error class; check if errors correlate with specific profile version.
  - Resolution: disable; provide audit event ID and request IDs to support.

Rollback instructions (customer-actionable)

- Disable at route level (Console + API snippet).
- Verify disablement and that requests are using baseline.

We should also include:

- “What information to include in a support ticket” checklist:
  - Org/tenant ID
  - Route name/ID
  - Model + variant
  - Profile ID/version
  - Region/deployment mode
  - Approx timeframe
  - Request IDs/traces
  - Observed metrics (fallback rate, p95 latency)

sections.section_path: Quantization Profiles Customer Docs Plan > Success criteria (docs)
sections.heading: Quantization Profiles Customer Docs Plan > Success criteria (docs)
sections.content:
Success criteria (docs)

- ≥80% of beta design partner enablements completed without synchronous Redwood help.
- Reduction in support tickets that are purely “how do I enable/disable?” (shift to higher-signal issues).
- Median time-to-rollback for customers (self-serve) < 10 minutes after following docs.

sections.heading: Quantization Profiles Customer Docs Plan > Information architecture (public docs) > Page 3: Compatibility + limitations
sections.content:
Page 3: Compatibility + limitations

**Proposed title:** “Compatibility, constraints, and fallback behavior”

**Include**

- What compatibility depends on:
  - Model ID + model variant
  - Deployment mode (Hosted/Dedicated/Private as applicable)
  - GPU class/SKU (expressed as customer-friendly names)
  - Max context / sequence length limits
  - Region constraints (if/when supported in route policy)

- Customer-facing compatibility matrix
  - If we can’t maintain a full matrix, we must at least publish:
    - “Supported GPUs by profile type” (e.g., INT8 supported on X, FP8 on Y)
    - “Max supported context per profile” for popular models
  - Decide format: table in docs + downloadable CSV updated weekly (recommended).

- Fallback semantics
  - Define what happens when incompatible:
    - If enablement time: block with clear error and remediation.
    - If request time: safe fallback to baseline; emit a signal; no infinite retry loops.

- Limitations / known caveats
  - Output differences are possible.
  - Some profiles may be labeled “Experimental” with narrower guardrails.
  - If customers pin to a profile version, it won’t change unless they update.
  - If we ever add “recommended” aliases, document that aliases may move and how we prevent silent changes (see Open Questions).

sections.section_path: Cross Role Tool Access Governance And Self Service Handbook 2027
sections.heading: Cross Role Tool Access Governance And Self Service Handbook 2027
sections.content:
- Emergency access (e.g., incident mitigation) uses the Fast-Track Exception flow:
  1) Requester files an incident-tagged access request with justification and incident ID.
  2) On-call approver (manager or designated incident commander) may grant a 4-hour temporary token via the Access Portal.
  3) Security must be notified within 1 hour and will follow up to convert to a formal exception or revoke.
- All emergency grants are logged and retroactively reviewed as part of the incident postmortem.

7) Deprovisioning and Offboarding

- Standard offboarding timeline:
  - Day 0: account disabled for interactive access within 4 hours of HR offboarding signal.
  - Day 1: short-lived API tokens invalidated; persistent service accounts rotated if necessary.
  - Day 7: cloud console roles removed; scheduled backup of any outstanding owner responsibilities.
- Manager responsibility: reassign ownership before final removal.
- Audit: people-ops runs weekly deprovisioning reports, security runs monthly verification.

8) Periodic Access Reviews

- Quarterly review for all high-risk roles.
- Biannual review for medium-risk.
- Annual review for low-risk.
- Review process: automated report produced by Access Portal -> owner validates or initiates deprovisioning -> people-ops enforces changes within 7 business days.

9) Tool Onboarding Checklist (for Tool Owners)

1. Identify required roles and map to least-privilege sets.
2. Document roles in the Role Catalog section of the owner page.
3. Define which roles are self-service vs require approval.
4. Provide an onboarding runbook with contact points and SLOs.
5. Register tool owner and escalation email in the Access Portal.
6. Provide a test account and verification steps for the access flow.

10) Technical Integration Patterns

- Recommended: integrate tool with SSO and SCIM for group sync.
- Fallback: if SCIM unavailable, implement an API-based provisioning endpoint with scoped tokens and change tracking.
- Example access request payload (JSON):

{
  "requester": "user@redwood.com",
  "tool": "grafana-prod",
  "role": "viewer",
  "justification": "Oncall rotation",
  "expires_at": "2026-02-28T23:59:00Z"
}

- Example CLI (Access Portal CLI):

$ rwd-access request --tool grafana-prod --role viewer --justification "oncall"

11) Monitoring, Auditing and KPIs

- KPIs to track: time-to-provision (median), percent self-service, number of active exceptions, time-to-deprovision after offboard.
- Reporting cadence: weekly provisioning dashboard, monthly audit exports (CSV) to security vault.
- Audit checks: verify no more than 5% of production-admin grants are older than 30 days without re-approval.

12) De-Escalation and Dispute Resolution

- If a manager or user disputes a grant or removal, escalate to people-ops with the ticket ID. People-ops will convene: manager, tool owner, and security to adjudicate within 5 business days.

13) Sample Runbook: Granting Prod-Read Access (Manager-Approved)

1. Manager submits request in Access Portal with business justification.
2. Portal routes to tool owner notification and manager approval.
3. On approval, provisioning job runs (SCIM or API).
4. Access granted; audit log written; notification sent to requester and manager.
5. After 90 days, system creates a renewal task for the manager.

14) Implementation Roadmap (next 18 months)

- Q2 2026: Complete SCIM integrations for top 10 tools.
- Q3 2026: Launch delegated team-admin roles for large product groups.
- Q4 2026: Build exception analytics dashboard and automatic expiration nudges.

entitlements-and-purchase-pathways-playbook-2030
Overview
=======

Purpose: This playbook consolidates company-wide procedures for entitlements (access and permissions), change governance, data handling expectations, procurement and expense approvals, vendor lifecycle management, and travel approvals. It is intended for all Redwood employees and contractors who request or approve resources, commit changes to production, or manage third-party relationships.

Scope: Applies to hosted, dedicated, and private deployment teams, platform and infra teams, procurement interactions, people-ops travel arrangements, and any third party that will access Redwood systems or customer data.

Quick links: Access Portal (Okta + Access Request), VendorHub (procurement back-end), ExpenseFlow (employee expenses), Legal intake form, Security questionnaire (security.redwood.local).

Roles and responsibilities
--------------------------

- Requestor: person initiating an access, change, purchase, vendor relationship, or travel booking. Responsible for completeness and business justification.
- Manager/Approver: direct manager who validates business need and budget availability.
- Approving Officer (Finance/Procurement): validates procurement thresholds, tax, and vendor classification.
- Security Reviewer: evaluates data access risk and mandatory controls (SOC2, encryption, contract clauses).
- Legal Reviewer: reviews contract terms for vendor agreements above threshold or with custom IP/data terms.
- Proc Ops (Vendor Onboarding): completes supplier setup, obtains W-9/COI as applicable.

Principles
----------

- Least privilege: grant minimal entitlements required for the job and set automatic expiration where practical.
- Segregation of duties: approval and provisioning paths must not be owned by the same individual for medium/high risk requests.
- Evidence-first approvals: all approvals must be attached to the request in VendorHub or Access Portal.
- Risk proportionality: stricter controls for vendors with data access, privileged infra access, or requests above financial thresholds.

Access & permissions (entitlement lifecycle)
-------------------------------------------
1) Request process

- Use the Access Portal (accessible from the Redwood Console > Tools > Access Request).
- Provide: justification, target systems (service name and environment), requested role (exact RBAC role), duration, and manager approval.
- For long-lived roles (>90 days), supply quarterly business justification and add reviewer in Access Portal.

2) Approval matrix (summary)

- Day-to-day access to non-prod systems: manager approval.
- Prod read-only access: manager + security notification.
- Prod privileged/infra access (SSH, K8s-admin, DB write): manager + security + infra-owner approval.
- Emergency elevated access: break-glass procedure (see Runbook ID: RG-2026-breakglass).

3) Provisioning and deprovisioning

- Provisioning is automated via Okta + Terraform runbooks (Infra-IAC). On approval, provisioning SLA is 2 business days for standard requests, 8 hours for emergency sprints.
- Access expirations are enforced: default 30 days for contractor requests, 90 days for internal hires unless renewed.

4) Periodic review

- Quarterly access attestation: team owners must validate active entitlements and remove stale accounts. Failure to respond triggers automated revocation notices.

Change management
-----------------

Scope: Any modification to production services, infra provisioning, IAM policies, or customer-facing configuration.

Change categories and approval paths:
