sections.section_path: Billing Meter Spec Hosted Api Tokens And Requests > 7. Token metering rules > 7.1 Canonical tokenization
sections.heading: Billing Meter Spec Hosted Api Tokens And Requests > 7. Token metering rules > 7.1 Canonical tokenization
sections.content:
7. Token metering rules

7.1 Canonical tokenization

Token counting uses the tokenizer associated with the **resolved billed model**.

- If routing selects a different compatible model variant than requested (fallback), the billed tokens MUST reflect the billed model’s tokenizer.
- Usage API must return both `requested_model` and `billed_model` when they differ.

sections.section_path: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Definitions (approved internal meanings) > 1) “Token”
sections.heading: Usage Based Pricing Legal Terms Playbook > Definitions (approved internal meanings) > 1) “Token”
sections.content:
1) “Token”

**Token** means a discrete unit of text as processed by the applicable model’s tokenization scheme. Tokenization is model-dependent.

Important internal positions:

- Token counts are **model-specific** and may differ between models and versions.
- For chat-style endpoints, token counts may include system/developer messages, tool call payloads, and structured output formatting as applicable.
- We support (and prefer to contract around) **billed tokens** as the invoicing unit, rather than raw “input + output tokens,” because billed tokens reflects caching/discounting rules.

Recommended terminology:

- **Input Tokens / Prompt Tokens**: tokens attributable to the request context provided by the customer.
- **Output Tokens / Completion Tokens**: tokens generated by the model in response.
- **Billed Tokens**: the token quantity used for billing after applying billing rules (e.g., caching adjustments, promotional discounts, free-tier inclusion), as shown on the invoice and/or usage reports.

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Quick triage checklist (Support)
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Quick triage checklist (Support)
sections.content:
Quick triage checklist (Support)

1) Confirm this is an overload-protection response (see “How to recognize” below).
2) Verify the customer is following recommended retry/backoff (or advise them to change).
3) Collect required debug info (IDs, time window, region/model, response headers).
4) Determine if this is expected transient overload vs a bug/misconfig (missing Retry-After, incorrect status mapping, fallback not triggering).
5) Escalate to Eng Oncall when criteria are met (see “When to escalate”).

sections.section_path: Metering To Invoice Reconciliation Playbook > Step-by-step reconciliation procedure > Step 7 — Drill-down playbook by failure mode > D) Missing/incorrect dimensions (region/model/route)
sections.heading: Metering To Invoice Reconciliation Playbook > Step-by-step reconciliation procedure > Step 7 — Drill-down playbook by failure mode > D) Missing/incorrect dimensions (region/model/route)
sections.content:
D) Missing/incorrect dimensions (region/model/route)

Signals:

- Null dimension rate > threshold
- Drift appears as “missing” in one bucket and “extra” in another

Actions:

- Determine whether ledger applies defaults/mappings that usage events do not.
- Backfill dimension fields if needed (with Finance approval if it changes customer exports).

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Paging and escalation triggers (when to page SRE / Infra) > Page Infra/Fleet On-Call when any of the following is true (often in parallel)
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Paging and escalation triggers (when to page SRE / Infra) > Page Infra/Fleet On-Call when any of the following is true (often in parallel)
sections.content:
Page Infra/Fleet On-Call when any of the following is true (often in parallel)

- GPU/node health signals indicate failures, evictions, ECC errors, or repeated container restarts.
- Saturation: GPU utilization pinned while throughput drops (suspected contention, thermal throttling, network bottleneck).
- Capacity: the deployment appears mapped to the wrong pool/shape or lacks the expected headroom.
- Region-wide capacity constraint impacting Dedicated pools.

sections.section_path: Sup 18421 Enterprise 429 Spike After Priority Routing Rollout > Steps to reproduce (customer)
sections.heading: Sup 18421 Enterprise 429 Spike After Priority Routing Rollout > Steps to reproduce (customer)
sections.content:
Steps to reproduce (customer)

1) Send ~800–1200 RPS bursts to /v1/chat/completions with streaming disabled.
2) Concurrently send embedding bursts (~2k RPS) during the same window.
3) Observe 429 rates rising from <0.2% to 6–12% during bursts.

sections.section_path: Billing Meter Spec Hosted Api Tokens And Requests > 4. Definitions > 4.1 Core terms
sections.heading: Billing Meter Spec Hosted Api Tokens And Requests > 4. Definitions > 4.1 Core terms
sections.content:
4. Definitions

4.1 Core terms

- **Request:** A single client call to a Hosted API endpoint.
- **Attempt:** A server-side execution attempt for a request (may include fallback routing or server-side retry).
- **Prompt tokens (input_tokens):** Tokens attributable to the serialized input to the model for an attempt.
- **Completion tokens (output_tokens):** Tokens generated by the model for an attempt.
- **Raw tokens:** input_tokens + output_tokens as observed for an attempt.
- **Billed tokens:** Token quantity used for charging. May differ from raw tokens when cache hits or policy-based adjustments apply.
- **Cache hit:** A case where a prefix/KV cache or response cache results in reduced compute for the request. Depending on pricing policy, cache-hit tokens may be billed differently (see §7).

sections.section_path: Metering To Invoice Reconciliation Playbook > Step-by-step reconciliation procedure > Step 7 — Drill-down playbook by failure mode > G) Timezone boundary mismatch (exports)
sections.heading: Metering To Invoice Reconciliation Playbook > Step-by-step reconciliation procedure > Step 7 — Drill-down playbook by failure mode > G) Timezone boundary mismatch (exports)
sections.content:
G) Timezone boundary mismatch (exports)

Signals:

- Customer sees day-over-day spikes at midnight local time

Actions:

- Confirm invoice period is UTC.
- If customer requires a local-time export, provide it as an informational report but do not change invoice basis unless contract specifies.

sections.content:
4) Check the Dedicated Throughput dashboard for that deployment

sections.section_path: Sup 18421 Enterprise 429 Spike After Priority Routing Rollout > Initial support response (guidance provided)
sections.heading: Sup 18421 Enterprise 429 Spike After Priority Routing Rollout > Initial support response (guidance provided)
sections.content:
Initial support response (guidance provided)

- Confirmed that the new system returns distinct reason codes and customers should key their retry/backoff behavior on:
  - "quota_exceeded" (respect quota windows; reduce steady-state rate)
  - "overload_protection_admission" (transient overload; respect Retry-After; use exponential backoff + jitter)
- Recommended changes:
  - Use exponential backoff with full jitter; cap concurrency; do not retry immediately.
  - Honor Retry-After; treat 429 as a signal to shed load client-side.

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > How to interpret and use correlation IDs > How Support should use them internally
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > How to interpret and use correlation IDs > How Support should use them internally
sections.content:
How Support should use them internally

- Paste the ID(s) into the internal log search / tracing tool.
- Capture:
  - the **error.code**
  - the **route** (e.g., `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/responses`, embeddings endpoint)
  - the **region** (requested + served)
  - whether **Retry-After** was present and its value

If Support cannot access dashboards/tracing, escalate with the IDs and all details in the escalation template below.

sections.section_path: Billing Meter Spec Hosted Api Tokens And Requests > 6. Request counting rules (request_count) > 6.3 Streaming and request_count
sections.heading: Billing Meter Spec Hosted Api Tokens And Requests > 6. Request counting rules (request_count) > 6.3 Streaming and request_count
sections.content:
6.3 Streaming and request_count

For streaming endpoints:

- `request_count` is emitted once per **deduped request**.
- If the client disconnects mid-stream, the request still counts if billing conditions are met (see §7.4).

sections.section_path: Metering To Invoice Reconciliation Playbook > Thresholds and SLOs (default) > Correctness/drift
sections.heading: Metering To Invoice Reconciliation Playbook > Thresholds and SLOs (default) > Correctness/drift
sections.content:
Correctness/drift

All drift thresholds are computed at the reconciliation grain.

- **Daily drift (Hosted API tokens):** absolute drift ≤ **0.25%** AND ≤ **$250** per account-day
- **Weekly drift:** absolute drift ≤ **0.10%** AND ≤ **$500** per account-week
- **Dedicated GPU-seconds:** absolute drift ≤ **0.20%** AND ≤ **$500** per account-day

sections.section_path: Billing Meter Spec Hosted Api Tokens And Requests > 7. Token metering rules > 7.2 Prompt tokens (prompt_tokens)
sections.heading: Billing Meter Spec Hosted Api Tokens And Requests > 7. Token metering rules > 7.2 Prompt tokens (prompt_tokens)
sections.content:
7.2 Prompt tokens (prompt_tokens)

Prompt tokens represent the total tokens in the model input for the billed attempt, including:

- System/developer/user messages (for chat)
- Tool schema/function definitions provided by the client (for tool calling)
- Any platform-inserted control tokens required by the serving runtime for the endpoint format

Rules:

- Count prompt tokens once for the billed attempt.
- If internal reformatting occurs (e.g., OpenAI-compatible -> canonical), token counting is performed after canonicalization.

sections.section_path: Metering To Invoice Reconciliation Playbook > Step-by-step reconciliation procedure > Step 5 — Compute drift and classify discrepancies
sections.heading: Metering To Invoice Reconciliation Playbook > Step-by-step reconciliation procedure > Step 5 — Compute drift and classify discrepancies
sections.content:
Step 5 — Compute drift and classify discrepancies

Join usage-event aggregates to ledger aggregates and compute:

- Token drift: (evt_billed_tokens - led_billed_tokens)
- Request drift
- Amount drift (if ledger contains pricing)

Classification (pick one primary label):
1) **Late-arriving usage events** (events present after ledger cut; freshness breach)
2) **Duplicate events / idempotency regression** (evt > ledger, duplicates elevated)
3) **Retry/fallback double-count** (streaming + server retry; known failure mode)
4) **Missing dimensions** (region/model/route nulls causing mis-bucketing)
5) **Token definition mismatch** (raw vs billed tokens; tool calls/structured output)
6) **Embeddings batch accounting bug** (per-input vs per-request counting)
7) **Timezone boundary mismatch** (customer export vs ledger day boundaries)
8) **Expected business rule difference** (e.g., free tier, minimums, rounding rules)

Decision rule:

- If drift is **within thresholds** and no systematic bias is observed: record as pass.
- If drift is **outside thresholds**: proceed to Step 6.

---

sections.section_path: Billing Meter Spec Hosted Api Tokens And Requests > 17. Changelog
sections.heading: Billing Meter Spec Hosted Api Tokens And Requests > 17. Changelog
sections.content:
17. Changelog

- 2026-02-07: Initial draft created (v1 scope, streaming + retry rules).
- 2026-02-18: Added tool calling attribution rules and execution_started requirement.
- 2026-02-24: Added explicit mapping to Usage API + invoice conventions; clarified prompt billing on disconnects.

sections.section_path: Billing Meter Spec Hosted Api Tokens And Requests > 7. Token metering rules > 7.4 Billed tokens (billed_tokens)
sections.heading: Billing Meter Spec Hosted Api Tokens And Requests > 7. Token metering rules > 7.4 Billed tokens (billed_tokens)
sections.content:
7.4 Billed tokens (billed_tokens)

`billed_tokens` is the default basis for charging and is computed as:

**billed_tokens = billed_prompt_tokens + billed_completion_tokens**

Unless otherwise specified by pricing policy, the default is:

- `billed_prompt_tokens = prompt_tokens`
- `billed_completion_tokens = completion_tokens`

Billing behavior by outcome:

- **Successful 2xx:** bill billed_tokens per above.
- **Client disconnect during streaming:** bill tokens actually generated and sent prior to disconnect (no future/estimated tokens). Request is billable if at least one token was streamed OR if prompt processing completed and policy bills prompt tokens (current policy: bill prompt tokens if the model began execution; see §7.6).
- **Server error after tokens produced:** bill tokens produced (prompt + completion as applicable). Must not bill tokens for attempts that never started execution.

sections.section_path: Metering To Invoice Reconciliation Playbook > Step-by-step reconciliation procedure > Step 7 — Drill-down playbook by failure mode > E) Token definition mismatch (raw vs billed)
sections.heading: Metering To Invoice Reconciliation Playbook > Step-by-step reconciliation procedure > Step 7 — Drill-down playbook by failure mode > E) Token definition mismatch (raw vs billed)
sections.content:
E) Token definition mismatch (raw vs billed)

Signals:

- Customer compares invoice to raw token counts from SDK logs
- Tool calls / structured output present

Actions:

- Confirm invoice uses **billed_tokens** per meter spec.
- Ensure customer usage export includes billed_tokens and is documented.
- If mismatch is due to OpenAI-compatible endpoint semantics: coordinate with Product + Docs.

sections.section_path: Billing Meter Spec Hosted Api Tokens And Requests > 3. Principles (must-haves)
sections.heading: Billing Meter Spec Hosted Api Tokens And Requests > 3. Principles (must-haves)
sections.content:
3. Principles (must-haves)

1. **Single source of truth for invoicing:** The billing ledger is the authoritative source for invoice totals. Telemetry events are authoritative for debugging and reconciliation.
2. **Idempotent billing:** Retries/fallbacks must not produce double-charges when the customer provided a stable idempotency key.
3. **Customer-observable semantics:** Usage API must explain billed vs raw tokens and any cache attribution.
4. **Consistency across endpoints:** OpenAI-compatible endpoints must align token counting semantics with the canonical Redwood endpoints (modulo model/tokenizer differences).
5. **Change control:** Any meter logic change requires shadow compare and Finance approval before impacting invoices.

---

sections.section_path: Metering To Invoice Reconciliation Playbook > Step-by-step reconciliation procedure > Step 2 — Confirm dedupe/idempotency posture
sections.heading: Metering To Invoice Reconciliation Playbook > Step-by-step reconciliation procedure > Step 2 — Confirm dedupe/idempotency posture
sections.content:
Step 2 — Confirm dedupe/idempotency posture

Many “overbilling” reports are actually duplicate-event issues during retries/backfills.

Controls:

- Use **deduped usage events** view for aggregates (never raw events) unless investigating.
- Verify dedupe key includes request_id + attempt_id + idempotency_key (as applicable).

Common symptoms:

- Drift spikes aligned to deploys
- Drift concentrated in streaming endpoints
- Duplicate rate increases in one region/cluster

---

sections.section_path: Billing Meter Spec Hosted Api Tokens And Requests > 2. Scope > 2.1 Included surfaces
sections.heading: Billing Meter Spec Hosted Api Tokens And Requests > 2. Scope > 2.1 Included surfaces
sections.content:
2. Scope

2.1 Included surfaces

This spec applies to Hosted API endpoints that return model outputs and therefore generate token usage:

- Chat / Responses-style generation endpoints
- Text completion endpoints
- Rerank endpoints **only if** they are billed per token (currently: billed per request; see notes)
- Embeddings endpoints are covered by a separate meter spec (batch semantics differ)

sections.section_path: Metering To Invoice Reconciliation Playbook > Purpose
sections.heading: Metering To Invoice Reconciliation Playbook > Purpose
sections.content:
Purpose

This playbook defines how Redwood Inference reconciles customer invoices back to underlying metering data.

It is designed to:

- Detect billing-impacting metering issues early (daily/weekly) and before invoices are sent (month-end).
- Provide a repeatable, audit-ready trail from: **request logs → usage events → billing ledger → invoice lines → customer usage exports**.
- Standardize discrepancy classification and remediation (forward fixes, credits, backfills) with clear sign-offs.

**Applies to:**

- Hosted API (tokens/requests, embeddings, reranking)
- Dedicated (GPU-seconds)

**Not covered:** tax, FX, payment collection, revenue allocation. For month-end close controls, see *Month-End Close: Usage Reconciliation Checklist*.

---

sections.section_path: Billing Meter Spec Hosted Api Tokens And Requests > 16. Open questions / TODOs
sections.heading: Billing Meter Spec Hosted Api Tokens And Requests > 16. Open questions / TODOs
sections.content:
16. Open questions / TODOs

- Confirm whether any rerank endpoints remain request-billed vs token-billed; update §2.1 and pricing tables accordingly.
- Finalize whether cache-hit billing will remain “full billed tokens” for all 2026 plans; if not, define plan-specific policies and required contract language.
- Confirm dedupe window target (24h vs 7d) with SDK and edge proxy behavior.

---

sections.section_path: Metering To Invoice Reconciliation Playbook > Definitions (canonical)
sections.heading: Metering To Invoice Reconciliation Playbook > Definitions (canonical)
sections.content:
Definitions (canonical)

**Billing Ledger:** The internal finance-grade table used to generate invoice line items. This is the **source of truth for invoicing** once the billing freeze occurs.

**Usage Events:** Telemetry events emitted per request (or per logical request segment) that contain metered quantities (e.g., billed_tokens, requests, cache_hit attribution, gpu_seconds).

**Customer Usage Export / Usage API:** Customer-facing aggregation derived from usage events and/or ledger with documented lag and schema. Used for customer validation and dispute resolution.

**Reconciliation Grain:**

- Hosted API: account_id × usage_date (UTC) × region × model × product_route (chat/completions/embeddings/rerank) × price_plan
- Dedicated: account_id × usage_date (UTC) × pool_id × region × sku

**Freeze Window:** A time after which we stop changing ledger totals for the close period except via an approved adjustment process. (See Finance Slack thread and the month-end checklist.)

---

sections.section_path: Billing Meter Spec Hosted Api Tokens And Requests > 7. Token metering rules > 7.6 When prompt tokens are billable for interrupted requests
sections.heading: Billing Meter Spec Hosted Api Tokens And Requests > 7. Token metering rules > 7.6 When prompt tokens are billable for interrupted requests
sections.content:
7.6 When prompt tokens are billable for interrupted requests

For streaming requests that fail or disconnect:

- If **model execution began** (i.e., prompt was tokenized and submitted to the runtime), then prompt_tokens are billable.
- If the request failed before runtime submission (auth failure, validation error, quota rejection), prompt_tokens are not billable.

Engineering signal:

- `execution_started = true/false` must be present on usage events.

---

sections.section_path: Billing Meter Spec Hosted Api Tokens And Requests > 6. Request counting rules (request_count) > 6.2 Partial success
sections.heading: Billing Meter Spec Hosted Api Tokens And Requests > 6. Request counting rules (request_count) > 6.2 Partial success
sections.content:
6.2 Partial success

If a request returns partial output (e.g., streaming interrupted after some tokens), it is still counted as a request if it is billable per §7.4.

sections.section_path: Sup 48377 Canary Traffic Split Not Matching Config
sections.heading: Sup 48377 Canary Traffic Split Not Matching Config
sections.content:
2025-04-18 16:22 UTC — Dev Patel (Support)
Acknowledged. We’re investigating a potential config propagation issue in us-east. Can you confirm the approximate timestamp when you changed the canary from 25% down to 10% in Console? Also, are you routing with a stable end-user identifier (e.g., user_id) or are requests unkeyed?
2025-04-18 16:36 UTC — Customer (Northstar Support AI)
We changed 25% -> 10% at ~15:52 UTC. We do pass a stable user_id in our app, but we’re not explicitly setting anything rollout-specific. The Console timeline shows the step change succeeded.
Also confirming: eu-west looks closer to 10% based on a quick spot check, but us-east is definitely around ~25%.
2025-04-18 17:05 UTC — Mina Haddad (Smart Routing)
Pulled us-east router logs. Seeing configured_canary_percent=25 for rollout rll_9f3c2d3a on a subset of pods. Others show 10. This is consistent with watch stream disconnect + no periodic resync.

2025-04-18 17:18 UTC — Sean Gallagher (SRE)
Confirmed: config-watch stream errors on router-canary in us-east starting 15:49 UTC. Some pods never re-established watch; they continued serving last known config.

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Signal flow (normative) > Runtime → telemetry → routing/gateway (aggregated)
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Signal flow (normative) > Runtime → telemetry → routing/gateway (aggregated)
sections.content:
Runtime → telemetry → routing/gateway (aggregated)

Runtime exports saturation metrics at pool/cluster granularity:

- scheduler_queue_depth (gauge)
- scheduler_backlog_ms (gauge)
- token_throughput_utilization (0..1)
- kv_cache_pressure (0..1)
- memory_pressure_proxy (0..1)

A telemetry aggregation layer produces:

- per-region/per-model “saturation state” (e.g., normal / elevated / critical)
- smoothed utilization signals (EMA or rolling windows)
- recommended admission modifiers (e.g., suggested shed percent)

Gateway and routing consume **aggregated** signals; they should not consume high-cardinality per-node metrics.

sections.section_path: Adr Hosted Rollout Cohorting And Traffic Splitting > Decision > 6) Fallback behavior and “effective cohort” telemetry
sections.heading: Adr Hosted Rollout Cohorting And Traffic Splitting > Decision > 6) Fallback behavior and “effective cohort” telemetry
sections.content:
6) Fallback behavior and “effective cohort” telemetry

If the intended cohort target cannot be served (e.g., canary model unavailable in a region, or hard failure triggers fallback), the system may serve from an alternate target.

Definitions:

- **intended_cohort:** baseline | canary (result of cohort function)
- **effective_target:** the model/version/config actually used after fallback
- **effective_cohort:** baseline | canary, derived from `effective_target` mapping

Telemetry requirements (must be emitted on every request):

- `rollout_id` (when applicable)
- `intended_cohort` (baseline/canary)
- `effective_cohort` (baseline/canary)
- `fallback_reason` (empty or one of: canary_unavailable, canary_error, capacity, policy_denied, region_failover, other)

Customer-facing metrics views:

- Default charts compare **effective_cohort** baseline vs canary (what was actually served).
- Secondary diagnostics show intended vs effective mismatch counts (to detect “phantom canary”).

Safety rule:

- If the rollout is in a state requiring canary availability guarantees (e.g., higher steps), policy may deny progressing if `canary_unavailable` is non-zero in any eligible region for a configured lookback window (guardrail; tracked separately).

sections.section_path: Pr 18458 Smart Routing Fallback When Breaker Open
sections.heading: Pr 18458 Smart Routing Fallback When Breaker Open
sections.content:
Elena Popov (author): Default is max 1 fallback attempt per request. There’s an internal config to allow 2 only for the (region hop -> model hop) path, but I kept it disabled by default and added a hard cap + test. Added explicit checks: Dedicated/Private never route into Hosted, and Hosted never routes into Dedicated.

Ravi Menon (review): Loop prevention looks good. One concern: you’re using requested_model as a label value in metrics. That can be high cardinality. Please bucket by model family or a normalized name.

Elena Popov (author): Good catch. Updated metrics to use requested_model_family (derived from the catalog) and route_group (chat/embeddings/rerank), and removed raw model IDs. Added a metrics test to enforce label set.

Peter Holtz (embedded SRE, review): What’s the trigger mapping? We should only fallback on overload-derived classifications, not generic 503s from downstream. Also ensure correlation ID is preserved for support.

Elena Popov (author): Added overload_mapping.ts and tests. We only fallback on explicit overload reasons (breaker_open, shed, capacity_unavailable) coming from gateway/runtime classification. Generic downstream 503/500 doesn’t trigger fallback. Correlation ID is preserved; added integration test asserting x-redwood-correlation-id is unchanged.

Rafael Mendes (SRE lead, review): Please add a guard against fallback storms: if the fallback target is also overloaded, we should not keep trying. Make sure we return the overload error and include a stable internal reason for dashboards.

Elena Popov (author): Implemented: if fallback attempt returns overload again, we stop (bounded) and return the overload classification. We emit fallback_exhausted with result=overload and include internal reason in routing decision logs (not as a metric label).

Jordan Lee (policy engine, review): Policy selection should be tenant-aware and route-aware. Ensure we validate that the fallback target is in the allowlist; no implicit compatibility.

Elena Popov (author): Done. Fallback targets must be explicitly configured via policy for the tenant + route selector; we also require compatibility check against catalog (same modality + context window constraints). No implicit model swaps.

Mina Haddad (review): Approved after last changes.
Ravi Menon (review): Approved.
Peter Holtz (review): Approved.

Rafael Mendes (review): Approved; please coordinate canary enablement with SRE runbook.

Elena Popov (author): Will do. Canary enablement tracked under ENG-4821 checklist.

sections.heading: Sup 2892 Fallback Model Not Triggering During Overload
sections.content:
2025-12-09 09:12 PT — Owen Phillips (Support): Customer (Banyan Search) reports fallback not triggering. They configured fallback from 70B -> 8B for overload, but still getting 503 OVERLOADED during peak. Provided correlation IDs and noted they are using streaming on /v1/chat/completions in us-east. Creating ticket and pulling in routing/SRE.
2025-12-09 09:28 PT — Dev Patel (Support readiness): Confirmed this aligns with multiple questions we’re getting since overload protection canary. Linking SUP-2860 as customer also mentioned missing Retry-After on a subset of responses.
2025-12-09 10:05 PT — Peter Holtz (Routing reliability): Looking at traces for rwcorr_01JEMNQZJ5J9P2G6E3R9K8V6M2 — request is being rejected at gateway admission (breaker open) with shed_reason=gateway_concurrency_cap before smart-routing service is called. So fallback cannot occur because routing is not invoked in this path. This matches ADR-015 layering behavior.
2025-12-09 10:19 PT — Peter Holtz (Routing reliability): Confirmed tenant policy has fallback configured, but current behavior: fallback is only evaluated on downstream overload signals (routing/runtime) and certain error codes. Gateway-level shedding is treated as terminal to stop retry storms and protect downstream. We need to align with Product whether we want optional 'fallback_when_breaker_open' semantics.
2025-12-09 10:42 PT — Nikhil Sharma (Product owner, Hosted API): For now, we should be explicit: fallback is best-effort and may not apply when admission control rejects early. However, for enterprise customers we can consider allowing fallback on gateway overload with strict guardrails (bounded retries, no loops, only within compatibility group). Please propose a safe tenant-scoped override if feasible.
2025-12-09 11:10 PT — Rafael Mendes (SRE lead): +1. If we allow fallback on gateway overload, need to ensure we’re not just shifting load to the fallback pool and causing broader instability. Suggest: only allow if fallback targets a different capacity pool/priority class and enforce additional max_tokens cap under duress.
2025-12-10 08:55 PT — Elena Popov (Routing signals integration): Found second issue: in cases where routing is invoked (runtime returns overload), fallback was suppressed for Banyan because loop-prevention saw attempted_models already populated from a previous internal retry. There’s a bug: we’re persisting attempted_models across an internal redirect even when the first attempt never reached the model backend due to a fast-fail overload. That makes the router think it already tried the fallback and stops.
2025-12-10 09:30 PT — Ravi Menon (Fallback routing architect): Root cause seems twofold:
(1) Most failures happen pre-routing (gateway admission sheds) => fallback not possible.
(2) In the subset that reaches routing, a header bookkeeping issue causes loop-prevention to incorrectly block fallback.
Proposed fix: clear attempted_models when the failure is classified as 'admission_shed' vs 'model_attempted'. We can hotfix routing to only append attempted_models after a backend attempt is made.
2025-12-10 10:15 PT — Amara Diallo (Gateway middleware): Confirmed gateway emits overload classification as 'gateway_admission_shed' with reason codes concurrency_cap / token_bucket. It does not call routing service in this path. If we want fallback here, it needs a design change (admission would have to consult routing policy, or we let some fraction through to routing for fallback evaluation).

sections.section_path: Sliced Ingest 429S Dedicated Pool Priority Class Debug Notes
sections.heading: Sliced Ingest 429S Dedicated Pool Priority Class Debug Notes
sections.content:
- A burst-pool weight recalculation occurs on route attach to a dedicated pool.
- Under high fanout (multipart chunk completion callbacks + interactive requests), an attach sequence can read stale bucket state and allow background borrow to temporarily draw from the interactive pool’s credits.
- Separately, when the edge proxy is under callback-related backpressure, it can return 429 before the normal header-enrichment path runs, producing opaque 429s.

Mitigations applied / tested (new since ticket)
Temporary customer-facing workaround (still valid)

- Stagger background multipart uploads and add jitter to the flush window.
- Reduce background upload concurrency (Streamly tested <= 6 workers) during peak interactive usage.

Config change (applied on 2026-03-12 call)

- On dp-132-usw we reserved burst capacity explicitly for interactive routes.
- Updated reservation target: reserve 30% (previous internal suggestion was 20%) of interactive burst credits exclusively for priority=high routes.
- Also separated the route groups so callbacks cannot share the same per-route window as interactive endpoints.

Patch status (updated)

- Rate-limiter fix was originally tracked as “target 1.14.1”.
- As of 2026-03-19: fix is in 1.14.1-rc2 and deployed to canary in us-west dedicated pools (including dp-132-usw) for validation.
- Early results: eliminates the negative token deltas we were seeing during attach bursts; interactive 429 rate decreased materially during the flush window.

Results from customer validation (new)

- 2026-03-12 (trial during scheduled flush):
  - Interactive error rate improved; remaining 429s clustered around callback spikes.
  - Customer confirmed jitter reduced the “all-at-once” failure mode.
- 2026-03-20 (post 1.14.1-rc2 canary + reserved burst config still in place):
  - No sustained 429s for /v1/chat during the 09:00–10:00 window.
  - A few 429s remain on background /v1/embed chunk callbacks (expected; acceptable if retried with backoff).

Open questions / TODO

- Edge proxy: ensure X-RateLimit headers are emitted even under backpressure for 429s originating from rate-limiter.
- Confirm whether signed URL callback endpoints should be assigned their own priority class (e.g., “callback-low”) distinct from generic background.
- Add a regression test: attach burst + high fanout + two priority classes should never allow cross-pool borrow that depletes interactive tokens.

Recommended next steps (updated plan)
1) Keep the reserved interactive burst split (30%) for dedicated pools with mixed interactive + bulk ingest traffic.
2) Promote rate-limiter 1.14.1 from rc to stable after 48h canary observation (watch: rlim.route.tokens.available deltas, interactive 429 rate, attach timing).
3) Edge proxy change: always populate rate-limit headers (or at least a stable error code) for 429s; avoid “opaque 429”.
4) Update the support playbook page with explicit guidance for signed URL callback fanout (jitter + concurrency caps + route separation).
5) Schedule a controlled load test with Streamly AI for 3 consecutive peak windows and collect traces + request IDs for closure criteria.

Notes / timeline crumbs (for internal use)

- 2026-03-10: incident window; strong correlation with cron flush.
- 2026-03-11: Eng suspected weight inversion / attach sequence sensitivity.
- 2026-03-12: customer call; implemented burst reservation + client-side jitter.
- 2026-03-19: 1.14.1-rc2 canary deployed to us-west dedicated.
- 2026-03-20: customer reports no sustained interactive 429s during flush.

Closure criteria (for SUP-864999)

sections.section_path: Sup 48377 Canary Traffic Split Not Matching Config
sections.heading: Sup 48377 Canary Traffic Split Not Matching Config
sections.content:
Sup 48377 Canary Traffic Split Not Matching Config

Source type: jira
Document ID: dsid_94f568e4161d4d78b0db60af2b611746
Release: v1.0.0
Benchmark: EnterpriseRAG-Bench synthetic upstream data
Hosted canary rollout: traffic split in us-east not matching Console config (canary receiving ~25% when set to 10%)

Issue summary
Customer reports that the canary cohort is receiving substantially more traffic than configured for a Hosted route rollout. Console shows canary set to 10% (after being reduced from 25%), but observed canary traffic remains ~22–27% in us-east.

Impact

- Customer sees increased cost/latency regression exposure compared to intended 10% canary.
- Customer is a beta design partner; they are using canary rollouts to validate a new quantization profile.

Customer report (via Support)

- Route: /v1/chat/completions (Hosted)
- Workspace/tenant: northstar-prod
- Rollout name/id (from customer screenshot): rll_9f3c2d3a
- Baseline: llama-3.1-70b-instruct v2025-04-03
- Canary: llama-3.1-70b-instruct v2025-04-16 (q8_0)
- Traffic schedule:
  - Step 1: 1% (ok)
  - Step 2: 5% (ok)
  - Step 3: 25% (ok)
  - Step 4: reduced to 10% (intended rollback in step) — mismatch started here

Environment

- prod, region: us-east
- Customer notes: eu-west appears closer to expected (not fully confirmed), but the majority of their traffic is us-east.

Evidence / reproduction
Customer provided:
1) Request logs showing response header X-Redwood-Rollout-Cohort=canary for ~1/4 of requests while Console shows 10%.
2) A sample of request IDs from a 10-minute window (2025-04-18 16:05–16:15 UTC) where cohort assignment was canary unexpectedly.

Support verification
Pulled routing decision logs in us-east for tenant northstar-prod and rollout rll_9f3c2d3a:

- router_decision fields observed:
  - rollout_id=rll_9f3c2d3a
  - configured_canary_percent=25 (unexpected)
  - console_step_target_percent=10 (expected)
  - cohort=canary
- Log example (redacted):
  - ts=2025-04-18T16:11:03Z request_id=req_01HV... tenant=northstar-prod route=/v1/chat/completions region=us-east rollout_id=rll_9f3c2d3a configured_canary_percent=25 hash_bucket=17 cohort=canary

Initial hypothesis
Smart Routing in us-east is using a stale rollout config (still at 25%) after a step change to 10% was applied in Console/control plane.

Immediate mitigation

- If confirmed stale config on a subset of router pods, restart/roll router deployment in us-east OR force a full config resync.
- Customer can also pause rollout to 0% canary as a safety measure (but report indicates Console changes are not reflecting, so may not be sufficient without router refresh).

Requested from customer

- Exact time they changed from 25% -> 10%
- Whether they use a consistent cohort key (e.g., user_id) vs relying on request_id (for sanity; not expected to cause systematic 2.5x increase, but helpful)

Internal notes
This resembles the beta incident in #incidents where a watch stream drop caused rollout config updates not to propagate to a subset of router pods in us-east. See related incident and upcoming router watchdog/resync change.

Next actions

- (Eng) Verify config watch health + last-applied rollout version on us-east router pods.
- (SRE) Check for watch lag / dropped stream in us-east around 15:40–16:00 UTC.
- (Support) Provide customer with mitigation steps and expected timeline.

sections.section_path: Runbook Rollout Stuck Or Bad Split > Symptoms and likely causes > B) Traffic split mismatch
sections.heading: Runbook Rollout Stuck Or Bad Split > Symptoms and likely causes > B) Traffic split mismatch
sections.content:
B) Traffic split mismatch

**Common symptoms:**

- Observed canary traffic differs significantly from configured percent.
- Split matches overall, but **per-region** mismatch (e.g., us-east OK, eu-west off).
- Mismatch only for streaming requests or retries.
- Canary sees 0% traffic despite non-zero configuration.

**Likely causes:**

- Deterministic cohort key mismatch (unexpected hashing input due to missing user/session key).
- Sticky assignment changes across retries (incorrect retry key usage).
- Multi-region propagation lag (config not yet applied everywhere).
- Data plane caching old route config.
- A/B test or fallback routing policy taking precedence (policy evaluation order).

---

sections.heading: 1740726110 Rollout Split Mismatch Us East
sections.content:
1740726110 Rollout Split Mismatch Us East

Source type: slack

Release: v1.0.0

incidents

Incident Bot: :rotating_light: *INCIDENT* (beta) - "rollout split mismatch" reported by Northstar in us-east. Expected canary=10%, observed ~35-45% over last 10m. Route: `hosted/chat/northstar-support-prod`. Rollout: `rlt_7f2c`.

Rafael Mendes: ack. is this impacting latency/error? customer-facing impact?

Sean Gallagher: error rate stable, but this is a safety issue if the new model is bad. We should treat as sev2-ish for beta. Let's contain.

Mina Haddad: on it. This is traffic-splitting enforcement in data plane. If it’s only us-east, could be hash input mismatch on that cluster or a config propagation issue.

Ravi Menon: +1. First check: are we using the same `cohort_key` in us-east? It’s supposed to be `tenant_id + route_id + stable_user_key` with fallback to request_id if missing.

Emily Zhao: I can check the us-east router build / config digest. Might be running slightly different commit?

Vikram Singh: grabbing router logs for rlt_7f2c in us-east. any recent deploy?

sections.section_path: Adr Hosted Rollout Cohorting And Traffic Splitting > Decision > 4) How configured percentages apply across regions
sections.heading: Adr Hosted Rollout Cohorting And Traffic Splitting > Decision > 4) How configured percentages apply across regions
sections.content:
4) How configured percentages apply across regions

Configured canary percentage is enforced **independently per region**, using the same deterministic function.

Meaning:

- The system does **not** attempt to maintain an exact global canary percentage across all regions combined.
- Each region will converge to the configured percentage for traffic that is routed to that region.

Rationale:

- Avoids cross-region coordination/state and reduces blast radius.
- Aligns canary metrics to the region where traffic was actually served.
- Prevents “global percentage drift” caused by sudden regional routing shifts.

Known consequence:

- If a single end user is routed to different regions on different requests (e.g., due to region failover or customer not using region affinity), they may land in different cohorts because the cohorting is evaluated after region selection and because the available model set can differ by region.

Mitigation:

- Customers who require strict consistency should use region pinning/affinity (where supported) and provide a stable `X-Redwood-Cohort-Key`.

sections.section_path: Pr 18458 Smart Routing Fallback When Breaker Open
sections.heading: Pr 18458 Smart Routing Fallback When Breaker Open
sections.content:
Pr 18458 Smart Routing Fallback When Breaker Open

Source type: github
Document ID: dsid_960a2981de674ebf844f7dc19d2e3cc0
Release: v1.0.0
Benchmark: EnterpriseRAG-Bench synthetic upstream data
Smart Routing: fallback model/region when overload breaker is open (bounded + loop-safe)

Context: As part of the hosted overload protection work, we want to degrade gracefully instead of cascading timeouts when a model/region is saturated. This PR adds a routing-side fallback attempt when the upstream admission layer reports an overload breaker open (or equivalent overload classification).

What this PR does: Implements a fallback resolution step in Smart Routing that can (optionally) route to a compatible fallback model and/or fallback region based on tenant + route policy. Adds strict loop prevention so we don’t bounce between model variants/regions, and bounds fallback attempts to a small fixed number to avoid amplifying load. Also ensures we do not fallback for non-overload failures (e.g., auth, invalid params, quota exceeded).

Key behaviors: (1) Trigger conditions: only when overload classification indicates breaker open / load shed / capacity unavailable (see mapping in code comments); not triggered on generic 5xx. (2) Fallback selection: consults policy engine for allowed fallbacks for the tenant + route + requested model; if none configured, behave as before. (3) Bounded attempts: max 1 fallback per request by default (configurable to 2 for region+model hop, but guarded); stops immediately if fallback target equals original target. (4) Loop prevention: propagates an internal routing context header across internal hops and records visited (model, region) pairs; if the candidate is already visited, we do not attempt it. (5) Observability: emits counters for fallback_attempted, fallback_succeeded, fallback_blocked_loop, and fallback_exhausted; dimensions intentionally low-cardinality (tenant_tier, route_group, requested_model_family, result).

Why routing (not gateway): The gateway admission layer is responsible for shedding early, but only routing knows compatibility constraints and tenant policy for fallback targets. This is consistent with the admission layering guidance (see ADR-015) — the gateway classifies overload; routing decides a safe alternate target; runtime remains the source of saturation signals.

Safety constraints: Dedicated and Private tenants are never routed to Hosted. Hosted self-serve can fallback within Hosted only. Enterprise Hosted can fallback only to configured allowlisted model variants and regions. We also explicitly disallow cross-AZ fallback within a region to avoid hiding infra issues; region fallback is an explicit opt-in.

Testing: Unit tests cover loop prevention, bounded retries, policy deny, and correct trigger mapping. Integration test fakes breaker-open signals and verifies we attempt exactly one fallback and preserve the correlation ID. Perf-canary scenario work is tracked separately.

Follow-ups: (a) tune default max attempts and error mapping once we have canary data; (b) add dashboard panel for fallback rates vs shed rate; (c) document customer-facing behavior once GA’d (docs owned by DevEx/Docs).

- Smart Routing can now attempt policy-configured fallback model/region when overload protection opens a circuit breaker, with bounded retries and loop prevention. No API surface changes; behavior is opt-in via policy.

Mina Haddad (review): Can you clarify the max attempts logic? I want to ensure we can’t end up trying multiple fallbacks and increasing traffic under overload. Also, please confirm we never cross Hosted/Dedicated boundaries.

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Context
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Context
sections.content:
Context

Redwood Inference’s Hosted API sees bursty and highly variable traffic (prompt length variance, streaming concurrency spikes, regional capacity dips). During overload, failures can cascade into:

- Tail-latency blowups (p95/p99), then timeouts
- Elevated 5xx from upstream retry storms and downstream saturation
- Noisy-neighbor effects across tenants and tiers
- Confusing customer experience (timeouts and generic 5xx instead of stable semantics)

We need a layered admission control strategy that:
1) Rejects or degrades traffic early and predictably.
2) Preserves tenant isolation and tier-aware behavior.
3) Avoids feedback loops (e.g., shedding causing routing thrash, or routing failover amplifying load elsewhere).
4) Produces consistent customer-facing overload errors (see ADR-014).

This ADR defines **where circuit breakers and load shedding “live”** across the request path (Gateway → Routing → Runtime) and how signals flow.

sections.section_path: Burst Capacity Retro Notes
sections.heading: Burst Capacity Retro Notes
sections.content:
- Symptom: customer asked why burst line item didn’t match dashboard usage; we found ~1.8–2.3% overcount in a specific retry pattern.
- Root cause: metering event emitted pre-idempotency; retried requests emitted duplicate usage increments.
- Fix: idempotency keys + reconciliation checks.
- Ref: GitHub:redwood/pr-24108, Jira:SUP-28488

D) Noisy neighbor scare (tail latency increase for a non-burst tenant)

- Symptom: p95/p99 latency increase for a non-burst tenant correlated with another tenant’s burst window.
- What we learned: even if pool isolation is “logical,” shared control-plane/routing and some shared fleet components can cause tail amplification under saturation.
- Mitigation used: reduced global cap + increased cooldown for bursting tenant + forced routing fallback for that tenant for 30 min.
- Ref: Jira:SUP-28455

E) Support confusion: 429s when burst cap reached (expected but poorly messaged)

- We returned 429/overload when both baseline+burst caps were reached; some customers expected queuing instead.
- For GA we need crisp guidance: recommended retry/backoff strategy and what will/won’t queue.
- Ref: Jira:SUP-28503

Guardrails that were too strict (beta feedback)
1) Cooldown windows were overly punitive for spiky-but-legit workloads

- Current behavior: once a tenant hits max burst ratio, cooldown kicks in even if they drop below quickly.
- Effect: denial bursts after short spikes; customers perceive “flaky burst.”
- Proposal: cooldown should be based on sustained saturation (e.g., N seconds over threshold) or make cooldown proportional to burst duration, not a flat window.

2) Max burst ratio default (x1.5) was too conservative for “weekly batch” customers

- Several beta tenants expected x2–x3 for short windows (10–30 min) and were willing to pay.
- But we must pair higher ratios with stronger fairness + fleet safety + SLO gates.

3) Admission determinism vs latency tradeoff

- We enforced determinism by evaluating multiple signals synchronously; in some cases this added controller latency and increased timeouts.
- Suggestion: determinism requirement should be: “same inputs => same decision” but inputs can be snapshot-based (cached) within a bounded TTL.

Guardrails that were too lax (or missing)
1) Retry amplification guard

- When customers got denials, some clients retried immediately with high concurrency.
- We need an explicit “retry-after” / backoff hint tied to denial reason codes, and optionally server-side throttling at gateway.

2) Alerting gaps for “telemetry freshness” and “admission controller dependency health”

- We lacked a strong, paging-quality indicator for telemetry freshness degradation (it showed in graphs but didn’t page until customers complained).
- Admission controller dependency p99 did not have an error-budget aligned alert.

3) Fairness under mixed priority tiers needs stronger anti-starvation proofs

- We introduced priority tiers late in beta; we didn’t run enough multi-tenant stress tests for gold/silver combos.
- Need explicit starvation bound (e.g., min guaranteed tokens) and test harness enforcement.

4) Config propagation / console staleness

- One customer ticket: burst limit updated but Console showed stale value for too long.
- Root cause likely caching/prop delay; not a safety issue but it undermines trust.
- Ref: Jira:SUP-28541

Key metrics from beta (rough, from dashboards)

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Definition > Definitions
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Definition > Definitions
sections.content:
Definitions

- **Deployment**: A Dedicated inference endpoint identified by `deployment_id` and bound to a region and hardware pool.
- **Route**: A logical API capability within a deployment (e.g., `chat.completions`, `completions`, `embeddings`). For this SLO, throughput is evaluated at the **deployment level**, with route breakdowns used for diagnostics.
- **Committed Throughput Floor (CTF)**: The minimum throughput Redwood commits to sustain for a deployment under defined conditions. Expressed as **tokens/sec** (canonical) or **requests/sec** (only for non-tokenized routes; see below).
- **Observed Throughput**: Throughput computed from Redwood-side metering and timing, scoped to eligible requests.
- **SLO Window**: The evaluation interval used to determine compliance for a point in time (5 minutes).
- **Error Budget**: The allowed fraction of SLO windows that can be below the committed floor over the compliance period.

sections.section_path: Adr Hosted Rollout Cohorting And Traffic Splitting > Decision > 2) Cohort key selection rules (stickiness)
sections.heading: Adr Hosted Rollout Cohorting And Traffic Splitting > Decision > 2) Cohort key selection rules (stickiness)
sections.content:
2) Cohort key selection rules (stickiness)

The data plane selects `cohort_key` using the following precedence order:

1. **Explicit Cohort Key header (preferred):**
   - `X-Redwood-Cohort-Key` (customer-provided stable identifier)
   - Recommended values: end_user_id, account_id, conversation_id, or a stable hash thereof

2. **Idempotency key (recommended for retries/streaming reconnects):**
   - `Idempotency-Key` (if present)
   - Intended to remain identical across client retries and stream reconnect attempts

3. **Request ID (best-effort fallback):**
   - `X-Request-Id` (if present)
   - If generated by Redwood, it is unique per attempt and does **not** provide end-user stickiness; it only makes repeated internal handling of the same request deterministic.

4. **Non-sticky fallback (last resort):**
   - A per-request generated UUID (ensures correct aggregate percentage but no per-user stickiness)

Console/Docs requirements:

- Console wizard and docs MUST recommend using `X-Redwood-Cohort-Key` or `Idempotency-Key` for best results.
- Console must warn when a customer’s observed request mix suggests low stickiness (optional; informational).

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Policy and configuration boundaries
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Policy and configuration boundaries
sections.content:
Policy and configuration boundaries

- Tier defaults (Hosted self-serve, enterprise Hosted, Dedicated) live in the overload policy engine and are enforced primarily at gateway.
- Per-tenant overrides are evaluated at gateway and must be validated with guardrails (e.g., cannot exceed global safety caps).
- Runtime receives only what it needs for execution and safety (e.g., max_tokens cap adjustments or feature flags), not tenant policy logic.

sections.section_path: Sup 2892 Fallback Model Not Triggering During Overload
sections.heading: Sup 2892 Fallback Model Not Triggering During Overload
sections.content:
Sup 2892 Fallback Model Not Triggering During Overload

Source type: jira
Document ID: dsid_6e528fa402c34043897649be6aa6df3d
Release: v1.0.0
Benchmark: EnterpriseRAG-Bench synthetic upstream data
Fallback model not triggering during overload (customer receives 503 OVERLOADED instead of routed fallback)

Issue summary
Banyan Search reports that their configured fallback model is not being used during overload events. Instead, requests fail with 503 and Redwood overload error codes.

Customer expectation
When primary model (rw-llama-3.1-70b-instruct) is overloaded, Redwood should route to configured fallback (rw-llama-3.1-8b-instruct) per their tenant policy.

Impact

- Customer sees elevated failed requests during traffic spikes rather than degraded (lower quality) responses.
- Affects production search assistant experience and increases client retry pressure.

Environment

- Hosted API
- Region: us-east
- Route: /v1/chat/completions
- Streaming: mostly enabled

Customer configuration (as described by customer)

- Primary: rw-llama-3.1-70b-instruct
- Fallback: rw-llama-3.1-8b-instruct
- Trigger condition: overload (customer referenced 'circuit breaker open')

What the customer is seeing (excerpt)

- HTTP 503
- Error payload (representative):
  code: OVERLOADED
  message: "Service temporarily overloaded. Please retry."
  correlation_id: rwcorr_01JEMNQZJ5J9P2G6E3R9K8V6M2
  retry_after: (present for some responses; missing for some per SUP-2860)

Steps to reproduce (internal)
1) Identify Banyan tenant_id and active routing policy.
2) Induce overload condition (or replay from perf-canary) where gateway admission control sheds requests.
3) Confirm whether routing attempts fallback model when overload is detected.

Initial hypothesis
Fallback routing is only attempted when overload is detected at routing/runtime stages. When overload occurs at the gateway admission layer (breaker open / shed), the request is rejected before routing executes, so no fallback can occur. Additional suspicion: loop-prevention logic may be suppressing fallback when the request already contains an attempted-model chain header.

Requested outcome

- Confirm whether fallback is expected to work under gateway-level shedding.
- If not currently supported, provide clear customer guidance and (if safe) enable fallback-on-gateway-overload for this tenant as an exception/feature flag.
- Ensure Retry-After is consistently present on overload errors.

- Today we mostly deny quickly; some customers want queuing.
- SRE view: queuing can hide fleet pain and increase tail; if we add queueing it must be bounded with clear max wait + cancellation and must not break determinism.

2) How much “degraded mode” behavior is acceptable?

- If telemetry is stale, do we:
  a) deny all burst? (safe but may be overly strict)
  b) allow small burst with conservative cap? (better UX)
  c) continue as-is with risk? (not acceptable)
- Tentative: (b) with tight global caps + explicit surfaced state.

3) GA scope: region/hardware allow list

- Recommendation: GA in us-east H100 first; add eu-west after EU-West latency fix + game day rerun.

Appendix: customer support learnings (from tickets)

- SUP-28411 (unexpected denials): customers interpret “burst enabled” as “guaranteed extra capacity.” We must emphasize “best-effort within guardrails,” with clear reasons.
- SUP-28503 (429s): customers need explicit guidance on client-side backoff, concurrency control, and how to detect “you are at cap.”
- SUP-28488 (billing question): customers will audit the burst line item against their own job schedule; we need accurate exports + transparent calculation.

sections.heading: Runbook Rollout Stuck Or Bad Split > “Bad split” deep diagnostics > A) Validate cohorting inputs

“Bad split” deep diagnostics

A) Validate cohorting inputs

**What to validate in routing decision logs:**

- Hash key inputs: tenant_id, route_id, stable request key (e.g., user_id/session_id if provided), plus rollout_id.
- Stickiness rules across retries and streaming reconnects.

**Common pitfalls:**

- Missing user/session key causes cohorting to fall back to request-id which changes frequently (appears non-deterministic).
- Retry path not preserving cohort assignment.

**Mitigation:**

- If cohorting is unstable: rollback and escalate to Smart Routing.

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Circuit breaker placement
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Circuit breaker placement
sections.content:
Circuit breaker placement

We define three breaker types:
1) **Gateway dependency breakers** (fast, local)

- Trips on: auth/usage service latency/timeouts, policy-engine unavailability, routing service brownout
- Action: fail closed with stable 503 (dependency_unavailable) or 429/503 overload class per ADR-014 mapping

2) **Gateway overload breakers** (regional, policy-driven)

- Trips on: sustained regional saturation state = critical AND shed budget exceeded OR error-budget protection triggers
- Action: shed by tier/tenant/route with predictable semantics; include Retry-After

3) **Runtime safety breakers** (hard stop)

- Trips on: queue depth hard limit, memory pressure beyond threshold, scheduler unable to admit
- Action: reject immediately; propagate internal reason for edge mapping

Routing uses “health gates” rather than circuit breakers for most target selection decisions. Routing may maintain a short-lived “avoid target” cache with hysteresis to reduce flapping.

sections.section_path: Adr Hosted Rollout Cohorting And Traffic Splitting > Decision > 3) Where cohorting is enforced
sections.heading: Adr Hosted Rollout Cohorting And Traffic Splitting > Decision > 3) Where cohorting is enforced
sections.content:
3) Where cohorting is enforced

Cohorting and split enforcement occur in the **Smart Routing / data plane** after route resolution and policy checks, and before final model selection.

Order (simplified):

1. Authenticate request / resolve tenant + route
2. Evaluate policy eligibility for rollout (RBAC, guardrails, rollout state)
3. Select region per existing routing policies (latency/capacity/affinity)
4. **Compute cohort (baseline/canary) in the chosen region’s data plane**
5. Select model version/config for the cohort
6. Apply existing fallback policies if the chosen target is unavailable

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Common failure modes and quick routing hints
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Common failure modes and quick routing hints
sections.content:
Common failure modes and quick routing hints

- **Customer sees lower throughput than Redwood reports:** often a measurement mismatch (streaming token accounting, end-to-end latency vs throughput, counting input tokens). Engage Observability if persistent.
- **Throughput drops with GPU pegged:** suspect contention, node health, thermal throttling, network bottleneck; page Infra.
- **Throughput drops with low utilization:** suspect admission control limiting, customer throttling, or workload shift to longer contexts; page SRE; ask customer for concurrency/workload details.
- **Regional capacity constraint / failover behavior:** check tier failover posture; page Infra and SRE; do not promise cross-region without tier/contract confirmation.

---

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Definition > Measurement semantics > Streaming token accounting
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Definition > Measurement semantics > Streaming token accounting
sections.content:
Streaming token accounting

For streaming responses:

- Output tokens are counted when emitted by the runtime, attributed to the originating request.
- We de-duplicate token counters to avoid double counting caused by stream chunk retries.

Operational note: streaming accounting semantics were corrected in **PR-19422** (“Fix throughput metric double counting streaming”). Any backfills or comparisons across that boundary must annotate the change.

sections.section_path: Runbook Rollout Stuck Or Bad Split > 1) Safe pause (recommended first action when unsure)
sections.heading: Runbook Rollout Stuck Or Bad Split > 1) Safe pause (recommended first action when unsure)
sections.content:
Mitigation playbooks

1) Safe pause (recommended first action when unsure)

**When to use:** Rollout health uncertain; need to stop automated progression.

**Effects:**

- Stops step progression.
- Depending on configuration, split may remain at current value (most common) or revert to previous safe step (tenant policy dependent).

**Procedure:**
1) Pause rollout from Console (preferred; ensures audit event):

   - Console → Hosted Route → Rollouts → Select rollout → **Pause**

2) Confirm in orchestrator that state is PAUSED and no scheduled transitions remain.
3) Monitor baseline/canary metrics for 10 minutes.

**If pause fails:** proceed to “Kill switch / forced rollback”.

---

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Consequences > Negative / tradeoffs
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Consequences > Negative / tradeoffs
sections.content:
Negative / tradeoffs

- More moving parts: three layers must align on semantics and observability.
- Tuning is non-trivial; requires careful rollout with canaries and dashboards.
- Signal aggregation adds latency; gateway decisions may lag rapid runtime changes (mitigated by runtime hard limits).

sections.section_path: Adr Hosted Rollout Cohorting And Traffic Splitting > Summary
sections.heading: Adr Hosted Rollout Cohorting And Traffic Splitting > Summary
sections.content:
Summary

This ADR defines how Redwood Hosted assigns requests to **baseline** vs **canary** cohorts during a hosted canary rollout, and how the configured canary percentage is enforced across regions. The decision prioritizes:

- Deterministic, reproducible cohort assignment (especially across retries)
- Sticky behavior when customers provide stable identifiers
- Minimal coordination/state across regions and data planes
- Observability clarity when effective serving differs from intended cohort

sections.section_path: Postmortem Perf Canary False Positive Alert Storm > Corrective and preventative actions (CPAs) > Implemented (completed)
sections.heading: Postmortem Perf Canary False Positive Alert Storm > Corrective and preventative actions (CPAs) > Implemented (completed)
sections.content:
Corrective and preventative actions (CPAs)

Implemented (completed)

- **Baseline key normalization:** Baseline lookup now uses a canonical key:
  - `model_id` (canonical registry ID)
  - `model_version` (registry version)
  - `runtime_build_id`
  - `hardware_sku`
  - `region`
  - (explicitly does *not* include prompt bucket or run IDs)
- **Metric label contract:** Reduced emitted labels to an approved set; added a CI check that fails if new labels are added without review.
- **Evaluator “baseline missing” behavior:** Baseline missing is now treated as **“canary unhealthy”** (warn once) rather than “assume default regression thresholds”.
- **Min-sample + dampening alignment:** Alert rules now match the evaluator grouping and require:
  - minimum N requests per grouping
  - sustained breach across multiple evaluation intervals
- **Incident-bot dedupe key update:** Dedupe keys now include (model_id, model_version, region, hardware_sku, runtime_build_id, alert_type).

sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Definition > Measurement semantics > Windowing and aggregation
sections.content:
Measurement semantics

Windowing and aggregation

- **Evaluation window:** 5 minutes (tumbling windows)
- **Compliance period:** 30 days (rolling)
- **Aggregation level:** `deployment_id` (primary); `deployment_id + route + model` (debug)

sections.section_path: Runbook Rollout Stuck Or Bad Split > Diagnostic procedure > Step 2 — Determine which failure mode you’re in
sections.heading: Runbook Rollout Stuck Or Bad Split > Diagnostic procedure > Step 2 — Determine which failure mode you’re in
sections.content:
Step 2 — Determine which failure mode you’re in

Use this table:

| Observation | Most likely area | Next check |
|---|---|---|
| Orchestrator state not changing; UI shows stuck in evaluation | Orchestrator / Telemetry | Telemetry delays; orchestrator worker health |
| Orchestrator progressed step, but traffic doesn’t reflect it | Smart Routing / propagation | Config version by region; routing cache |
| Only one region mismatched | Propagation / region-specific dataplane | Route config apply status in that region |
| Canary traffic is 0% despite >0% config | Cohort tagging / eligibility filter | Cohort eligibility decision logs |
| Canary traffic is ~100% unexpectedly | Routing precedence or config corruption | Policy evaluation order; rollback immediately |

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Decision > 2) Routing admission + fallback (secondary protection and graceful degradation)
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Decision > 2) Routing admission + fallback (secondary protection and graceful degradation)
sections.content:
2) Routing admission + fallback (secondary protection and graceful degradation)

**Routing owns “where it goes”** and **controlled degradation**, not global rate limiting.

Routing responsibilities:

- Choose region/model deployment target using policy (latency/cost/availability) and health signals.
- If gateway-admitted traffic hits a saturated target, routing may:
  - Attempt **configured fallback model/region** (bounded, loop-safe) when policy allows.
  - Otherwise, return an overload response consistent with ADR-014.

Routing must not create uncontrolled amplification (e.g., fan-out retries across regions). Routing is permitted to do **at most one** fallback attempt per request, and must enforce loop-prevention.

sections.section_path: Burst Capacity Retro Notes
sections.heading: Burst Capacity Retro Notes
sections.content:
Burst Capacity Retro Notes

Source type: google_drive
Document ID: dsid_95c7aa5238f94570a8e0a8684736b666
Release: v1.0.0
Benchmark: EnterpriseRAG-Bench synthetic upstream data
Dedicated Burst Capacity — Post-beta retro notes (SRE)
Doc goal
Capture what we learned from the Dedicated Burst Capacity beta (May 2025): what broke, which guardrails were too strict/too lax, what we changed during beta, and what must be completed before GA.

Retro logistics

- Date: 2025-05-28 (60 min)
- Facilitator: Rafael Mendes (SRE)
- Notetaker: Peter Holtz (Routing SRE)
- Beta window covered: 2025-05-06 to 2025-05-24
- Scope: burst pools (regional/hardware), admission controller, routing integration, SLO gates, dashboards/alerts, metering/billing hooks, supportability

Attendees (high signal contributors)

- SRE/Obs: Sean G., Rafael M., Peter H., Allison G., Sergio C.
- Infra/Fleet: Vanessa O., Keiko Y.
- Control plane/policy: Jordan L.
- Routing: Mina H.
- Billing/metering: Cole S., Nadia R.
- CS feedback: Rachel K.

What went well (keep)
1) Global safety cap + circuit breaker concept worked in practice

- We hit the cap once in staging and once “near miss” in prod beta; breaker prevented runaway neighbor impact.
- The playbook of “reduce caps -> drain queues -> disable burst for lowest tiers first” is operationally sound.

2) Denial reason codes improved triage materially

- Support/CS could distinguish “cap reached” vs “pool saturated” vs “cooldown” vs “telemetry stale”.
- Routing logs + reason codes made it clear where to look first.

3) Dashboards were mostly the right primitives

- Saturation, queue depth, admit/deny rates, and p95 deltas by tenant were enough to debug 80% of issues.
- SLO gate signal (non-burst tenant latency regression) is a good north star even if thresholds need tuning.

4) Rollout gating/feature flags prevented blast radius

- Per-region allow list + per-tenant enablement meant we could pause EU-West issues without impacting US-East.

What broke / painful incidents
A) Telemetry lag caused unfair denials + occasional starvation

- Symptom: a few tenants saw denial spikes while pool appeared underutilized; the “laggy” telemetry made the controller think they were still consuming burst tokens.
- Customer-visible effect: burst requests denied unexpectedly; some clients retried aggressively and amplified load.
- Root cause (likely): our admission controller relied on near-real-time usage signals; when signals were delayed, the smoothing window + token bucket refill behavior effectively penalized active tenants.
- Fix during beta: hotfix added smoothing + guard conditions + conservative fallback when telemetry freshness is below threshold.
- Ref: GitHub:redwood/pr-23944

B) EU-West burst admission timeouts (controller dependency chain)

- Symptom: admission calls intermittently timed out in eu-west under high request rate; routing fell back but increased gateway error rates briefly.
- Root cause: admission controller p99 latency spiked due to dependency (policy evaluation + fleet telemetry query) not being bounded; threadpool saturation.
- Mitigation: enable circuit breaker + temporarily tighten per-tenant caps + disable burst in eu-west allow list until patched.
- Ref: Jira:SUP-28579

C) Billing: burst usage double-counted on retry paths

sections.heading: Postmortem Perf Canary False Positive Alert Storm > Resolution and immediate mitigations
sections.content:
Resolution and immediate mitigations

Actions taken during the incident:

1. **Disabled paging rules** for perf-canary regressions (kept warning-level visibility). (Owner: SRE on-call)
2. **Rolled back canary model coverage** to the previously stable 3-model configuration. (Owner: Runtime on-call)
3. **Pinned evaluator to fixed baseline artifacts** (no rolling updates) until schema/keys were corrected. (Owner: Nadia Rahman)
4. **Hotfix to drop high-cardinality labels** from canary metrics (`workload_run_id`, `prompt_template_id`, full `route`). (Owner: Logan Wright)

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Warm pool / startup considerations
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Warm pool / startup considerations
sections.content:
Warm pool / startup considerations

Some tiers include warm pool guarantees (or faster recovery expectations). During triage, identify if the customer is within a warm-up window:

- Did the deployment recently scale from zero?
- Was there a recent model reload, config change, or node replacement?
- Did traffic resume after prolonged inactivity?

If warm-up is suspected, note it explicitly in the customer thread and ask SRE to confirm whether the event is excluded by policy.

---

sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Definition > Change log

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Implementation notes (non-normative)
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Implementation notes (non-normative)
sections.content:
Implementation notes (non-normative)

- Gateway admission should use a combination of:
  - token bucket (QPS) per tenant/route
  - concurrency caps for streaming endpoints
  - “regional overload state” multiplier for dynamic throttling (with hysteresis)
- Runtime should expose clear “reject reasons” that map into ADR-014 overload codes without leaking internals.
- Routing should mark fallback attempts and enforce max_attempts=1. Any further attempt must be a client retry honoring Retry-After.

sections.heading: Adr Hosted Rollout Cohorting And Traffic Splitting > Implementation notes (non-normative)

Implementation notes (non-normative)

- Data plane should compute cohort as early as possible after route resolution, but after any bypass/policy deny checks.
- Keep the hash implementation identical across languages (gateway, edge proxies, and routing services). Add a golden test vector suite.
- Add integration tests to validate:
  - Stable assignment across retries with same idempotency key
  - Step increases are monotonic superset of canary population
  - Fallback produces intended/effective mismatch telemetry

sections.section_path: Postmortem Perf Canary False Positive Alert Storm > Follow-up validation plan
sections.heading: Postmortem Perf Canary False Positive Alert Storm > Follow-up validation plan
sections.content:
Follow-up validation plan

Before re-enabling paging and using signals as rollout gates, we will:

1. Run a **7-day warning-only bake** with expanded coverage and confirm:
   - baseline hit-rate > 99.5%
   - no unexpected label growth (cardinality budget)
   - alert volume within noise budget
2. Re-enable paging for **one top model** in one region with clear success criteria.
3. Only after stable paging, enable rollout gate consumption in “advisory” mode for 2 weeks, then move to “blocking” mode.

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Operational guidance (brief)
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Operational guidance (brief)
sections.content:
Operational guidance (brief)

- When overload happens, prefer adjusting gateway policy thresholds and shed behavior before touching runtime queue settings.
- Use routing fallback only for tenants that have explicitly opted in and where compatible models are defined.
- Watch for oscillation: frequent breaker open/close events or high fallback attempt rates are indicators of unstable thresholds.

sections.section_path: Runbook Rollout Stuck Or Bad Split > 3) Fix split mismatch without rollback (only if impact is low)
sections.heading: Runbook Rollout Stuck Or Bad Split > 3) Fix split mismatch without rollback (only if impact is low)
sections.content:
3) Fix split mismatch without rollback (only if impact is low)

**When to use:**

- Split mismatch exists but canary/baseline are both healthy.
- Customer is blocked but no production regression.

**Options (in order):**
1) **Re-apply step / re-sync config**

   - Trigger a “reconcile/apply” action in orchestrator (if available to oncall).
   - Confirm apply ack in every region.

2) **Lower canary percent**

   - If canary is receiving more than expected, reduce target to a safe value (e.g., 0–1%) while investigating.

3) **Pause and hold**

   - Stop changes; coordinate with owner team for deeper fix.

Do not repeatedly “nudge” percentages quickly; it increases confusion and complicates audit timelines.

---

sections.heading: Adr Hosted Rollout Cohorting And Traffic Splitting > Options considered > Option A: Pure random assignment per request

Options considered

Option A: Pure random assignment per request

- Pros: simple; aggregate percentage correct
- Cons: not sticky; terrible for user experience comparisons; retries change cohort; noisy metrics
- Rejected.

sections.heading: Postmortem Perf Canary False Positive Alert Storm > Corrective and preventative actions (CPAs) > Planned (in progress)
sections.content:
Planned (in progress)

- **Region/SKU-aware thresholds:** Allow thresholds that differ by SKU/region where variance is known to differ (documented + versioned).
- **Baseline drift guardrails:** Rolling baselines require an explicit “baseline update window” and block updates during rollout expansion or telemetry schema changes.
- **Canary alert gating:** Rollout gates will consume only “high-confidence” regression signals (enforced min samples + stable baseline + low ingestion lag).

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Alternatives considered
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Alternatives considered
sections.content:
Alternatives considered

1) **Single global breaker at gateway only**

- Rejected: insufficient fidelity; cannot protect runtime safety in all cases; still allows deep queueing.

2) **Runtime-only backpressure (let everything in)**

- Rejected: overload manifests as queued latency/timeouts; poor customer semantics; wastes upstream work.

3) **Routing-driven global admission control**

- Rejected: routing is not the best place to enforce tenant fairness and local dependency breakers; risks complex control loops.

B) Policy precedence causing unexpected routing

**Checks:**

- Fallback routing policy may override canary selection.
- Region routing constraints may redirect canary traffic to baseline in some regions.
- Quota/rate limiting policy may shed canary disproportionately.

**Mitigation:**

- Prefer rollback if behavior is not easily explained.
- Escalate to Policy Engine if denies/overrides suspected.

When paging SRE/Infra, include:
