sections.section_path: Ci Eval Determinism And Flake Mitigation > RNG handling (current standard) > Framework flags
sections.heading: Ci Eval Determinism And Flake Mitigation > RNG handling (current standard) > Framework flags
sections.content:
Framework flags

We enable deterministic flags when `deterministic: true`:

- `torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)`
- `torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic = True`
- `torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = False`

Caveat:

- Quantized/int8 kernels may not fully respect these flags. Treat the flags as best-effort rather than a guarantee.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Implementation Notes / Requirements
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Implementation Notes / Requirements
sections.content:
Implementation Notes / Requirements

1. Baseline artifacts must be stored in an access-controlled, versioned store with auditability (who/when created).
2. Canary config must support per-model overrides:
   - thresholds by severity
   - whether region-specific keys are enabled
   - “top model” flag affecting paging eligibility
3. Alert payloads must include:
   - observed value, baseline value, percent change
   - sample counts and token counts
   - runtime_build_id, kernel_set_id, hardware_sku, region
   - links to dashboards, traces, and runbook
4. Changes to default thresholds must go through an ADR update or SRE-approved change request.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Baseline Computation > Rolling health baseline (calibration only)
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Baseline Computation > Rolling health baseline (calibration only)
sections.content:
Rolling health baseline (calibration only)

- Window: trailing 7 days, excluding periods marked as “rollout” or “incident.”
- Aggregation: daily aggregates with robust statistics (median-of-daily-p95) to reduce sensitivity to short spikes.
- Purpose:
  - detect slow drift (e.g., fleet changes) that may warrant generating a new fixed baseline
  - suggest region/SKU overrides when variance is consistently higher

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Alternatives Considered > A) Pure rolling baseline (always updated)
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Alternatives Considered > A) Pure rolling baseline (always updated)
sections.content:
Alternatives Considered

A) Pure rolling baseline (always updated)

Pros:

- Adapts to drift without explicit re-baselining.

Cons:

- Risk of masking slow regressions (baseline chases the regression).
- Hard to use for rollout gating (“moving goalposts”).
- Susceptible to alert storms if rolling logic is impacted by label bugs or ingestion gaps.

Decision: Rejected for paging/gating. Allowed only as a secondary calibration signal.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Baseline Computation > Fixed baseline artifact
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Baseline Computation > Fixed baseline artifact
sections.content:
Baseline Computation

Fixed baseline artifact

- Source: controlled perf-canary runs using the approved synthetic prompt distribution.
- For each baseline key, we store:
  - distribution summaries (p50/p95/p99) for each latency metric
  - mean and standard deviation where stable enough to be meaningful
  - tokens/sec distribution summaries
  - run metadata (time range, sample count, canary config version)
- Baseline validity: baseline is considered valid only if it meets minimum sample size requirements (see below) and passes sanity checks (no telemetry gaps, no error-rate spikes).

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Rollout Guidance
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Rollout Guidance
sections.content:
Rollout Guidance

- Phase 1 (single region): warnings only, tune per-model overrides until noise is acceptable.
- Phase 2: enable paging only for top models with proven low variance and stable baselines.
- Phase 3: integrate gating with release engineering once paging signal is trusted (warning can gate early as “soft fail,” paging as “hard fail”).

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Appendix B: Ownership
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Appendix B: Ownership
sections.content:
Appendix B: Ownership

- Baseline pipeline and artifact integrity: Telemetry Platform (Logan Wright) + Metrics/Baselines (Nadia Rahman)
- Threshold standards and paging hygiene: SRE (Sean Gallagher, Allison Grant)
- Model list and rollout gating integration: Serving Runtime (Noah Patel) + Release Engineering (Connor O'Brien)

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Consequences > Negative / Tradeoffs
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Consequences > Negative / Tradeoffs
sections.content:
Negative / Tradeoffs

- Requires baseline artifact generation whenever major runtime/kernel changes land for covered models/SKUs.
- Some true regressions may be detected slightly later due to sustained-breach requirements.
- Optional region/tier overrides add complexity when enabled.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Alternatives Considered > C) Per-region baselines always on
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Alternatives Considered > C) Per-region baselines always on
sections.content:
C) Per-region baselines always on

Pros:

- Reduces false positives due to cross-region fleet differences.

Cons:

- Baseline explosion (more artifacts and config), operational overhead.

Decision: Region is optional and only enabled for models/regions where observed variance requires it.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Consequences > Positive
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Consequences > Positive
sections.content:
Consequences

Positive

- Stable, versioned baselines support rollout gates and high-confidence paging.
- Rolling health baseline provides drift visibility without undermining safety.
- Anti-flap controls reduce alert noise and prevent incident-bot storms.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Alternatives Considered > B) Pure fixed baseline (never updated unless manual)
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Alternatives Considered > B) Pure fixed baseline (never updated unless manual)
sections.content:
B) Pure fixed baseline (never updated unless manual)

Pros:

- Extremely stable; easy to reason about.

Cons:

- Becomes stale as fleet/hardware/driver changes accumulate; increases false positives over time.
- Forces frequent manual work to remain relevant.

Decision: Rejected as the only strategy. Adopted as primary baseline with explicit regeneration workflows.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Anti-Flap, Dedupe, and Hysteresis > Sustained breach logic
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Anti-Flap, Dedupe, and Hysteresis > Sustained breach logic
sections.content:
Anti-Flap, Dedupe, and Hysteresis

Sustained breach logic

We use “M out of N windows” to reduce sensitivity to transient spikes:

- Warning: 2/3 consecutive windows breach
- Paging: 3/4 consecutive windows breach

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Minimum Sample Sizes and Windowing > Evaluation window
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Minimum Sample Sizes and Windowing > Evaluation window
sections.content:
Minimum Sample Sizes and Windowing

Evaluation window

- Default evaluation window: **10 minutes**.
- Windows are evaluated continuously and require sustained breach rules (see anti-flap).

sections.section_path: Ci Eval Determinism And Flake Mitigation > RNG handling (current standard) > Root seed and per-example seeds
sections.heading: Ci Eval Determinism And Flake Mitigation > RNG handling (current standard) > Root seed and per-example seeds
sections.content:
RNG handling (current standard)

Root seed and per-example seeds

- The runner accepts a `--seed` root seed.
- For each example, derive a stable per-example seed:
  - `example_seed = root_seed + example_index`
- Construct a generator on the active device and pass it explicitly to generation.

Operational guidance:

- Ensure `example_index` is stable across runs (do not use worker-local indices unless they are globally consistent).
- If sharding is used, include `shard_id` in the seed derivation only if shard assignments are stable across runs.

sections.section_path: Ci Eval Determinism And Flake Mitigation > Ownership and change control
sections.heading: Ci Eval Determinism And Flake Mitigation > Ownership and change control
sections.content:
Ownership and change control

- Owner: Applied ML & Evals
- Any change to determinism semantics (`--deterministic` behavior, seed derivation, gating thresholds) requires review from Applied ML & Evals + Serving Runtime.

sections.section_path: Ci Eval Determinism And Flake Mitigation > Runner CLI (current)
sections.heading: Ci Eval Determinism And Flake Mitigation > Runner CLI (current)
sections.content:
Runner CLI (current)

Required runner options for reproducibility testing:

- `--repeat N` : runs the same suite N times with the same config and seed
- `--deterministic {true|false}` : enforces deterministic mode when true
- `--seed SEED` : sets the root seed

Example:

- `evals/onboarding --suite quantized-v2 --repeat 3 --deterministic true --seed 42`

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Regression Definition
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Regression Definition
sections.content:
Regression Definition

We define regression as a statistically and operationally meaningful deviation from the fixed baseline.

sections.section_path: Ci Eval Determinism And Flake Mitigation > Definitions > Flake
sections.heading: Ci Eval Determinism And Flake Mitigation > Definitions > Flake
sections.content:
Flake

A flake is a CI failure caused by nondeterministic variation rather than a real change in model/code.

sections.section_path: Quantization Profiles Customer Docs Plan > Audience and use cases
sections.heading: Quantization Profiles Customer Docs Plan > Audience and use cases
sections.content:
Audience and use cases

**Primary audiences**

- Software engineers and ML engineers integrating Redwood routes who want to reduce cost/token.
- Platform teams managing production change control (audit logs, RBAC, rollbacks).

**Customer use cases we need to support in docs**

1. Enable an approved quantization profile for a single route (hosted API).
2. Enable profile for a route with region/tier constraints (Dedicated + multi-region hosted).
3. Validate quality and latency before expanding traffic.
4. Diagnose output changes, elevated fallback rate, or latency regressions.
5. Roll back (route-level disable; global kill-switch is internal-only but mention its existence at a high level).

sections.section_path: Quantization Profiles Customer Docs Plan > Information architecture (public docs) > Page 4: Evaluation best practices
sections.heading: Quantization Profiles Customer Docs Plan > Information architecture (public docs) > Page 4: Evaluation best practices
sections.content:
Page 4: Evaluation best practices

**Proposed title:** “How to evaluate quality and latency before rollout”

**Customer-friendly guidance**

- Suggested evaluation approach:
  - Identify representative prompts (production samples + edge cases).
  - Run baseline vs profile-enabled comparisons.
  - Use A/B sampling (e.g., 1–5% traffic) with a rollback threshold.

- What to measure
  - Quality: task-specific metrics (pass@k, exact match, ranking metrics) + human review where appropriate.
  - Latency: p50/p95 decode latency and time-to-first-token.
  - Cost: cost/token and throughput.

- Rollout strategy
  1) Enable in staging on a non-critical route
  2) Canary in production (small % traffic)
  3) Expand gradually with monitoring

- Provide explicit “stop conditions”
  - Elevated fallback rate
  - Increased error rate
  - Statistically meaningful quality regression on a defined slice

**Note:** We cannot publish Redwood’s internal thresholds verbatim if they are considered sensitive, but we can publish recommended guardrails (e.g., “predefine acceptable deltas and require sign-off”). We will align with Selene Huang (quality guardrails) on what’s safe to disclose.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Decision
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Decision
sections.content:
Decision

We adopt a **hybrid baseline strategy**:

1) **Primary baseline = Fixed, versioned baseline per (model, model_version, runtime_build, kernel_set_id, hardware_sku) with optional region override**

- Baselines are generated from controlled canary runs (prod-like load) and stored as immutable artifacts.
- Baselines are explicitly tied to the runtime build and kernel selection identifiers so comparisons remain meaningful.
- This is the baseline used for rollout gating and for paging.

2) **Secondary baseline = Rolling “health baseline” used for drift monitoring and threshold calibration (not for paging)**

- We compute a rolling reference from recent stable periods (default: last 7 days) to detect slow environmental drift and to inform recalibration.
- Rolling baseline is not used to auto-suppress a fixed-baseline regression; it is used as a triage and tuning signal.

3) **Baseline freeze rules**

- During a runtime rollout (canary/gradual), the baseline used for alerts is **frozen** to the most recent fixed baseline for the currently active runtime build on that ring.
- If an incident is declared for a perf regression, baseline updates are **paused** for affected keys until incident closure.

4) **Threshold evaluation requires minimum sample size + sustained breach + hysteresis**

- Alerts require both a minimum number of canary requests and sustained breach across multiple evaluation windows.
- Alert clear conditions are stricter than trigger conditions (hysteresis) to reduce flapping.

sections.section_path: Ci Eval Determinism And Flake Mitigation > Recommended CI strategy (current) > 2) Nightly: multi-seed + tolerance-based comparison
sections.heading: Ci Eval Determinism And Flake Mitigation > Recommended CI strategy (current) > 2) Nightly: multi-seed + tolerance-based comparison
sections.content:
2) Nightly: multi-seed + tolerance-based comparison

Purpose: catch real regressions and quantify expected variance.

- Environment: target infra (A100 for quantized-v2)
- Mode: `deterministic: false` (sampling allowed when the eval is designed to measure sampled behavior)
- Seeds: 3 seeds (default: 13, 37, 101)
- Decision rule: compare against the golden baseline using metric tolerance thresholds; alert on sustained shifts (median across seeds).

sections.section_path: Ci Eval Determinism And Flake Mitigation > Recommended CI strategy (current) > 3) On failure: auto-trigger repro debug job
sections.heading: Ci Eval Determinism And Flake Mitigation > Recommended CI strategy (current) > 3) On failure: auto-trigger repro debug job
sections.content:
3) On failure: auto-trigger repro debug job

Purpose: make investigations fast and data-rich.

- Auto-collect artifacts listed in the Logging and Artifacts section.
- Include a run summary that states whether variance is:
  - decode-level (different token sequences)
  - metric-only (same outputs but metric computation drift)
  - environment-level (hardware/container mismatch)

sections.section_path: Ci Eval Determinism And Flake Mitigation > Troubleshooting playbook
sections.heading: Ci Eval Determinism And Flake Mitigation > Troubleshooting playbook
sections.content:
Troubleshooting playbook

If you see nondeterminism with `deterministic: true`:
1) Confirm the run is on the expected hardware class and container digest.
2) Confirm output hashes differ (decode nondeterminism) vs metrics differ (metric computation drift).
3) If decode nondeterminism:

   - verify generator is passed explicitly
   - verify stable ordering of examples and stable batch shape
   - check for any remaining sampling knobs being set by a suite override

4) If still nondeterministic on A100 quantized kernels:

   - capture artifacts and escalate to eng-serving-runtime for kernel-level investigation
   - consider switching the suite’s CI gate to tolerance-based comparison if bitwise repeatability is unattainable

sections.section_path: Ci Eval Determinism And Flake Mitigation > Recommended CI strategy (current) > 1) Per-commit (PR) gate: deterministic quick eval
sections.heading: Ci Eval Determinism And Flake Mitigation > Recommended CI strategy (current) > 1) Per-commit (PR) gate: deterministic quick eval
sections.content:
Recommended CI strategy (current)

1) Per-commit (PR) gate: deterministic quick eval

Purpose: prevent random sampling jitter from blocking merges.

- Environment: standardized runner image + target GPU class when available (A10 preferred for cost; A100 acceptable).
- Mode: `deterministic: true`
- Repeats: `--repeat 3`
- Decision rule: gate on the median metric across repeats; also fail if output hashes differ across repeats (for suites that require bitwise stability).

sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Open Questions (tracked outside ADR)
sections.content:

sections.section_path: Ci Eval Determinism And Flake Mitigation > Metric gating rules > Per-commit deterministic gate
sections.heading: Ci Eval Determinism And Flake Mitigation > Metric gating rules > Per-commit deterministic gate
sections.content:
Metric gating rules

Per-commit deterministic gate

- Compute metric per repeat.
- Report: median, min, max, and standard deviation.
- Fail conditions:
  - Any repeat differs in output token hash (for deterministic suites).
  - Std dev exceeds threshold (default threshold: 0.005 BLEU-equivalent; suite owners may override).

sections.section_path: Ci Eval Determinism And Flake Mitigation > Definitions > Deterministic (harness-level)
sections.heading: Ci Eval Determinism And Flake Mitigation > Definitions > Deterministic (harness-level)
sections.content:
Definitions

Deterministic (harness-level)

A run is considered deterministic (for CI purposes) if repeated executions on the same hardware + container image + model revision produce identical decoded token sequences for the same prompts.

Notes:

- Hardware drift (A100 vs K80) is not expected to be bitwise identical.
- Some quantized kernels may still be nondeterministic even when framework-level deterministic flags are enabled.

sections.section_path: Quantization Profiles Customer Docs Plan > Product language and terminology
sections.heading: Quantization Profiles Customer Docs Plan > Product language and terminology
sections.content:
Product language and terminology

We need consistent, customer-friendly wording:

- **Quantization profile**: A versioned, Redwood-validated configuration for running a specific model variant using a specific quantization method/precision combination.
- **Profile library**: The set of published profiles per model variant. Customers choose a profile for a route.
- **Route-level enablement**: Profiles are enabled per route, not globally for all tenant traffic (v1).
- **Fallback**: If a request is incompatible (hardware/sequence length constraints) or profile application fails safe checks, Redwood serves using baseline precision for that request (or route) while emitting an event.

Avoid ambiguous language:

- Avoid saying “Redwood automatically picks the best profile.”
- Avoid “lossless” claims. Use “aims to preserve quality” and emphasize eval/monitoring.

sections.section_path: Quantization Profiles Customer Docs Plan > Information architecture (public docs) > Page 5: Troubleshooting + rollback
sections.heading: Quantization Profiles Customer Docs Plan > Information architecture (public docs) > Page 5: Troubleshooting + rollback
sections.content:
Page 5: Troubleshooting + rollback

**Proposed title:** “Troubleshooting quantization profiles”

**Structure: symptom → likely cause → how to confirm → resolution**

Required symptoms:

- Console says profile is incompatible
  - Common causes: wrong model variant, unsupported GPU class, context length exceeds profile limit.
  - Resolution: choose another profile; reduce max tokens/context; use baseline.

- Output quality changed unexpectedly
  - Confirm: compare baseline vs profile, check whether fallback occurred (mixed behavior can look inconsistent).
  - Resolution: disable profile; run eval; contact support with request IDs.

- p95 latency increased
  - Confirm: look at per-route latency panels; check TTFT vs decode; check batching/caching changes.
  - Resolution: disable profile; adjust route concurrency/batching; consult Redwood support.

- Elevated fallback rate
  - Confirm: dashboard panel + route events.
  - Likely causes: requests exceed profile constraints; region/GPU mismatch; deployment drift.
  - Resolution: tighten route constraints; pick compatible profile; disable.

- 5xx errors after enabling
  - Confirm: error class; check if errors correlate with specific profile version.
  - Resolution: disable; provide audit event ID and request IDs to support.

Rollback instructions (customer-actionable)

- Disable at route level (Console + API snippet).
- Verify disablement and that requests are using baseline.

We should also include:

- “What information to include in a support ticket” checklist:
  - Org/tenant ID
  - Route name/ID
  - Model + variant
  - Profile ID/version
  - Region/deployment mode
  - Approx timeframe
  - Request IDs/traces
  - Observed metrics (fallback rate, p95 latency)

sections.section_path: Ci Eval Determinism And Flake Mitigation > Deterministic decoding mode (required behavior)
sections.heading: Ci Eval Determinism And Flake Mitigation > Deterministic decoding mode (required behavior)
sections.content:
Deterministic decoding mode (required behavior)

When `deterministic: true`, the harness MUST enforce:

- `do_sample = false`
- `temperature = 0.0`
- `top_k = 1`
- `top_p = 1.0`
- `num_beams = 1` (unless the suite explicitly tests beam search)
- Explicit generator passed into generation APIs
- Stable batching order (no data-loader shuffling; stable sort by example_id)

Rationale:

- Simply setting a global seed is insufficient when generation draws randomness in parallel or across different batch shapes.

sections.section_path: Quantization Profiles Customer Docs Plan > Non-goals (docs)
sections.heading: Quantization Profiles Customer Docs Plan > Non-goals (docs)
sections.content:
Non-goals (docs)

- Do not position this as automatic tuning/recommendations (out of scope for v1).
- Do not publish internal-only implementation details (artifact signing specifics, internal service names, kill-switch runbooks).
- Do not promise universal profile coverage across all models/GPU SKUs.

sections.heading: Quantization Profiles Customer Docs Plan > Success criteria (docs)

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Regression Definition > Threshold levels
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Regression Definition > Threshold levels
sections.content:
Threshold levels

Two alert levels exist:

- **Warning**: actionable signal for runtime team triage; routed to #eng-runtime.
- **Paging**: sustained, high-confidence regression on top models; routed to on-call rotation.

sections.section_path: Ci Eval Determinism And Flake Mitigation > Metric gating rules > Nightly tolerance-based gate
sections.heading: Ci Eval Determinism And Flake Mitigation > Metric gating rules > Nightly tolerance-based gate
sections.content:
Nightly tolerance-based gate

- Compare nightly medians to golden medians.
- Default tolerances (may be tuned per suite):
  - BLEU: 0.03 absolute
  - chrF: 0.02 absolute
  - Task accuracy: 0.5 percentage points absolute

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Summary
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Summary
sections.content:
Summary

This ADR defines how the production performance canary computes baselines and evaluates regressions for per-model serving performance (primarily p95 latency and tokens/sec). It documents:

- Baseline computation approach (rolling vs fixed) and when each is used.
- Regression thresholds (warning vs paging) and how they are applied.
- Minimum sample sizes and confidence requirements to avoid noisy alerts.
- Anti-flap / dedupe logic to prevent alert storms during drift, telemetry delays, or small-sample variance.

sections.section_path: Quantization Profiles Customer Docs Plan > Summary
sections.heading: Quantization Profiles Customer Docs Plan > Summary
sections.content:
Summary

This page defines the plan for customer-facing documentation for the Quantization Profile Library (opt-in). The goal is to help customers safely enable quantization profiles per route, understand limitations and compatibility, run appropriate evaluations, interpret observability signals, and roll back quickly if needed.

This is an internal planning doc for Redwood Docs + DevEx and will be used as the source of truth for docs IA, required examples, and cross-team review gates.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Default Thresholds (v1) > Throughput (tokens/sec)
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Default Thresholds (v1) > Throughput (tokens/sec)
sections.content:
Throughput (tokens/sec)

- Warning: tokens/sec **-8%** vs baseline for **2 out of 3** windows.
- Paging: tokens/sec **-15%** vs baseline for **3 out of 4** windows.

sections.section_path: Ci Eval Determinism And Flake Mitigation > Logging and artifacts (required)
sections.heading: Ci Eval Determinism And Flake Mitigation > Logging and artifacts (required)
sections.content:
Logging and artifacts (required)

Each eval run must emit the following into the run artifact directory:

- `run_metadata.json`: model revision, container digest, GPU type, torch version, eval suite name, config snapshot
- RNG details:
  - root seed
  - per-example seed derivation scheme
  - `torch.get_rng_state()` (hex or base64)
  - `torch.cuda.get_rng_state_all()` (per device; hex or base64)
- Generation parameters:
  - do_sample, temperature, top_p, top_k, num_beams, max_new_tokens
- Outputs:
  - `outputs_run_{i}.jsonl` for each repeat
  - include decoded text and decoded token ids
- Summary:
  - `metrics_run_{i}.json`
  - `summary.json` with median/std and output hash comparisons

sections.heading: Quantization Profiles Customer Docs Plan > Information architecture (public docs) > Page 2: Enablement guide (Console + API/SDK)
sections.content:
Page 2: Enablement guide (Console + API/SDK)

**Proposed title:** “Enable a quantization profile for a route”

**Required elements**

- Console walkthrough (with screenshots once UX is final):
  1) Navigate to Route → Performance/Optimize → Quantization
  2) Choose model variant + eligible profiles
  3) Read compatibility warnings
  4) Confirm change (modal) and review expected impact
  5) Verify enablement and view change history

- API example (REST) for updating route config
  - Show setting `quantization_profile_ref` to a specific profile ID/version.
  - Show how to reset to `default` / disable.

- SDK examples
  - Python and TypeScript: configure route setting; retrieve route state; handle incompatibility errors.

**Verification steps**

- Confirm in Console that route shows “Enabled” and which profile is selected.
- Show how to verify in request metadata (e.g., response headers or trace attributes) that a profile was applied vs fallback.
- Show where to find fallback/latency/cost deltas in dashboards.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Anti-Flap, Dedupe, and Hysteresis > Alert clear (hysteresis)
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Anti-Flap, Dedupe, and Hysteresis > Alert clear (hysteresis)
sections.content:
Alert clear (hysteresis)

Alerts clear only when performance returns closer to baseline:

- Warning clears when Δ < +6% (latency) and Δ > -5% (tokens/sec) for 3/3 windows.
- Paging clears when Δ < +12% (latency) and Δ > -10% (tokens/sec) for 4/4 windows.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Default Thresholds (v1)
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Default Thresholds (v1)
sections.content:
Default Thresholds (v1)

Thresholds are configurable per model, with these platform defaults used unless overridden.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Anti-Flap, Dedupe, and Hysteresis > Cooldown
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Anti-Flap, Dedupe, and Hysteresis > Cooldown
sections.content:
Cooldown

After an alert transitions to firing, we enforce a cooldown before re-triggering a new incident thread for the same key:

- Warning cooldown: 60 minutes
- Paging cooldown: 120 minutes

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Decision Drivers
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Decision Drivers
sections.content:
Decision Drivers

1. **Low noise / high trust**: warnings should be useful; pages should be rare and high-confidence.
2. **Fast detection**: detect regressions within ~10–30 minutes for top models in covered regions.
3. **Attribution**: baseline keys must align to dimensions needed for root cause (runtime build, kernel tags, SKU).
4. **Operational simplicity**: SRE/on-call should have a predictable interpretation of “regression vs baseline,” including during ongoing rollouts.
5. **Guardrails against drift and telemetry issues**: avoid alert storms caused by baseline drift, delayed metric ingestion, and label cardinality errors.

sections.section_path: Ci Eval Determinism And Flake Mitigation > What changed since the initial investigation
sections.heading: Ci Eval Determinism And Flake Mitigation > What changed since the initial investigation
sections.content:
What changed since the initial investigation

The original debugging thread identified sampling parameters and missing explicit generators as primary contributors. The current harness incorporates the same core ideas, with the following updates:

- We now treat deterministic decoding as the default for per-commit CI gates for onboarding suites.
- The determinism flag is implemented as `--deterministic` / `deterministic: true` in eval config, and it hard-enforces decoding parameters (see below).
- The runner always constructs and passes an explicit `torch.Generator` for generation, derived from a root seed plus a stable per-example index.
- CI gating moved from single-run metrics to median-of-repeats, and flakiness is measured explicitly.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Anti-Flap, Dedupe, and Hysteresis > Telemetry delay protection
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Anti-Flap, Dedupe, and Hysteresis > Telemetry delay protection
sections.content:
Telemetry delay protection

If telemetry ingestion delay exceeds 2x the evaluation window (e.g., >20 minutes), alert evaluation is suspended and a separate “telemetry delay” warning is emitted to #eng-platform.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Context / Problem
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Context / Problem
sections.content:
Context / Problem

Redwood’s serving runtime changes frequently (kernel selection updates, scheduler heuristics, model config changes, GPU fleet changes, and staged rollouts). We need an always-on canary that:

- Detects real p95 latency regressions and throughput drops early.
- Produces actionable signals for attribution (kernel vs scheduler vs infra).
- Avoids paging on expected variance and baseline drift (e.g., slow fleet mix changes or regional differences).

The key design tension is baseline choice:

- A **fixed baseline** is stable and easy to reason about during rollouts, but can become stale as hardware/driver stacks and workloads evolve.
- A **rolling baseline** adapts over time, but can drift (masking regressions) or create false positives if drift is misinterpreted as regression.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Anti-Flap, Dedupe, and Hysteresis > Dedupe key
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Anti-Flap, Dedupe, and Hysteresis > Dedupe key
sections.content:
Dedupe key

Incident-bot dedupes based on:

- model_id + model_version + runtime_build_id + kernel_set_id + hardware_sku (+ region if present) + metric_type + severity

sections.section_path: Quantization Profiles Customer Docs Plan > Open questions
sections.heading: Quantization Profiles Customer Docs Plan > Open questions
sections.content:
Open questions

1. **Alias semantics:** Will we expose “recommended/latest” aliases in v1 GA or only pinned profile IDs/versions? If aliases exist, we must document how we prevent silent changes (e.g., aliases only change on customer action vs Redwood updates).
2. **Customer-facing compatibility matrix:** What is the minimum viable matrix we can keep current without excessive operational load? (Proposal: publish for top 10 models + major GPU classes first.)
3. **What can we safely publish about quality thresholds?** We should align with Applied ML on whether to include specific numeric deltas or keep it as qualitative guidance.
4. **Request metadata surface:** What is the final customer-visible mechanism to confirm applied profile (headers, response fields, trace attribute)? This must be stable.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Appendix A: Example Per-Model Overrides (illustrative)
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Appendix A: Example Per-Model Overrides (illustrative)
sections.content:
Appendix A: Example Per-Model Overrides (illustrative)

- Top model (customer-critical): paging at +15% p95 E2E, -12% tokens/sec, stricter min token count.
- High-variance model: warning only, wider thresholds (+15% / -10%), region-specific baseline enabled.
- New kernel rollout candidate: temporary tighter warning (+8%) during rollout ring, but paging remains at default until validated.

sections.heading: Quantization Profiles Customer Docs Plan > Notes

Notes

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Minimum Sample Sizes and Windowing > Minimum samples (per key K, per window)
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Minimum Sample Sizes and Windowing > Minimum samples (per key K, per window)
sections.content:
Minimum samples (per key K, per window)

- **Latency metrics**: minimum **200 successful canary requests** per window.
- **Tokens/sec**: minimum **200 successful canary requests** per window AND minimum **50,000 total generated tokens** per window.

If sample requirements are not met:

- No alert state change is allowed (prevents flapping in low-coverage periods).
- Dashboard panels display “insufficient sample” annotation.

Rationale:

- Tail latency (p95/p99) is unreliable with very small N.
- Tokens/sec needs sufficient token volume to smooth per-request variance.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Regression Definition > Core comparison method (v1)
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Regression Definition > Core comparison method (v1)
sections.content:
Core comparison method (v1)

For each metric M and key K in each evaluation window W:

- Compute observed metric value O(K, W).
- Fetch baseline value B(K) and baseline variability estimates when available.
- Compute percent change: Δ = (O - B) / B.

We use percent change thresholds with guardrails (min samples + sustained breach). Percent thresholds are chosen because:

- Different models have different absolute latencies.
- p95 is the primary SLO-relevant tail metric.

sections.section_path: 1751234567 Nondet Seed Top P Ci Gate
sections.heading: 1751234567 Nondet Seed Top P Ci Gate
sections.content:
Priya Rao: Heads-up — our eval runner is flaky on the quantized-v2 onboarding suite. CI reported a 0.04 drop in BLEU on one run, then back to baseline on rerun. stack: `evals/runner.py::run_all`
Mike Chen: Ugh. Did the job show differing lengths or just metric jitter?
Priya Rao: Metric jitter mostly. Same prompts, same seeds (we thought). Logs show `seed=42` passed but outputs diff across runs.
Alyssa Gomez: Common culprits: sampling params (temp/top_p), nondeterministic CUDA kernels, or RNG not propagated to all libs. Are we doing do_sample=True anywhere?
Jordan Li: We default to sampling with `temperature=0.8, top_p=0.9` for some evals. That will be nondet even with same seed if decode uses sampling across threads.
Priya Rao: The eval config for quantize tests uses the canonical config from onboarding.yaml — it sets `do_sample: true`. The weird bit is we see differences even when we change to `do_sample: false` for some runs.
Mike Chen: If `do_sample=false` but we still see nondet, then it's likely from floating point / kernel order or dropout/amp. Which runtime? cudnn, torch 2.x?
Priya Rao: Runner is on a K80 prod node for CI debug and on A100 infra for nightly. Torch 2.1 in both. Quantized model uses int8 kernels on A100 (faster) and fallback ops on K80.
Alyssa Gomez: A100 int8 kernels sometimes reorder operations; also make sure `torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)` and `torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic = True` are set during eval setup. But note that quantized kernels may not be covered by those flags.
Jordan Li: Another angle — are we resetting RNGs per example? We seed at process start, but token sampling can be parallel across batch dim so RNG streams differ per batch ordering. I usually do `generator = torch.Generator(device).manual_seed(seed + shard_id)` and pass explicit generator to sampling operations.
Priya Rao: Good point. Our runner calls `model.generate(...)` without explicit `generator=`.
Mike Chen: Patch suggestion: always pass an explicit generator built from root seed + example index. Also add a small harness for reproducibility: run the same eval N times (N=5) and compute median metric and std. Fail CI if std > threshold.
Alyssa Gomez: Agreed. Also: add a deterministic decode mode for evaluations where we want bit-for-bit repeatability. It would enforce `do_sample=False`, `temperature=0`, `top_k=1`, and `generator` usage. Name it `deterministic=True` in eval config.
Priya Rao: I can add `deterministic` flag to eval schema. What about GPU-level nondet from quant kernels?
Jordan Li: For that, record a golden artifact (reference outputs) from a chosen baseline environment (A100 with Intel RT kernels) and treat other runs as comparators. We can compute a stable similarity metric (e.g., chrF/BLEU diff tolerance) and allow small differences due to quantization. For CI gating of regressions, gate on median across 3 seeds run on the same hardware.
Mike Chen: For CI wiring: 1) run per-commit quick eval in cheap env with deterministic mode, 2) nightly multi-seed non-deterministic checks on target infra (A100) comparing to golden baseline, 3) on-failure, auto-run debug job with expanded logging.
Priya Rao: What expanded logging do we need? I propose: seed, generator states (torch.get_rng_state hex), torch.cuda.get_rng_state_all for GPUs, model version, quantization config, and full decode tokens.
Alyssa Gomez: Yes. Also log sampling params: temperature, top_p, top_k, do_sample, and beam params. And artifacts:

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Decision > 3) Runtime admission/backpressure (last-line protection)
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Decision > 3) Runtime admission/backpressure (last-line protection)
sections.content:
3) Runtime admission/backpressure (last-line protection)

**Runtime owns “what can actually execute”** on a given GPU pool/node.

Runtime responsibilities:

- Enforce hard safety limits: queue depth, scheduler backlog, token/sec saturation, memory/KV-cache pressure.
- Apply backpressure locally (e.g., refuse new admissions to a saturated scheduler; clamp optional features if configured).
- Export saturation signals at bounded cardinality for upstream decisions.

Runtime should be able to reject quickly with an internal reason that maps to stable overload error codes at the edge (ADR-014). Runtime should not attempt cross-region balancing.

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Alerting (paging + ticketing) > Overload protection operational alerts
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Alerting (paging + ticketing) > Overload protection operational alerts
sections.content:
Overload protection operational alerts

These are predictive/guardrail alerts. Configure as:

- **Page (Sev2):** enterprise overload shedding sustained
  - enterprise `shed_rate` > **0.1%** for **10 minutes** (any protected route)
- **Ticket:** best-effort shedding unexpectedly high at low utilization
  - best-effort `shed_rate` > **20%** for **15 minutes** AND GPU utilization < **65%** (indicates policy mis-tuning or signal errors)
- **Ticket:** queue depth / scheduler lag sustained without corresponding shedding
  - queue depth > threshold for **10 minutes** with `admission_control_active=false` (indicates missing trigger wiring)

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Decision > Summary: decision table
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Decision > Summary: decision table
sections.content:
Summary: decision table

| Layer | Owns | Should do | Must not do |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gateway | Early rejection + tenant/tier fairness | Token bucket / concurrency caps, dependency circuit breakers, consistent overload responses | GPU-level scheduling decisions, multi-step retry/fallback loops |
| Routing | Target selection + bounded graceful degradation | Single bounded fallback attempt (if configured), loop prevention, target health gating | Global rate limiting, unbounded retries, per-GPU fairness |
| Runtime | Local safety + scheduling viability | Backpressure, queue/kv/memory safety, feature clamping (policy-controlled), export saturation signals | Cross-region routing decisions, customer-specific policy interpretation |

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Definitions > Route tiers
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Definitions > Route tiers
sections.content:
Definitions

Route tiers

We classify requests into one of the following tiers at the gateway/policy engine:

- **Enterprise (Protected):** SLA-bearing tenants and allowlisted enterprise accounts for protected routes. These requests receive priority admission and are protected during fleet pressure.
- **Best-effort:** all other traffic. Best-effort may be throttled earlier and more aggressively to preserve fleet health and enterprise budgets.

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Rationale > Avoiding feedback loops
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Rationale > Avoiding feedback loops
sections.content:
Avoiding feedback loops

Layering introduces risks of control loops where:

- Gateway sheds → routing sees less traffic and declares healthy → gateway admits more → oscillation
- Runtime rejects → routing fails over → overload moves to another region → cascading rejection

We mitigate these via:

- **Hysteresis and smoothing** on saturation signals used by gateway and routing.
- **Single-step bounded fallback** (no multi-hop) and strict loop-prevention.
- **Separation of timescales** (runtime reacts fastest; gateway/routing react slower with stabilized aggregates).

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Implementation notes (non-normative)
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Implementation notes (non-normative)
sections.content:
Implementation notes (non-normative)

- Gateway admission should use a combination of:
  - token bucket (QPS) per tenant/route
  - concurrency caps for streaming endpoints
  - “regional overload state” multiplier for dynamic throttling (with hysteresis)
- Runtime should expose clear “reject reasons” that map into ADR-014 overload codes without leaking internals.
- Routing should mark fallback attempts and enforce max_attempts=1. Any further attempt must be a client retry honoring Retry-After.

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Signal flow (normative) > Routing → gateway/runtime (bounded outcomes)
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Signal flow (normative) > Routing → gateway/runtime (bounded outcomes)
sections.content:
Routing → gateway/runtime (bounded outcomes)

Routing returns one of:

- Success (target selected)
- Overload response (with stable overload code)
- Success after single fallback attempt (internally recorded)

Routing should not instruct gateway to immediately open/close breakers. Gateway breaker state changes must come from its own breaker logic using stabilized aggregates and its local dependency health.

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Consequences > Positive
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Consequences > Positive
sections.content:
Consequences

Positive

- Earlier, clearer shedding reduces tail latency and incident severity.
- Tenant/tier fairness is enforced consistently at the edge.
- Runtime remains protected even if gateway/routing misestimate load.
- Routing provides graceful degradation (fallback) without turning into a retry storm engine.

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Consequences > Negative / tradeoffs
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Consequences > Negative / tradeoffs
sections.content:
Negative / tradeoffs

- More moving parts: three layers must align on semantics and observability.
- Tuning is non-trivial; requires careful rollout with canaries and dashboards.
- Signal aggregation adds latency; gateway decisions may lag rapid runtime changes (mitigated by runtime hard limits).

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Rationale > Why involve routing?
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Rationale > Why involve routing?
sections.content:
Why involve routing?

Routing is the only layer that can safely implement **graceful degradation** (fallback model/region) and integrate capacity/health signals across targets. However, routing must be strictly bounded to avoid shifting overload around the system.

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Circuit breaker placement
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Circuit breaker placement
sections.content:
Circuit breaker placement

We define three breaker types:
1) **Gateway dependency breakers** (fast, local)

- Trips on: auth/usage service latency/timeouts, policy-engine unavailability, routing service brownout
- Action: fail closed with stable 503 (dependency_unavailable) or 429/503 overload class per ADR-014 mapping

2) **Gateway overload breakers** (regional, policy-driven)

- Trips on: sustained regional saturation state = critical AND shed budget exceeded OR error-budget protection triggers
- Action: shed by tier/tenant/route with predictable semantics; include Retry-After

3) **Runtime safety breakers** (hard stop)

- Trips on: queue depth hard limit, memory pressure beyond threshold, scheduler unable to admit
- Action: reject immediately; propagate internal reason for edge mapping

Routing uses “health gates” rather than circuit breakers for most target selection decisions. Routing may maintain a short-lived “avoid target” cache with hysteresis to reduce flapping.

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > SLIs (what we measure) > 1) Availability SLI (server success)
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > SLIs (what we measure) > 1) Availability SLI (server success)
sections.content:
1) Availability SLI (server success)

**Definition:** percentage of requests that return an eligible success response.

- Success codes: `2xx` (and `3xx` if any internal redirects apply; typically none)
- Failures: `5xx`, `408`, `499` (client disconnect) are counted as failures unless explicitly excluded by route-specific rules below.

**Tier handling of 429:**

- **Enterprise:** `429` due to *overload shedding/admission control* counts as **unavailable** (because enterprise is protected; overload shed should be rare and indicates under-provisioning or misconfiguration).
- **Best-effort:** `429` due to overload shedding/admission control does **not** count as unavailable (it is expected behavior under pressure). Quota/rate-limit 429s are not counted as availability failures for either tier.

**Note:** 429 classification must be based on the reason code emitted by gateway/policy engine, not inferred from rate.

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Ownership
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Ownership
sections.content:
Ownership

- SLO definitions and alert policy: **SRE (Rafael Mendes / Aisha Bello)**
- Metric correctness and tagging: **Telemetry (Logan Wright)**
- Enforcement behavior (429 reason codes, gateway semantics): **API Gateway (Amara Diallo)**
- Priority routing/admission control behavior: **Smart Routing (Mina Haddad)**

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Operational guidance > How to interpret 429s for SLOs
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Operational guidance > How to interpret 429s for SLOs
sections.content:
Operational guidance

How to interpret 429s for SLOs

- **Enterprise 429 overload-shed:** treat as incident-worthy and investigate capacity signals, admission thresholds, route budgets, and pool weights.
- **Best-effort 429 overload-shed:** expected under pressure; use this to validate the protection is working (enterprise should remain stable).
- **Quota 429 (any tier):** not an SLO failure; route to Support/Solutions for policy adjustment if needed.

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > SLIs (what we measure) > 2) Latency SLI
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > SLIs (what we measure) > 2) Latency SLI
sections.content:
2) Latency SLI

Latency is measured at the gateway edge (request receive to first byte / completion) and reported as:

- **TTFB (time-to-first-byte)** for streaming endpoints.
- **E2E response time** for non-streaming.

We maintain distinct latency SLO targets per tier and route (see tables below).

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Alerting (paging + ticketing) > Paging routing
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Alerting (paging + ticketing) > Paging routing
sections.content:
Paging routing

- Primary: **#eng-oncall** and SRE pager rotation
- Secondary: **#eng-platform** for policy/gateway issues, **#eng-runtime** for scheduler lag/queue depth anomalies

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Operational guidance > Change management
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Operational guidance > Change management
sections.content:
Change management

Changes that affect enterprise SLOs require:

- Feature flag + region canary
- Dashboard annotation
- Rollback plan
- Confirmed alert routing and runbook link in incident-bot message

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > SLIs (what we measure)
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > SLIs (what we measure)
sections.content:
SLIs (what we measure)

All SLIs are computed per **route x region x tier** using the standard metrics set.

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Dashboard requirements (minimum)
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Dashboard requirements (minimum)
sections.content:
Dashboard requirements (minimum)

Every protected route must have:

- Availability by tier (enterprise vs best-effort)
- Latency p95/p99 by tier (and TTFB for streaming)
- 429 rate split by reason code (quota vs overload)
- shed_rate and admission_control_active
- queue depth and scheduler lag for backing pools
- Annotations for config changes, feature flag toggles, fallback activation

See the dashboard spec for panel/query naming conventions.

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Alerting (paging + ticketing) > Enterprise latency alerts
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Alerting (paging + ticketing) > Enterprise latency alerts
sections.content:
Enterprise latency alerts

For each protected route x region:

- **Page (Sev2):** p99 latency SLO violated for **15 minutes** AND admission control active (or queue depth high)
- **Ticket:** p95 latency SLO violated for **60 minutes**

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Signal flow (normative)
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Signal flow (normative)
sections.content:
Signal flow (normative)

This section is normative for implementation.

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Signal flow (normative) > Runtime → telemetry → routing/gateway (aggregated)
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Signal flow (normative) > Runtime → telemetry → routing/gateway (aggregated)
sections.content:
Runtime → telemetry → routing/gateway (aggregated)

Runtime exports saturation metrics at pool/cluster granularity:

- scheduler_queue_depth (gauge)
- scheduler_backlog_ms (gauge)
- token_throughput_utilization (0..1)
- kv_cache_pressure (0..1)
- memory_pressure_proxy (0..1)

A telemetry aggregation layer produces:

- per-region/per-model “saturation state” (e.g., normal / elevated / critical)
- smoothed utilization signals (EMA or rolling windows)
- recommended admission modifiers (e.g., suggested shed percent)

Gateway and routing consume **aggregated** signals; they should not consume high-cardinality per-node metrics.

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Operational guidance (brief)
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Operational guidance (brief)
sections.content:
Operational guidance (brief)

- When overload happens, prefer adjusting gateway policy thresholds and shed behavior before touching runtime queue settings.
- Use routing fallback only for tenants that have explicitly opted in and where compatible models are defined.
- Watch for oscillation: frequent breaker open/close events or high fallback attempt rates are indicators of unstable thresholds.

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Error budgets > Error budget policy (what we do when we burn)
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Error budgets > Error budget policy (what we do when we burn)
sections.content:
Error budget policy (what we do when we burn)

**Enterprise (Protected) routes**

- If burn is elevated, the default stance is **protect SLOs over throughput**.
- Allowed mitigations (in priority order):
  1) Tighten best-effort admission control thresholds (shed earlier)
  2) Temporarily reduce best-effort burst allowances
  3) Increase enterprise reserved capacity / pool weights (if available)
  4) Enable guarded fallback policies where contractually allowed
  5) As last resort: temporary enterprise throttling with exec/on-call approval and proactive comms

**Best-effort routes**

- Best-effort can be shed under pressure; we do not page purely on best-effort 429 shedding.
- If best-effort availability drops due to 5xx (not 429 overload-shed), we investigate as a normal reliability regression.

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Decision > 1) Gateway admission control (primary front-door protection)
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Decision > 1) Gateway admission control (primary front-door protection)
sections.content:
1) Gateway admission control (primary front-door protection)

**Gateway owns “who gets in”** based on:

- Tenant/tier policy (Hosted self-serve vs enterprise Hosted vs Dedicated routing paths)
- Per-route/model caps (concurrency, QPS/token-bucket style limits)
- Coarse-grained regional overload state (from aggregated signals)
- Dependency health gates for gateway-local dependencies (auth, quota/usage checks, policy engine, routing service)

Gateway behavior under overload:

- Return customer-facing errors per ADR-014 (typically 429 or 503 with stable overload error codes).
- Include correlation_id and consistent Retry-After semantics.
- Prefer **fail fast** when signals indicate sustained overload (avoid letting requests queue indefinitely).

Gateway does **not** attempt fine-grained GPU scheduling decisions.

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Open questions / follow-ups
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Open questions / follow-ups
sections.content:
Open questions / follow-ups

- Define standard hysteresis parameters for “regional saturation state” (window sizes, open/close thresholds) and document in the policy engine page.
- Confirm SLO accounting and error budget treatment for overload-induced errors (tracked in Hosted API SLO policy update).
- Validate that runtime exported signals remain bounded cardinality and are stable under rolling deploys.

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Policy and configuration boundaries
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Policy and configuration boundaries
sections.content:
Policy and configuration boundaries

- Tier defaults (Hosted self-serve, enterprise Hosted, Dedicated) live in the overload policy engine and are enforced primarily at gateway.
- Per-tenant overrides are evaluated at gateway and must be validated with guardrails (e.g., cannot exceed global safety caps).
- Runtime receives only what it needs for execution and safety (e.g., max_tokens cap adjustments or feature flags), not tenant policy logic.

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Decision > 2) Routing admission + fallback (secondary protection and graceful degradation)
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Decision > 2) Routing admission + fallback (secondary protection and graceful degradation)
sections.content:
2) Routing admission + fallback (secondary protection and graceful degradation)

**Routing owns “where it goes”** and **controlled degradation**, not global rate limiting.

Routing responsibilities:

- Choose region/model deployment target using policy (latency/cost/availability) and health signals.
- If gateway-admitted traffic hits a saturated target, routing may:
  - Attempt **configured fallback model/region** (bounded, loop-safe) when policy allows.
  - Otherwise, return an overload response consistent with ADR-014.

Routing must not create uncontrolled amplification (e.g., fan-out retries across regions). Routing is permitted to do **at most one** fallback attempt per request, and must enforce loop-prevention.

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Alternatives considered
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Alternatives considered
sections.content:
Alternatives considered

1) **Single global breaker at gateway only**

- Rejected: insufficient fidelity; cannot protect runtime safety in all cases; still allows deep queueing.

2) **Runtime-only backpressure (let everything in)**

- Rejected: overload manifests as queued latency/timeouts; poor customer semantics; wastes upstream work.

3) **Routing-driven global admission control**

- Rejected: routing is not the best place to enforce tenant fairness and local dependency breakers; risks complex control loops.

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Definitions > Overload / throttling semantics
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Definitions > Overload / throttling semantics
sections.content:
Overload / throttling semantics

Requests may be rejected with HTTP **429** for:

- **Quota/rate limit enforcement** (tenant policy)
- **Overload shedding/admission control** (fleet protection)

We distinguish causes via standardized reason code headers/payloads (see Support doc for exact fields). For SLO accounting, we treat quota-throttled and overload-shed requests differently by tier (see SLI rules below).

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Context
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Context
sections.content:
Context

Redwood Inference’s Hosted API sees bursty and highly variable traffic (prompt length variance, streaming concurrency spikes, regional capacity dips). During overload, failures can cascade into:

- Tail-latency blowups (p95/p99), then timeouts
- Elevated 5xx from upstream retry storms and downstream saturation
- Noisy-neighbor effects across tenants and tiers
- Confusing customer experience (timeouts and generic 5xx instead of stable semantics)

We need a layered admission control strategy that:
1) Rejects or degrades traffic early and predictably.
2) Preserves tenant isolation and tier-aware behavior.
3) Avoids feedback loops (e.g., shedding causing routing thrash, or routing failover amplifying load elsewhere).
4) Produces consistent customer-facing overload errors (see ADR-014).

This ADR defines **where circuit breakers and load shedding “live”** across the request path (Gateway → Routing → Runtime) and how signals flow.

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Rationale > Why not “only runtime”?
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Rationale > Why not “only runtime”?
sections.content:
Why not “only runtime”?

Runtime-only rejection is too late:

- Wastes work in upstream services (auth, routing, logging, request parsing)
- Increases tail latency due to queue buildup
- Fails to enforce tenant/tier fairness consistently across services

Gateway is best suited to shed early and protect downstreams.

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Alerting (paging + ticketing) > Alert principles
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Alerting (paging + ticketing) > Alert principles
sections.content:
Alerting (paging + ticketing)

Alert principles

- Page on **enterprise** impact (availability/latency) and on conditions that predict imminent enterprise impact.
- Do not page on expected best-effort shedding unless it indicates misconfiguration or runaway protection (e.g., shedding at low utilization).
- Use multi-window burn rate to avoid flapping.

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > SLOs (targets) > Latency SLOs by route and tier
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > SLOs (targets) > Latency SLOs by route and tier
sections.content:
Latency SLOs by route and tier

Latency objectives are defined in terms of:

- **Chat streaming:** TTFB p95/p99
- **Non-streaming:** E2E p95/p99

| Route | Tier | Latency SLO (primary) | Latency SLO (secondary) | Measurement |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| `/v1/chat/completions` (streaming) | Enterprise (Protected) | TTFB p95 ≤ 450ms | TTFB p99 ≤ 900ms | Gateway TTFB |
| `/v1/chat/completions` (streaming) | Best-effort | TTFB p95 ≤ 900ms | (informational) p99 ≤ 1800ms | Gateway TTFB |
| `/v1/chat/completions` (non-streaming) | Enterprise (Protected) | E2E p95 ≤ 1.8s | E2E p99 ≤ 3.5s | Gateway E2E |
| `/v1/embeddings` | Enterprise (Protected) | E2E p95 ≤ 350ms | E2E p99 ≤ 800ms | Gateway E2E |
| `/v1/embeddings` | Best-effort | E2E p95 ≤ 700ms | (informational) p99 ≤ 1.5s | Gateway E2E |
| `/v1/rerank` | Enterprise (Protected) | E2E p95 ≤ 550ms | E2E p99 ≤ 1.2s | Gateway E2E |
| `/v1/rerank` | Best-effort | E2E p95 ≤ 1.2s | (informational) p99 ≤ 2.5s | Gateway E2E |

**Notes / caveats**

- Latency SLOs assume nominal prompt and response sizes. Excessive prompt length or extreme max_tokens increases may be subject to policy limits; those requests are still included in latency metrics unless explicitly rejected by policy.
- Where fallback is permitted (route/model policy), latency SLI measures the actual served path; dashboards must annotate fallback activations.

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > SLOs (targets) > General notes
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > SLOs (targets) > General notes
sections.content:
SLOs (targets)

General notes

- SLOs are evaluated over a **rolling 28-day window**.
- Unless specified, targets apply per region (e.g., us-east, eu-west).
- We define both **p95 and p99** latency objectives for enterprise; best-effort uses p95 as primary.

Gateway → routing (request-scoped hints)

When gateway admits a request, it may attach request-scoped metadata:

- tenant_id, tier

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Purpose
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Purpose
sections.content:
Purpose

This document defines **per-route SLOs and error budget policy** for Redwood Inference’s **Hosted API** as it relates to **hot-route capacity protection** (tier-aware quotas, priority routing, and controlled shedding).

The intent is to:

- Explicitly define **enterprise vs best-effort** expectations for the highest-traffic routes.
- Make overload behavior **measurable and supportable** (clear SLIs + dashboards + alerts).
- Align alerting to overload protection so we page on **enterprise degradation**, not expected best-effort shedding.

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Scope
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Scope
sections.content:
Scope

**In scope**

- Hosted API routes: `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/embeddings`, `/v1/rerank`, `/v1/completions`.
- Tiered behavior: **Enterprise (Protected)** vs **Best-effort (Standard/Self-serve)**.
- SLOs for **availability**, **latency**, and **overload responses (429)**.
- Alert thresholds and error budget burn policy.

**Out of scope**

- Dedicated and Private SLOs (tracked separately).
- Model-quality or semantic correctness SLIs.

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Error budgets > Error budget calculation
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Error budgets > Error budget calculation
sections.content:
Error budgets

Error budget calculation

For an SLO target **T** over a 28-day window:

- Error budget = **1 − T**

Examples:

- 99.95% availability ⇒ 0.05% error budget (≈ 21.6 minutes of downtime equivalent over 28 days)
- 99.5% availability ⇒ 0.5% error budget

We track budgets separately per:

- route
- region
- tier

sections.content:
Budget stop-the-line triggers

For enterprise protected routes, any of the following triggers a “stop the line” review in the weekly reliability sync (or async in #eng-sre if urgent):

- Availability error budget burn ≥ **50%** in 7 days
- p99 latency SLO violated for ≥ **2 hours** in a day (sustained)
- Overload shedding observed for enterprise traffic (non-zero sustained) outside planned game day / load test windows

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Rationale > Why not “only gateway”?
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Rationale > Why not “only gateway”?
sections.content:
Rationale

Why not “only gateway”?

Gateway-only decisions lack the most accurate, immediate view of per-pool saturation. If the gateway admits traffic without runtime backpressure, overload still manifests as long queues/timeouts. Runtime is the source of truth for “can this execute now?”.

sections.section_path: Metering To Invoice Reconciliation Playbook > Definitions (canonical)
sections.heading: Metering To Invoice Reconciliation Playbook > Definitions (canonical)
sections.content:
Definitions (canonical)

**Billing Ledger:** The internal finance-grade table used to generate invoice line items. This is the **source of truth for invoicing** once the billing freeze occurs.

**Usage Events:** Telemetry events emitted per request (or per logical request segment) that contain metered quantities (e.g., billed_tokens, requests, cache_hit attribution, gpu_seconds).

**Customer Usage Export / Usage API:** Customer-facing aggregation derived from usage events and/or ledger with documented lag and schema. Used for customer validation and dispute resolution.

**Reconciliation Grain:**

- Hosted API: account_id × usage_date (UTC) × region × model × product_route (chat/completions/embeddings/rerank) × price_plan
- Dedicated: account_id × usage_date (UTC) × pool_id × region × sku

**Freeze Window:** A time after which we stop changing ledger totals for the close period except via an approved adjustment process. (See Finance Slack thread and the month-end checklist.)

---

sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Metrics Covered
sections.content:
Metrics Covered

Baselines and regressions are computed for:

- End-to-end latency: p50, p95, p99 (ms)
- Runtime-only latency: p50, p95, p99 (ms) (excludes network/client)
- Prefill latency and decode latency (ms)
- Queueing time (ms) (scheduler-level)
- Tokens/sec (overall, and decode tokens/sec where available)
- Batch size distribution (for attribution)
- KV cache hit rate (where applicable; informational at v1)

sections.section_path: 2025 05 28 Private Upgrades Technical Deep Dive
sections.heading: 2025 05 28 Private Upgrades Technical Deep Dive
sections.content:
[01:30] Fatima Noor: Sure. So the direction is: the installer generates an upgrade plan first, it’s a versioned artifact that lists stages and steps. Before doing anything, we run preflight checks—cluster health, storage headroom, DNS/TLS, RBAC, database connectivity, and also artifact availability. Then we orchestrate backups. After that we execute the plan in phases: control plane first, then data plane, with readiness gates. If something fails, we have deterministic rollback entry points that use stored state from the plan execution.

[02:05] Priya Raman: When you say installer—this is the redwood-private-installer CLI, right? Not Helm itself?

[02:10] Fatima Noor: Correct. Helm still does the actual apply of charts, but we wrap it with an orchestrator so we can be consistent and auditable.

[02:19] Marisol Chen: Auditable meaning we can show, like, exactly what checks ran and what was backed up?

[02:24] Fatima Noor: Exactly. Plan output persisted, precheck results, backup IDs, and upgrade start/stop events.

[02:31] Irene Choi: And timestamps, plus versions: current version, target version, and what artifacts were used.

[02:39] Marisol Chen: Okay.

[02:41] Markus Klein: Evan, can you describe your on-prem constraints? Like how air-gapped are we talking.

[02:47] Evan Wu: Fully. No outbound internet. We have an internal artifact mirror for container images and we can host a chart repo internally, but it’s manual. Also we need checksums for everything. Our security team won’t allow “curl random thing during upgrade.”

[03:06] Marisol Chen: And signatures if possible. Checksums alone are… better than nothing, but ideally there’s a signing chain.

[03:13] Fatima Noor: Yep. So we’re adding bundle verification: manifest, checksums, and optional signatures. The installer will fail early if the bundle doesn’t match.

[03:24] Priya Raman: Can it operate with, like, a USB drop? We sometimes do physical transfer to the restricted enclave.

[03:30] Fatima Noor: That’s a supported model. The bundle is basically a directory or tarball with a manifest file plus all referenced artifacts.

[03:40] Bruno Silva: And on the Terraform side for VPC it’s a bit different, but for on-prem we’ll document “offline registry endpoint” variables too, so the installer knows where to pull from without going to the public registry.

[03:54] Evan Wu: Okay. Biggest pain for us is, if Helm upgrade fails, we don’t know what state we’re in. Like, was the database migrated? Was it halfway? And then we get stuck.

[04:08] Sean Gallagher: Right. So we’re defining “rollback hooks” as part of the plan. The critical part is: schema migrations have to be guarded. We’re implementing idempotency checks and lock timeouts. Also, we’re biasing to backwards-compatible changes when possible so rollback doesn’t require “un-migrating” data.

[04:28] Jake Miller: That’s good in theory but we’ve seen migration jobs hold locks for a long time.

[04:32] Sean Gallagher: Yep. We’ve been tuning defaults—like statement timeouts and lock timeouts—so a bad migration doesn’t freeze the cluster. And the precheck will also test DB connectivity and maybe space.

[04:45] Priya Raman: Can we dig into prechecks? Which ones are blocking? Because we don’t want the system to block over something we accept risk on.

sections.section_path: Pr 27463 Fix Double Counting On Stream Retry
sections.heading: Pr 27463 Fix Double Counting On Stream Retry
sections.content:
- This change is behind feature flag billing.metering_stream_retry_dedupe_v1 (default off). Plan: enable in staging for 48h, then canary 5% of hosted traffic (US-East + two high-volume accounts), then ramp to 50% and 100% if drift checks remain within thresholds.
- Shadow-billing: for the canary phase, ledger will compute both old and new billable usage in parallel (annotated in the recon export) to quantify deltas; Finance/RevRec sign-off required before 100% rollout.
- Backfill: no backfill in this PR. If shadow-billing indicates material historical impact, we’ll follow the RevRec playbook for corrective credits rather than retroactive invoice edits.

Customer impact: Fixes an overbilling bug in specific streaming retry/fallback scenarios (primarily server-side retries). In most cases, customers should see billed token counts decrease slightly for affected days; usage API exports will show clearer attempt attribution fields once the related API surface PR lands.

Checklist:

- [x] Added unit coverage for streaming retry + fallback paths
- [x] Added integration coverage for forced retry in staging
- [x] Added metrics + logs for superseded attempts
- [x] Rollout plan documented + flag added
- [x] Linked to support escalation SUP-28463 and Linear ENG-4430

Notes for reviewers: Please focus on (a) dedupe key stability across OpenAI-compatible endpoints, (b) ensuring we never bill SUPERSEDED attempts, and (c) any edge cases where SUCCESS could be emitted after partial stream termination.
Logan Wright (review): The dedupe_key derivation uses request_id for non-idempotent requests — do we normalize OpenAI-compat request IDs the same way as native endpoints? Author (Cole): Good catch. I added normalization to strip the gateway-generated suffix and included a regression test for /v1/chat/completions streaming. Nadia Rahman (review): Can we guarantee terminal_reason cannot be SUCCESS for the superseded attempt if the client disconnects? Also please document semantics of CLIENT_DISCONNECT vs SUPERSEDED. Author: Updated the state machine so SUCCESS is only emitted from the finalization path that sees a completed stream; client disconnect now emits CLIENT_DISCONNECT and short-circuits retries. Added inline docs and tests. Aisha Bello (review): Please add a metric we can alert on for high superseded rates per route/model; also add log fields so SRE can join events. Author: Added usage_events_superseded_total with route+model labels (bounded), and structured log fields usage_dedupe_key/attempt_seq. Connor O'Brien (review): Rollout plan needs an explicit canary and revert procedure. Author: Expanded rollout section with percentages, regions, and revert steps (flag off, keep shadow-billing for 24h). Monica Patel (review): Ensure SDK retries using idempotency_key don’t change dedupe semantics. Author: Dedupe prefers idempotency_key when present; added a test that simulates client retry with same idempotency key and confirms single billable attempt. Final: Approved after changes; merged squash.
Fixes a bug where streaming retries/fallbacks could double-count billed tokens by ensuring only the final successful attempt is billable; adds retry attempt attribution fields and regression coverage; rolled out behind feature flag billing.metering_stream_retry_dedupe_v1 with shadow-billing support.

sections.section_path: Quantization Profiles Customer Docs Plan > Information architecture (public docs) > Page 4: Evaluation best practices
sections.heading: Quantization Profiles Customer Docs Plan > Information architecture (public docs) > Page 4: Evaluation best practices
sections.content:
Page 4: Evaluation best practices

**Proposed title:** “How to evaluate quality and latency before rollout”

**Customer-friendly guidance**

- Suggested evaluation approach:
  - Identify representative prompts (production samples + edge cases).
  - Run baseline vs profile-enabled comparisons.
  - Use A/B sampling (e.g., 1–5% traffic) with a rollback threshold.

- What to measure
  - Quality: task-specific metrics (pass@k, exact match, ranking metrics) + human review where appropriate.
  - Latency: p50/p95 decode latency and time-to-first-token.
  - Cost: cost/token and throughput.

- Rollout strategy
  1) Enable in staging on a non-critical route
  2) Canary in production (small % traffic)
  3) Expand gradually with monitoring

- Provide explicit “stop conditions”
  - Elevated fallback rate
  - Increased error rate
  - Statistically meaningful quality regression on a defined slice

**Note:** We cannot publish Redwood’s internal thresholds verbatim if they are considered sensitive, but we can publish recommended guardrails (e.g., “predefine acceptable deltas and require sign-off”). We will align with Selene Huang (quality guardrails) on what’s safe to disclose.
