sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Definitions > Overload / throttling semantics
sections.content:
Overload / throttling semantics

Requests may be rejected with HTTP **429** for:

- **Quota/rate limit enforcement** (tenant policy)
- **Overload shedding/admission control** (fleet protection)

We distinguish causes via standardized reason code headers/payloads (see Support doc for exact fields). For SLO accounting, we treat quota-throttled and overload-shed requests differently by tier (see SLI rules below).

sections.section_path: Pr 18458 Smart Routing Fallback When Breaker Open
sections.heading: Pr 18458 Smart Routing Fallback When Breaker Open
sections.content:
Pr 18458 Smart Routing Fallback When Breaker Open

Source type: github
Document ID: dsid_960a2981de674ebf844f7dc19d2e3cc0
Release: v1.0.0
Benchmark: EnterpriseRAG-Bench synthetic upstream data
Smart Routing: fallback model/region when overload breaker is open (bounded + loop-safe)

Context: As part of the hosted overload protection work, we want to degrade gracefully instead of cascading timeouts when a model/region is saturated. This PR adds a routing-side fallback attempt when the upstream admission layer reports an overload breaker open (or equivalent overload classification).

What this PR does: Implements a fallback resolution step in Smart Routing that can (optionally) route to a compatible fallback model and/or fallback region based on tenant + route policy. Adds strict loop prevention so we don’t bounce between model variants/regions, and bounds fallback attempts to a small fixed number to avoid amplifying load. Also ensures we do not fallback for non-overload failures (e.g., auth, invalid params, quota exceeded).

Key behaviors: (1) Trigger conditions: only when overload classification indicates breaker open / load shed / capacity unavailable (see mapping in code comments); not triggered on generic 5xx. (2) Fallback selection: consults policy engine for allowed fallbacks for the tenant + route + requested model; if none configured, behave as before. (3) Bounded attempts: max 1 fallback per request by default (configurable to 2 for region+model hop, but guarded); stops immediately if fallback target equals original target. (4) Loop prevention: propagates an internal routing context header across internal hops and records visited (model, region) pairs; if the candidate is already visited, we do not attempt it. (5) Observability: emits counters for fallback_attempted, fallback_succeeded, fallback_blocked_loop, and fallback_exhausted; dimensions intentionally low-cardinality (tenant_tier, route_group, requested_model_family, result).

Why routing (not gateway): The gateway admission layer is responsible for shedding early, but only routing knows compatibility constraints and tenant policy for fallback targets. This is consistent with the admission layering guidance (see ADR-015) — the gateway classifies overload; routing decides a safe alternate target; runtime remains the source of saturation signals.

Safety constraints: Dedicated and Private tenants are never routed to Hosted. Hosted self-serve can fallback within Hosted only. Enterprise Hosted can fallback only to configured allowlisted model variants and regions. We also explicitly disallow cross-AZ fallback within a region to avoid hiding infra issues; region fallback is an explicit opt-in.

Testing: Unit tests cover loop prevention, bounded retries, policy deny, and correct trigger mapping. Integration test fakes breaker-open signals and verifies we attempt exactly one fallback and preserve the correlation ID. Perf-canary scenario work is tracked separately.

Follow-ups: (a) tune default max attempts and error mapping once we have canary data; (b) add dashboard panel for fallback rates vs shed rate; (c) document customer-facing behavior once GA’d (docs owned by DevEx/Docs).

- Smart Routing can now attempt policy-configured fallback model/region when overload protection opens a circuit breaker, with bounded retries and loop prevention. No API surface changes; behavior is opt-in via policy.

Mina Haddad (review): Can you clarify the max attempts logic? I want to ensure we can’t end up trying multiple fallbacks and increasing traffic under overload. Also, please confirm we never cross Hosted/Dedicated boundaries.

sections.section_path: Sup 2892 Fallback Model Not Triggering During Overload
sections.heading: Sup 2892 Fallback Model Not Triggering During Overload
sections.content:
2025-12-09 09:12 PT — Owen Phillips (Support): Customer (Banyan Search) reports fallback not triggering. They configured fallback from 70B -> 8B for overload, but still getting 503 OVERLOADED during peak. Provided correlation IDs and noted they are using streaming on /v1/chat/completions in us-east. Creating ticket and pulling in routing/SRE.
2025-12-09 09:28 PT — Dev Patel (Support readiness): Confirmed this aligns with multiple questions we’re getting since overload protection canary. Linking SUP-2860 as customer also mentioned missing Retry-After on a subset of responses.
2025-12-09 10:05 PT — Peter Holtz (Routing reliability): Looking at traces for rwcorr_01JEMNQZJ5J9P2G6E3R9K8V6M2 — request is being rejected at gateway admission (breaker open) with shed_reason=gateway_concurrency_cap before smart-routing service is called. So fallback cannot occur because routing is not invoked in this path. This matches ADR-015 layering behavior.
2025-12-09 10:19 PT — Peter Holtz (Routing reliability): Confirmed tenant policy has fallback configured, but current behavior: fallback is only evaluated on downstream overload signals (routing/runtime) and certain error codes. Gateway-level shedding is treated as terminal to stop retry storms and protect downstream. We need to align with Product whether we want optional 'fallback_when_breaker_open' semantics.
2025-12-09 10:42 PT — Nikhil Sharma (Product owner, Hosted API): For now, we should be explicit: fallback is best-effort and may not apply when admission control rejects early. However, for enterprise customers we can consider allowing fallback on gateway overload with strict guardrails (bounded retries, no loops, only within compatibility group). Please propose a safe tenant-scoped override if feasible.
2025-12-09 11:10 PT — Rafael Mendes (SRE lead): +1. If we allow fallback on gateway overload, need to ensure we’re not just shifting load to the fallback pool and causing broader instability. Suggest: only allow if fallback targets a different capacity pool/priority class and enforce additional max_tokens cap under duress.
2025-12-10 08:55 PT — Elena Popov (Routing signals integration): Found second issue: in cases where routing is invoked (runtime returns overload), fallback was suppressed for Banyan because loop-prevention saw attempted_models already populated from a previous internal retry. There’s a bug: we’re persisting attempted_models across an internal redirect even when the first attempt never reached the model backend due to a fast-fail overload. That makes the router think it already tried the fallback and stops.
2025-12-10 09:30 PT — Ravi Menon (Fallback routing architect): Root cause seems twofold:
(1) Most failures happen pre-routing (gateway admission sheds) => fallback not possible.
(2) In the subset that reaches routing, a header bookkeeping issue causes loop-prevention to incorrectly block fallback.
Proposed fix: clear attempted_models when the failure is classified as 'admission_shed' vs 'model_attempted'. We can hotfix routing to only append attempted_models after a backend attempt is made.
2025-12-10 10:15 PT — Amara Diallo (Gateway middleware): Confirmed gateway emits overload classification as 'gateway_admission_shed' with reason codes concurrency_cap / token_bucket. It does not call routing service in this path. If we want fallback here, it needs a design change (admission would have to consult routing policy, or we let some fraction through to routing for fallback evaluation).
2025-12-10 11:05 PT — Peter Holtz (Routing reliability): Action items:

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Default Thresholds (v1) > Runtime-only attribution signals (non-paging by default)
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Default Thresholds (v1) > Runtime-only attribution signals (non-paging by default)
sections.content:
Runtime-only attribution signals (non-paging by default)

These are emitted to dashboards and included in alert payloads, but do not page unless explicitly enabled for a model:

- Queueing time p95 +25% (suggests scheduler/fleet saturation)
- Prefill p95 +15% (suggests kernel/model config regressions)
- Decode p95 +15% (suggests kernel/model config regressions)

Rationale:

- Paging should be driven by end-to-end customer-impact proxy (E2E p95 and tokens/sec).
- Breakdown metrics improve triage but are often noisier and more sensitive to load mix.

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Decision > Summary: decision table
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Decision > Summary: decision table
sections.content:
Summary: decision table

| Layer | Owns | Should do | Must not do |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gateway | Early rejection + tenant/tier fairness | Token bucket / concurrency caps, dependency circuit breakers, consistent overload responses | GPU-level scheduling decisions, multi-step retry/fallback loops |
| Routing | Target selection + bounded graceful degradation | Single bounded fallback attempt (if configured), loop prevention, target health gating | Global rate limiting, unbounded retries, per-GPU fairness |
| Runtime | Local safety + scheduling viability | Backpressure, queue/kv/memory safety, feature clamping (policy-controlled), export saturation signals | Cross-region routing decisions, customer-specific policy interpretation |

sections.section_path: Burst Capacity Retro Notes
sections.heading: Burst Capacity Retro Notes
sections.content:
- Total burst attempts: dominated by 2 tenants with scheduled batch jobs.
- Denial rate: ranged 0–18% by tenant depending on time-of-day; spikes correlated with telemetry lag and cooldown behavior.
- Admission controller p99: stable in us-east; spiky in eu-west (timeouts).
- Neighbor impact: one validated event (SUP-28455) where non-burst p99 regressed ~12–18% for ~20 minutes before mitigation.
- Billing reconciliation: identified retry double-counting bug; now fixed but we need ongoing automated checks.

What we changed during beta (already merged or in progress)

- Telemetry smoothing / prevent starvation under lag: GitHub:redwood/pr-23944
- Global circuit breaker for burst pools: GitHub:redwood/pr-23919
- SLO-based auto-gating (reduce/disable burst on non-burst regression): GitHub:redwood/pr-23988
- Billing idempotency + prevent double-counting: GitHub:redwood/pr-24108

GA readiness action items (must do)
P0 (blockers)
1) Telemetry freshness as a first-class signal

- Add metric + alert: “telemetry freshness seconds” by region/hardware + admission controller decision mode (fresh vs degraded).
- In degraded mode: enforce safer decisions (lower caps) + include explicit denial reason “TELEMETRY_STALE_DEGRADED_MODE”.
- Owner: Allison Grant + Logan Wright
- Target: by 2025-06-07

2) EU-West admission controller latency hardening

- Bound dependency calls with strict timeouts; add cached snapshots; add load shedding in controller.
- Define routing behavior when controller is slow: deterministic fallback decision + do not hammer controller.
- Owner: Jordan Lee + Mina Haddad
- Target: by 2025-06-10

3) Retry guidance + “Retry-After” semantics tied to reason codes

- Standardize: which denials are immediate (cap reached) vs transient (pool saturated) and include a backoff hint.
- Update docs + support macros.
- Owner: Peter Holtz + Kira Thompson
- Target: by 2025-06-12

4) Billing reconciliation automation

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Definition > Canonical SLI and SLO > Canonical throughput metric (SLI)
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Definition > Canonical SLI and SLO > Canonical throughput metric (SLI)
sections.content:
Canonical SLI and SLO

Canonical throughput metric (SLI)

**SLI name:** Dedicated Throughput Floor Attainment
**SLI definition (per deployment):**
For each `deployment_id`, compute the fraction of eligible 5-minute windows in which the **observed output token rate** meets or exceeds the committed floor.

A 5-minute window is considered **good** if:

- `observed_tps(deployment_id, window) >= committed_tps(deployment_id) * 1.00`

A window is **bad** if:

- `observed_tps(deployment_id, window) < committed_tps(deployment_id) * 1.00`

**Why tokens/sec:** Token throughput is the most stable cross-model, cross-request indicator for generation routes and aligns with customer-perceived capacity for streaming/chat.

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > How to recognize overload-protection responses > Common HTTP statuses
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > How to recognize overload-protection responses > Common HTTP statuses
sections.content:
How to recognize overload-protection responses

Common HTTP statuses

- **429 Too Many Requests**
  - Used for admission controls such as per-tenant concurrency caps, token buckets, or tier limits.
  - Usually safe to retry with backoff if Retry-After is provided.

- **503 Service Unavailable**
  - Used when the platform is overloaded at the regional/model level (breaker open) or actively shedding load to protect SLOs.
  - Usually safe to retry with backoff and/or reduce load. May persist until capacity recovers.

sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Appendix: Minimal internal handoff note (for paging)
sections.content:
Appendix: Minimal internal handoff note (for paging)

When paging SRE/Infra, include:

- “Dedicated Throughput SLO: suspected/confirmed”
- Deployment ID
- Tier + region
- Time window and whether ongoing
- Customer-confirmed load/concurrency (if available)
- Dashboard link
- Any correlated symptoms (timeouts, 5xx, queue depth)

This reduces back-and-forth and speeds mitigation.

sections.section_path: Policy Engine Failover Extensions Draft
sections.heading: Policy Engine Failover Extensions Draft
sections.content:
- decision_id (stable hash of route_id + tenant_id + evaluation_time + policy_version)
- policy_version
- evaluation_time
- decision_type
- chosen_reason
- target_state (string encoding; owned by controller)
- requested_actions (string encoding; empty in recommend mode)
- evidence (string encoding; ordered)
- annotations (string encoding; includes thresholds, staleness, hold-down state)

Note: In our implementation we’ll likely use structured objects, but for logging/audit we must generate a stable, versioned string representation.

Safety constraints (ADR-043 alignment)

- Anti-flap:
  - Enforce hold-down between flips for non-reachability triggers.
  - Any rollback decision must respect a separate rollback hold-down (avoid ping-pong between primary and fallback).
- Rate limiting:
  - flip_budget_ok must be true, else HOLD.
- Approval hooks:
  - If require_approval is true, decision_type can still be FAILOVER but requested_actions must be empty and “approval_required=true” annotation set.
- Tenant/tier gates:
  - Enterprise/Dedicated can be configured with stricter “do not cross data residency boundary” constraint (policy engine should surface “constraint_violation:data_residency” rather than attempt partial shifts).

Edge cases and expected behavior
1) Partial outage in primary region

- Reachability degraded (not down), 5xx burn elevated, capacity OK in fallback.
- Expected: PARTIAL_SHIFT (e.g., shift 25–50% depending on max_traffic_shift_percent) if corroborated. If sustained and escalates to reachability down or error burn becomes severe => FAILOVER.

2) Signal missing / ingestion delayed

- Any authoritative signal is stale beyond max_staleness_seconds.
- Expected: HOLD. Evidence must explicitly call out staleness and which signal blocked action.

3) Fallback region constrained

- Primary is failing (5xx burn), fallback capacity_hard_gate true.
- Expected: HOLD + annotate “fallback_unhealthy_due_to_capacity”. Controller should invoke load shedding and retry-after rather than shifting load.

4) Control plane degraded

- Control plane health degraded; data plane signals ambiguous.
- Expected: HOLD unless reachability down is authoritative. (Avoid flipping policies when control plane is suspect.)

5) Multi-fallback selection

- If multiple eligible fallback regions are healthy, selection tie-breakers:
  1) policy-specified order
  2) lowest latency probe (if available in inputs)
  3) highest capacity headroom
  4) stable sort by region name

Testing plan (draft)
Unit tests

- Determinism:
  - Same payload with randomized key order => same decision_id, decision_type, evidence ordering.
- Staleness gating:
  - Stale error burn + fresh reachability OK => HOLD.
- Priority:
  - Reachability DOWN overrides hold-down.
  - 5xx burn overrides latency burn when both exceed thresholds.

Integration tests

- Replay recorded signal snapshots from staging incidents + controlled game day traces.
- Validate output is compatible with controller dry-run UX (must contain reasons + evidence).

Performance considerations

- Evaluation must be cheap; do not add per-eval remote calls.
- Evidence strings must be bounded in size. Cap rejected_candidates and evidence list.

Operational / observability hooks

- Emit a single log line per decision with:
  - decision_id, route_id, tenant_id (hashed in shared Hosted contexts), decision_type, chosen_reason
  - key thresholds and freshness
- Export metrics:
  - policy_engine_decisions_total{decision_type, chosen_reason, tier}
  - policy_engine_hold_reasons_total{reason}
  - policy_engine_eval_latency_ms

Open questions

sections.section_path: Go Live Protocols Cross Org Communications Escalation 2027
sections.heading: Go Live Protocols Cross Org Communications Escalation 2027
sections.content:
| Level | Trigger example | Primary contact | Secondary contact | Action required |
|-------|-----------------|-----------------|-------------------|-----------------|
| L1 (CSM) | Customer questions, minor errors | CSM | SE | Acknowledge to customer within 15m, open internal thread |
| L2 (SRE) | Error rate >5% | Oncall SRE | SRE Lead | Execute diagnostics, apply mitigations (rate-limit, route switch) |
| L3 (SE/PM) | Persistent degradation >30m | Solutions Engineer | Product Manager | Coordinate config changes, model fallback, communicate to customer executives |
| L4 (Exec) | SLA breach or major incident | Head of Customer Success | Head of Engineering | Declare incident, engage legal/finance if SLA credits likely |

Note: The table above is intended as a quick reference. The full escalation paging list with phone numbers and PagerDuty IDs is stored in /confluence/people-ops/rosters and in the private channel pinned messages.

Common Mitigations (ordered by lowest customer impact first)
----------------------------------------------------------

- Increase routing to a higher-capacity pool (if Dedicated: burst pool)
- Apply tenant-level throttles to protect shared resources (quota reduce to 30% of projected steady-state)
- Enable model fallback: route to last-known-stable model snapshot
- Temporarily switch customer to hosted API endpoint (if allowed by contract)
- Quiesce long-running batch jobs from the customer side

Rollback and Safe-fail Strategies
--------------------------------

1. Safe rollback to previous routing config (SE executes):
   - Command: curl -X POST https://ops-api.internal.redwood/v1/route/revert -d '{"tenant":"<tenant-id>","to_config":"<previous-config-id>"}' 
   - Confirm routing table via: kubectl get svc ingress-<tenant> -o yaml (requires ops role)
2. Tenant quiesce API (customer-facing graceful shutdown):
   - POST https://api.redwood.com/v1/tenants/<tenant>/quiesce?actor=ops
   - Expected behavior: existing requests drain, new requests return 429 with Retry-After header.
3. Emergency switchback to hosted region: update DNS TTL and apply traffic policy TTL=30s for faster re-routing.

Communication Templates
-----------------------

- Customer-facing 1-line (acknowledge): "We are investigating increased latency for your production routes and will provide an update within 15 minutes. No action required from your side unless we ask."
- Customer-facing status update (10m cadence): include short bullet list: observed metric, action taken, owner, ETA for next update.
- Internal P0 page message sample:
  - "P0: <customer> production routes returning 503s since 08:12 UTC. Oncall SRE investigating. Initial hypothesis: ingress proxy thread exhaustion. Paging SRE Lead and SE. Next update in 5 minutes"

Telemetry checks / Queries (examples)
----------------------------------

- PromQL (errors): sum(rate(http_requests_total{tenant="<tenant>",status=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{tenant="<tenant>"}[5m])) > 0.05
- Token consumption anomaly (example):
  - Query: increase(token_count_total{tenant="<tenant>"}[30m]) / expected_token_rate > 2.0
- Synthetic validation command (curl):
  - curl -s -X POST https://api.redwood.com/v1/generate -H "Authorization: Bearer <key>" -d '{"input":"synthetic health check"}' | jq '.latency_ms'

Post-Cutover (T+4 to T+72 hours)
--------------------------------

- Stability window monitoring: SRE to keep watch for 72 hours; escalate on any SLO breach.
- Cost and quota reconciliation: Finance Ops and CSM to review token consumption, forecast delta, and apply quota protections if needed.
- Customer QBR prep: collect first-week metrics and any incident notes for the 30-day QBR.

Runbook Ownership and RACI
-------------------------

sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Decision > 3) Runtime admission/backpressure (last-line protection)
sections.content:
3) Runtime admission/backpressure (last-line protection)

**Runtime owns “what can actually execute”** on a given GPU pool/node.

Runtime responsibilities:

- Enforce hard safety limits: queue depth, scheduler backlog, token/sec saturation, memory/KV-cache pressure.
- Apply backpressure locally (e.g., refuse new admissions to a saturated scheduler; clamp optional features if configured).
- Export saturation signals at bounded cardinality for upstream decisions.

Runtime should be able to reject quickly with an internal reason that maps to stable overload error codes at the edge (ADR-014). Runtime should not attempt cross-region balancing.

sections.section_path: Burst Capacity Retro Notes
sections.heading: Burst Capacity Retro Notes
sections.content:
Burst Capacity Retro Notes

Source type: google_drive
Document ID: dsid_95c7aa5238f94570a8e0a8684736b666
Release: v1.0.0
Benchmark: EnterpriseRAG-Bench synthetic upstream data
Dedicated Burst Capacity — Post-beta retro notes (SRE)
Doc goal
Capture what we learned from the Dedicated Burst Capacity beta (May 2025): what broke, which guardrails were too strict/too lax, what we changed during beta, and what must be completed before GA.

Retro logistics

- Date: 2025-05-28 (60 min)
- Facilitator: Rafael Mendes (SRE)
- Notetaker: Peter Holtz (Routing SRE)
- Beta window covered: 2025-05-06 to 2025-05-24
- Scope: burst pools (regional/hardware), admission controller, routing integration, SLO gates, dashboards/alerts, metering/billing hooks, supportability

Attendees (high signal contributors)

- SRE/Obs: Sean G., Rafael M., Peter H., Allison G., Sergio C.
- Infra/Fleet: Vanessa O., Keiko Y.
- Control plane/policy: Jordan L.
- Routing: Mina H.
- Billing/metering: Cole S., Nadia R.
- CS feedback: Rachel K.

What went well (keep)
1) Global safety cap + circuit breaker concept worked in practice

- We hit the cap once in staging and once “near miss” in prod beta; breaker prevented runaway neighbor impact.
- The playbook of “reduce caps -> drain queues -> disable burst for lowest tiers first” is operationally sound.

2) Denial reason codes improved triage materially

- Support/CS could distinguish “cap reached” vs “pool saturated” vs “cooldown” vs “telemetry stale”.
- Routing logs + reason codes made it clear where to look first.

3) Dashboards were mostly the right primitives

- Saturation, queue depth, admit/deny rates, and p95 deltas by tenant were enough to debug 80% of issues.
- SLO gate signal (non-burst tenant latency regression) is a good north star even if thresholds need tuning.

4) Rollout gating/feature flags prevented blast radius

- Per-region allow list + per-tenant enablement meant we could pause EU-West issues without impacting US-East.

What broke / painful incidents
A) Telemetry lag caused unfair denials + occasional starvation

- Symptom: a few tenants saw denial spikes while pool appeared underutilized; the “laggy” telemetry made the controller think they were still consuming burst tokens.
- Customer-visible effect: burst requests denied unexpectedly; some clients retried aggressively and amplified load.
- Root cause (likely): our admission controller relied on near-real-time usage signals; when signals were delayed, the smoothing window + token bucket refill behavior effectively penalized active tenants.
- Fix during beta: hotfix added smoothing + guard conditions + conservative fallback when telemetry freshness is below threshold.
- Ref: GitHub:redwood/pr-23944

B) EU-West burst admission timeouts (controller dependency chain)

- Symptom: admission calls intermittently timed out in eu-west under high request rate; routing fell back but increased gateway error rates briefly.
- Root cause: admission controller p99 latency spiked due to dependency (policy evaluation + fleet telemetry query) not being bounded; threadpool saturation.
- Mitigation: enable circuit breaker + temporarily tighten per-tenant caps + disable burst in eu-west allow list until patched.
- Ref: Jira:SUP-28579

C) Billing: burst usage double-counted on retry paths

sections.section_path: Policy Engine Failover Extensions Draft
sections.heading: Policy Engine Failover Extensions Draft
sections.content:
- Decision must include:
  - decision_type (NO_OP | FAILOVER | PARTIAL_SHIFT | ROLLBACK | HOLD)
  - chosen_reason (canonical enum)
  - evidence: ordered list of signals used, with values, freshness, and thresholds.
  - rejected_candidates: (optional) top 1–3 alternatives and why they were not selected.

Proposed changes to policy engine
A) New predicates / functions
1) region_health(region, signal_type) -> {status, value, confidence, freshness_seconds}

- Wrapper that pulls normalized data from payload and enforces freshness calculations.

2) is_authoritative_reachability_down(region) -> bool

- True only if:
  - reachability.status == down
  - confidence >= configured_min_confidence (default 0.9)
  - freshness_seconds <= reachability_max_staleness (default 30s)

3) burn_rate_exceeded(region, metric, window, threshold) -> bool

- Works for errors_5xx_burn and tail_latency_burn.
- Window must be one of approved windows (e.g., 1m/5m/30m) to avoid configuration drift.

4) capacity_hard_gate(region) -> bool

- True if headroom below threshold AND capacity signal confidence is high.
- Intended to prevent shifting into an already overloaded region.

5) corroborated(primary_signal, secondary_signal) -> bool

- Enforces ADR-042 “required corroboration signals” when configured.
- Example: if tail latency burn triggers, require either 5xx burn OR reachability degraded/down OR control plane degraded.

6) hold_down_active(last_flip_at, min_hold_down_seconds) -> bool

- If true, policy engine returns HOLD unless reachability down is authoritative.

7) flip_budget_ok(tenant_id, route_id, max_flips_per_hour) -> bool

- Input includes a precomputed counter from controller/state store (policy engine does not store state).

8) blast_radius_ok(tenant_tier, requested_action) -> bool

- Enforces “can’t shift more than X% traffic for tier Y without approval”.
- For Hosted, blast radius is route-scoped; for Dedicated, pool-scoped.

B) Deterministic evaluation mode (required)

- Add an “evaluation_mode” field:
  - recommend: compute decision + evidence; do not mark as executable
  - enforce: compute decision; include explicit requested_action(s)
- Engine must produce identical decision_type and evidence in both modes (action packaging differs).

C) Signal hierarchy evaluation (ADR-042)
Priority order (proposed canonical order for v1):
1) Reachability DOWN (authoritative) => FAILOVER (unless no healthy fallback)
2) Errors (5xx) fast burn (high severity) => FAILOVER or PARTIAL_SHIFT depending on blast radius and capacity
3) Tail latency burn (p99/p95) => PARTIAL_SHIFT first; escalate to FAILOVER if corroborated and sustained
4) Capacity exhaustion / hard gate => HOLD + load shed (controller action), avoid shifting into constrained region
5) Control plane degradation => HOLD (do not flip rapidly; prevent oscillation)

Notes:

- “No healthy fallback” means every eligible fallback region fails capacity_hard_gate OR reachability is down OR stale beyond threshold.
- If no healthy fallback, decision should be HOLD and include “degrade_allowed=true” hint (controller can activate load shedding / retry-after).

D) Policy language / config schema additions
Add new fields (names tentative):

- failover:
  - enabled: boolean
  - eligible_regions: [us-east, eu-west, ...]
  - signal_requirements:
    - primary_trigger: enum
    - corroboration: [enum]
    - min_confidence: float
    - max_staleness_seconds: int
  - dampening:
    - min_hold_down_seconds: int
    - require_sustain_seconds: int (for non-reachability triggers)
  - safety:
    - require_approval: boolean (default true for prod initially)
    - max_flips_per_hour: int
    - max_traffic_shift_percent: int
    - rollback:
      - auto_rollback_enabled: boolean
      - rollback_after_seconds: int
      - rollback_require_healthy_primary_seconds: int

E) Output schema
Decision output (single object, JSON):

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > What changed (customer-facing)
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > What changed (customer-facing)
sections.content:
What changed (customer-facing)

When the platform is saturated (GPU capacity, scheduler backlog, downstream dependency brownout), Redwood may reject requests *early* and predictably rather than allowing them to time out or generate random 5xx.

Customers may now see:

- **429** responses for admission / quota / per-tenant caps.
- **503** responses when a regional/model circuit breaker is open or the system is actively shedding load.

These responses:

- Include stable **error codes** and a machine-readable JSON payload.
- Typically include a **Retry-After** header to indicate safe retry timing.
- Include Redwood request/correlation IDs for tracing.

sections.content:
Go Live Protocols Cross Org Communications Escalation 2027

Source type: confluence
Document ID: dsid_9c8cb10d65324c03a8ededbd98c1b058
Release: v1.0.0

Go-Live Protocols: Cross-Org Communications & Escalation
Summary
-------
This document defines the cross-organizational go-live protocol used by Redwood Inference for enterprise tenant cutovers. It focuses on communications, stakeholder coordination, and an escalation ladder tailored for high-risk or high-visibility customers. Use this runbook as the canonical checklist for the 72 hours before, during, and 72 hours after a cutover where multiple teams (Customer Success, SRE, Solutions Engineering, Product, and Sales) must be coordinated.

Scope
-----

- Applies to: Dedicated and Private deployment go-lives and tenant migrations with SLA commitments (any customer with an enterprise contract or > $50k monthly spend).
- Out of scope: self-serve trial accounts, routine model-only updates without routing changes.

Goals and SLOs to Protect
-------------------------

- Availability SLA target to protect during cutover: 99.9% (monthly) for production routes.
- Immediate remediation thresholds (trigger escalation):
  - Error rate spike: sustained >5% errors for 5 minutes across tenant endpoints.
  - Latency spike: P95 latency >2000ms for 10 minutes.
  - Token cost anomaly: >200% of projected token spend in 30 minutes.
  - KV cache miss-rate >30% sustained for 15 minutes (for cache-sensitive workloads).

Pre-Cutover (T-72 to T-1 hours)
-------------------------------

1. Confirm stakeholders and channels
   - Primary CSM (Customer Success Manager): name + mobile number.
   - Tech lead (Customer): contact + escalation path.
   - Solution Engineer (SE): responsible for ingress, API contract verification.
   - Oncall SRE/Platform owner: PagerDuty schedule and runbook owner.
   - Slack channels: #cs-<customer>-go-live (private channel), #oncall-redwood, #se-ops.
2. Telemetry sanity checks — must pass before proceeding:
   - Synthetic journey (happy path) passes end-to-end: <customer> -> Redwood API -> response < 1s.
   - PromQL checks: error_rate/instance < 0.005 for 10m; p95_latency_query < 1500ms.
3. Canary plan and acceptance criteria
   - Canary traffic: route 1% of production for 30 minutes with zero critical errors.
   - Acceptance: no P0/P1 incidents during canary and no regression in model quality metrics (if applicable).
4. Whitelist and firewall confirmations
   - Verify ingress IP ranges, customer egress rules, and TLS client certs.

----------------------------------------------------

- Primary communications protocol:
  - All updates posted to #cs-<customer>-go-live every 10 minutes during the first hour, then every 30 minutes until stable.
  - The CSM posts customer-facing status updates; technical details posted to private channel only.
- Live monitoring dashboard (owner: Oncall SRE):
  - Tenant-specific dashboard showing throughput, p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate, KV cache hits, token consumption.
- Escalation triggers (first responder must escalate within 5 minutes if triggered):
  1) P0: service unavailable for customer routes — immediate page to P1 oncall and notify Engineering Director.
  2) P1: sustained SLO breach (see thresholds above) — page SE and PM, start RCA and mitigation steps.
  3) P2: model quality regression detected — notify Applied ML and SE; consider traffic switch to verified model snapshot.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Baseline Keys (What defines “like-for-like”)
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Baseline Keys (What defines “like-for-like”)
sections.content:
Baseline Keys (What defines “like-for-like”)

Baseline artifacts and regression evaluation are keyed by the following dimensions:

**Required baseline key fields (v1):**

- model_id (canonical model identifier)
- model_version (registry version / hash)
- runtime_build_id (serving runtime build tag)
- kernel_set_id (kernel selection/version identifier)
- hardware_sku (e.g., H100-80GB, A100-80GB)

**Optional fields (only when variance requires it):**

- region (enabled for regions with materially different fleet/network characteristics)
- capacity_tier (hosted vs dedicated pools) when pools differ materially

Notes:

- We do NOT key baselines by customer, endpoint, or prompt content (privacy + cardinality constraints).
- Scheduler configuration flags that materially change behavior must be reflected either in runtime_build_id or an explicit scheduler_profile tag (introduced only if needed; kept off by default to control cardinality).

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Decision > 1) Gateway admission control (primary front-door protection)
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Decision > 1) Gateway admission control (primary front-door protection)
sections.content:
1) Gateway admission control (primary front-door protection)

**Gateway owns “who gets in”** based on:

- Tenant/tier policy (Hosted self-serve vs enterprise Hosted vs Dedicated routing paths)
- Per-route/model caps (concurrency, QPS/token-bucket style limits)
- Coarse-grained regional overload state (from aggregated signals)
- Dependency health gates for gateway-local dependencies (auth, quota/usage checks, policy engine, routing service)

Gateway behavior under overload:

- Return customer-facing errors per ADR-014 (typically 429 or 503 with stable overload error codes).
- Include correlation_id and consistent Retry-After semantics.
- Prefer **fail fast** when signals indicate sustained overload (avoid letting requests queue indefinitely).

Gateway does **not** attempt fine-grained GPU scheduling decisions.

sections.section_path: Sup 2892 Fallback Model Not Triggering During Overload
sections.heading: Sup 2892 Fallback Model Not Triggering During Overload
sections.content:
Sup 2892 Fallback Model Not Triggering During Overload

Source type: jira
Document ID: dsid_6e528fa402c34043897649be6aa6df3d
Release: v1.0.0
Benchmark: EnterpriseRAG-Bench synthetic upstream data
Fallback model not triggering during overload (customer receives 503 OVERLOADED instead of routed fallback)

Issue summary
Banyan Search reports that their configured fallback model is not being used during overload events. Instead, requests fail with 503 and Redwood overload error codes.

Customer expectation
When primary model (rw-llama-3.1-70b-instruct) is overloaded, Redwood should route to configured fallback (rw-llama-3.1-8b-instruct) per their tenant policy.

Impact

- Customer sees elevated failed requests during traffic spikes rather than degraded (lower quality) responses.
- Affects production search assistant experience and increases client retry pressure.

Environment

- Hosted API
- Region: us-east
- Route: /v1/chat/completions
- Streaming: mostly enabled

Customer configuration (as described by customer)

- Primary: rw-llama-3.1-70b-instruct
- Fallback: rw-llama-3.1-8b-instruct
- Trigger condition: overload (customer referenced 'circuit breaker open')

What the customer is seeing (excerpt)

- HTTP 503
- Error payload (representative):
  code: OVERLOADED
  message: "Service temporarily overloaded. Please retry."
  correlation_id: rwcorr_01JEMNQZJ5J9P2G6E3R9K8V6M2
  retry_after: (present for some responses; missing for some per SUP-2860)

Steps to reproduce (internal)
1) Identify Banyan tenant_id and active routing policy.
2) Induce overload condition (or replay from perf-canary) where gateway admission control sheds requests.
3) Confirm whether routing attempts fallback model when overload is detected.

Initial hypothesis
Fallback routing is only attempted when overload is detected at routing/runtime stages. When overload occurs at the gateway admission layer (breaker open / shed), the request is rejected before routing executes, so no fallback can occur. Additional suspicion: loop-prevention logic may be suppressing fallback when the request already contains an attempted-model chain header.

Requested outcome

- Confirm whether fallback is expected to work under gateway-level shedding.
- If not currently supported, provide clear customer guidance and (if safe) enable fallback-on-gateway-overload for this tenant as an exception/feature flag.
- Ensure Retry-After is consistently present on overload errors.

sections.section_path: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Alerting (paging + ticketing) > Overload protection operational alerts
sections.heading: Hosted Api Slos Enterprise Route Tiers > Alerting (paging + ticketing) > Overload protection operational alerts
sections.content:
Overload protection operational alerts

These are predictive/guardrail alerts. Configure as:

- **Page (Sev2):** enterprise overload shedding sustained
  - enterprise `shed_rate` > **0.1%** for **10 minutes** (any protected route)
- **Ticket:** best-effort shedding unexpectedly high at low utilization
  - best-effort `shed_rate` > **20%** for **15 minutes** AND GPU utilization < **65%** (indicates policy mis-tuning or signal errors)
- **Ticket:** queue depth / scheduler lag sustained without corresponding shedding
  - queue depth > threshold for **10 minutes** with `admission_control_active=false` (indicates missing trigger wiring)

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Definition > Canonical SLI and SLO > Requests/sec as a secondary metric
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Definition > Canonical SLI and SLO > Requests/sec as a secondary metric
sections.content:
Requests/sec as a secondary metric

Requests/sec may be used for:

- Non-generative routes where token accounting is not meaningful (rare in Dedicated scope), or
- As an internal diagnostic view (e.g., “QPS at steady state”) alongside tokens/sec.

If requests/sec is used, it is explicitly labeled as a **non-canonical** SLI and must not be substituted for compliance without SRE sign-off.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Severity levels (Support/CS view)
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Severity levels (Support/CS view)
sections.content:
Severity levels (Support/CS view)

Use these severities to standardize response; SRE may map to their incident severities.

**SEV-1 (Critical, likely customer-impacting breach)**

- Premium tier customer reports sustained throughput below floor OR SRE burn-rate alert is firing.
- Clear production impact (e.g., queue buildup, timeouts, user-visible latency spikes).
- Immediate paging required.

**SEV-2 (High, likely degradation / at-risk of breach)**

- Throughput is below expected but not yet confirmed as an SLO breach.
- Customer impact is moderate OR limited to a subset of traffic/routes.
- Paging may be required depending on tier and duration.

**SEV-3 (Moderate, investigation / metrics discrepancy)**

- Conflicting metrics (customer vs Redwood dashboards), short-lived dips, or suspected measurement artifacts.
- No clear production impact.

---

sections.section_path: Burst Capacity Retro Notes
sections.heading: Burst Capacity Retro Notes
sections.content:
- Symptom: customer asked why burst line item didn’t match dashboard usage; we found ~1.8–2.3% overcount in a specific retry pattern.
- Root cause: metering event emitted pre-idempotency; retried requests emitted duplicate usage increments.
- Fix: idempotency keys + reconciliation checks.
- Ref: GitHub:redwood/pr-24108, Jira:SUP-28488

D) Noisy neighbor scare (tail latency increase for a non-burst tenant)

- Symptom: p95/p99 latency increase for a non-burst tenant correlated with another tenant’s burst window.
- What we learned: even if pool isolation is “logical,” shared control-plane/routing and some shared fleet components can cause tail amplification under saturation.
- Mitigation used: reduced global cap + increased cooldown for bursting tenant + forced routing fallback for that tenant for 30 min.
- Ref: Jira:SUP-28455

E) Support confusion: 429s when burst cap reached (expected but poorly messaged)

- We returned 429/overload when both baseline+burst caps were reached; some customers expected queuing instead.
- For GA we need crisp guidance: recommended retry/backoff strategy and what will/won’t queue.
- Ref: Jira:SUP-28503

Guardrails that were too strict (beta feedback)
1) Cooldown windows were overly punitive for spiky-but-legit workloads

- Current behavior: once a tenant hits max burst ratio, cooldown kicks in even if they drop below quickly.
- Effect: denial bursts after short spikes; customers perceive “flaky burst.”
- Proposal: cooldown should be based on sustained saturation (e.g., N seconds over threshold) or make cooldown proportional to burst duration, not a flat window.

2) Max burst ratio default (x1.5) was too conservative for “weekly batch” customers

- Several beta tenants expected x2–x3 for short windows (10–30 min) and were willing to pay.
- But we must pair higher ratios with stronger fairness + fleet safety + SLO gates.

3) Admission determinism vs latency tradeoff

- We enforced determinism by evaluating multiple signals synchronously; in some cases this added controller latency and increased timeouts.
- Suggestion: determinism requirement should be: “same inputs => same decision” but inputs can be snapshot-based (cached) within a bounded TTL.

Guardrails that were too lax (or missing)
1) Retry amplification guard

- When customers got denials, some clients retried immediately with high concurrency.
- We need an explicit “retry-after” / backoff hint tied to denial reason codes, and optionally server-side throttling at gateway.

2) Alerting gaps for “telemetry freshness” and “admission controller dependency health”

- We lacked a strong, paging-quality indicator for telemetry freshness degradation (it showed in graphs but didn’t page until customers complained).
- Admission controller dependency p99 did not have an error-budget aligned alert.

3) Fairness under mixed priority tiers needs stronger anti-starvation proofs

- We introduced priority tiers late in beta; we didn’t run enough multi-tenant stress tests for gold/silver combos.
- Need explicit starvation bound (e.g., min guaranteed tokens) and test harness enforcement.

4) Config propagation / console staleness

- One customer ticket: burst limit updated but Console showed stale value for too long.
- Root cause likely caching/prop delay; not a safety issue but it undermines trust.
- Ref: Jira:SUP-28541

Key metrics from beta (rough, from dashboards)

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Retry & backoff guidance (what we should recommend) > Streaming-specific guidance
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Retry & backoff guidance (what we should recommend) > Streaming-specific guidance
sections.content:
Streaming-specific guidance

Streaming workloads can worsen overload if clients open many concurrent streams.

- Recommend **lower streaming concurrency** during peak periods.
- If the customer can tolerate it, recommend **shorter outputs** (reduce `max_tokens`) and/or **shorter prompts**.
- If a stream fails mid-response with an overload error on reconnect attempts, advise them to back off and resume with a bounded number of attempts.

sections.section_path: Policy Engine Failover Extensions Draft
sections.heading: Policy Engine Failover Extensions Draft
sections.content:
- Exact shape of “target_state” string: should it be a controller-owned serialization of desired weights, or should the policy engine output high-level intent only?
- Do we want PARTIAL_SHIFT as a first-class decision type (recommended), or represent it as FAILOVER with weight < 100%?
- How strict should corroboration be for tail latency burn? (ADR-042 indicates corroboration required; we need the exact default set.)
- Where should data residency constraints live?
  - Option A: policy engine validates “region set allowed” and blocks action.
  - Option B: upstream policy compilation prevents invalid eligible_regions.

Near-term next steps

- Align with Miles/Ravi on canonical signal enum + reason enum.
- Draft schema PR for policy config additions (behind feature flag).
- Implement deterministic ordering + evidence output in policy engine.
- Wire to dry-run mode (ENG-2415) so the controller can display “recommended action + confidence + evidence” on game day.

sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Implementation notes (non-normative)
sections.content:
Implementation notes (non-normative)

- Gateway admission should use a combination of:
  - token bucket (QPS) per tenant/route
  - concurrency caps for streaming endpoints
  - “regional overload state” multiplier for dynamic throttling (with hysteresis)
- Runtime should expose clear “reject reasons” that map into ADR-014 overload codes without leaking internals.
- Routing should mark fallback attempts and enforce max_attempts=1. Any further attempt must be a client retry honoring Retry-After.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Common failure modes and quick routing hints
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Common failure modes and quick routing hints
sections.content:
Common failure modes and quick routing hints

- **Customer sees lower throughput than Redwood reports:** often a measurement mismatch (streaming token accounting, end-to-end latency vs throughput, counting input tokens). Engage Observability if persistent.
- **Throughput drops with GPU pegged:** suspect contention, node health, thermal throttling, network bottleneck; page Infra.
- **Throughput drops with low utilization:** suspect admission control limiting, customer throttling, or workload shift to longer contexts; page SRE; ask customer for concurrency/workload details.
- **Regional capacity constraint / failover behavior:** check tier failover posture; page Infra and SRE; do not promise cross-region without tier/contract confirmation.

sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Definition > Measurement semantics > Streaming token accounting
sections.content:
Streaming token accounting

For streaming responses:

- Output tokens are counted when emitted by the runtime, attributed to the originating request.
- We de-duplicate token counters to avoid double counting caused by stream chunk retries.

Operational note: streaming accounting semantics were corrected in **PR-19422** (“Fix throughput metric double counting streaming”). Any backfills or comparisons across that boundary must annotate the change.

sections.section_path: Policy Engine Failover Extensions Draft
sections.heading: Policy Engine Failover Extensions Draft
sections.content:
Policy Engine Failover Extensions Draft

Source type: google_drive
Document ID: dsid_184be937d34a412ab5e61366d54d8ed6
Release: v1.0.0
Benchmark: EnterpriseRAG-Bench synthetic upstream data
Draft Spec: Policy Engine Extensions for Regional Failover Automation

Context / why this exists

- We’re upgrading regional failover automation as part of Reliability Program (Q1–Q2 2026). Today, routing policy evaluation has a few gaps:
  - Non-deterministic behavior in edge cases (e.g., multiple signals firing, partial signal availability, time-window ambiguity).
  - Hard to reason about priority across trigger signals (reachability, 5xx burn, tail latency burn, capacity exhaustion).
  - No first-class “hold-down” / dampening in evaluation; logic is split between policy rules and external controller.
  - No consistent mechanism to enforce safety constraints per tenant/tier (max flips, blast radius caps, required approval).

Goals

- Add policy engine primitives so failover decisioning is:
  - Deterministic and auditable (same inputs => same decision; explainability built-in).
  - Compatible with ADR-042 (signal priority + corroboration) and ADR-043 (rollback + anti-flap).
  - Safe by default (rate limits, required corroboration, blast radius constraints).
- Support both:
  - “Recommend” (dry-run) mode: compute candidate flips + evidence.
  - “Enforce” mode: same evaluation but returns executable actions.

Non-goals

- Replace the automation controller. The controller still orchestrates execution, approvals, and cross-system workflow.
- Re-architect signal ingestion. We consume normalized, time-bucketed signals from Region Health + SLO toolkit.
- Build customer-facing UI here.

Terminology

- Policy: configuration describing routing behavior for a route/service/model/tier.
- Region set: primary and fallback regions eligible for this route.
- Trigger signal: normalized boolean or scalar indicating regional impairment or risk.
- Decision: computed outcome (no-op, failover, partial shift, rollback, hold).
- Action: executable change (policy flip, weight adjustment, circuit breaker mode) emitted by controller.

Inputs / data model assumptions

- Policy engine receives inputs as a single evaluation payload, including:
  - route_id (e.g., hosted.chat.completions, dedicated.pool.<pool_id>)
  - tenant_id (optional for shared Hosted; required for Dedicated)
  - tenant_tier (free/pro/enterprise/dedicated)
  - current_routing_state (primary region, weights, last_flip_at)
  - signals (per region, per signal type):
    - reachability: ok|degraded|down + confidence + last_updated
    - errors_5xx_burn: burn_rate + window + confidence
    - tail_latency_burn: burn_rate + p95/p99 deltas + confidence
    - capacity_headroom: percent + “hard gate” boolean
    - control_plane_health (optional): ok|degraded|down
  - evaluation_time (UTC epoch + monotonic sequence)
  - constraints (policy-level + tenant-level): max_flips_per_hour, min_hold_down_seconds, require_approval, blast_radius_limit

Determinism requirements (core)
1) Stable ordering

- Evaluation must not depend on map iteration order.
- Rule matching must define explicit ordering: by priority, then by tie-breakers.

2) Stable time semantics

- All windowed signals must be anchored to evaluation_time and include:
  - effective_start, effective_end, and a “freshness” timestamp.
- Engine must treat stale signals consistently:
  - If authoritative signals are stale beyond threshold, decision = HOLD (do not fail over) unless reachability is explicitly DOWN with high confidence.

3) Single decision per evaluation

- For a given (route_id, tenant_id, evaluation_time), engine emits exactly one decision object, even if multiple actions are possible.
- Multi-step actions (e.g., drain -> shift weights -> finalize) must be represented as a sequence recommendation but still within a single decision record.

4) Explainability

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Alternatives considered
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Alternatives considered
sections.content:
Alternatives considered

1) **Single global breaker at gateway only**

- Rejected: insufficient fidelity; cannot protect runtime safety in all cases; still allows deep queueing.

2) **Runtime-only backpressure (let everything in)**

- Rejected: overload manifests as queued latency/timeouts; poor customer semantics; wastes upstream work.

3) **Routing-driven global admission control**

- Rejected: routing is not the best place to enforce tenant fairness and local dependency breakers; risks complex control loops.

sections.section_path: Burst Capacity Retro Notes
sections.heading: Burst Capacity Retro Notes
sections.content:
- Today we mostly deny quickly; some customers want queuing.
- SRE view: queuing can hide fleet pain and increase tail; if we add queueing it must be bounded with clear max wait + cancellation and must not break determinism.

2) How much “degraded mode” behavior is acceptable?

- If telemetry is stale, do we:
  a) deny all burst? (safe but may be overly strict)
  b) allow small burst with conservative cap? (better UX)
  c) continue as-is with risk? (not acceptable)
- Tentative: (b) with tight global caps + explicit surfaced state.

3) GA scope: region/hardware allow list

- Recommendation: GA in us-east H100 first; add eu-west after EU-West latency fix + game day rerun.

Appendix: customer support learnings (from tickets)

- SUP-28411 (unexpected denials): customers interpret “burst enabled” as “guaranteed extra capacity.” We must emphasize “best-effort within guardrails,” with clear reasons.
- SUP-28503 (429s): customers need explicit guidance on client-side backoff, concurrency control, and how to detect “you are at cap.”
- SUP-28488 (billing question): customers will audit the burst line item against their own job schedule; we need accurate exports + transparent calculation.

Next steps

- Rafael to turn P0s into a GA gate checklist and review in SRE staff meeting (2025-06-04).
- Schedule a short follow-up retro after GA week 1 to validate assumptions and update runbooks.

sections.section_path: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Minimum Sample Sizes and Windowing > Minimum samples (per key K, per window)
sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Minimum Sample Sizes and Windowing > Minimum samples (per key K, per window)
sections.content:
Minimum samples (per key K, per window)

- **Latency metrics**: minimum **200 successful canary requests** per window.
- **Tokens/sec**: minimum **200 successful canary requests** per window AND minimum **50,000 total generated tokens** per window.

If sample requirements are not met:

- No alert state change is allowed (prevents flapping in low-coverage periods).
- Dashboard panels display “insufficient sample” annotation.

Rationale:

- Tail latency (p95/p99) is unreliable with very small N.
- Tokens/sec needs sufficient token volume to smooth per-request variance.

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Rationale > Why not “only runtime”?
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Rationale > Why not “only runtime”?
sections.content:
Why not “only runtime”?

Runtime-only rejection is too late:

- Wastes work in upstream services (auth, routing, logging, request parsing)
- Increases tail latency due to queue buildup
- Fails to enforce tenant/tier fairness consistently across services

Gateway is best suited to shed early and protect downstreams.

Appendix A: Example Per-Model Overrides (illustrative)

- Top model (customer-critical): paging at +15% p95 E2E, -12% tokens/sec, stricter min token count.
- High-variance model: warning only, wider thresholds (+15% / -10%), region-specific baseline enabled.
- New kernel rollout candidate: temporary tighter warning (+8%) during rollout ring, but paging remains at default until validated.

sections.section_path: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Canonical mapping: status → meaning → what we tell customers
sections.heading: Overload Errors And Retry Guidance > Canonical mapping: status → meaning → what we tell customers
sections.content:
Canonical mapping: status → meaning → what we tell customers

Use this table to drive consistent customer guidance.

| HTTP | Typical meaning | What Support should say | Customer action |
|------|------------------|--------------------------|-----------------|
| 429 | Admission control / rate limiting / tier cap hit | “Your request was rejected to protect system stability. This is not a model failure; it indicates you are sending requests faster than the current allowed rate/concurrency.” | Respect Retry-After; implement exponential backoff + jitter; reduce concurrency; consider batching; if persistent, discuss tier/capacity options. |
| 503 | Regional/model breaker open or load shedding | “Redwood is temporarily overloaded in the requested region/model. We are rejecting early to avoid timeouts and protect overall reliability.” | Respect Retry-After; backoff + jitter; optionally route to another region/model if configured; reduce max_tokens/streaming concurrency; retry with bounded attempts. |

Notes:

- If the customer reports **timeouts** with no JSON error, treat as a separate issue (possible client/network or upstream timeouts) and escalate based on impact.
- If the customer gets **5xx** without the overload payload, collect details; it may be an unrelated incident.

sections.section_path: Dedicated Throughput Slo Definition > Metrics (source of truth) > Canonical metrics (Prometheus-style names)
sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Definition > Metrics (source of truth) > Canonical metrics (Prometheus-style names)

Canonical metrics (Prometheus-style names)

sections.content:
4) Check the Dedicated Throughput dashboard for that deployment

- Rolling-window throughput vs committed floor

- Recent routing pool changes or failovers

sections.section_path: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Consequences > Positive
sections.heading: Adr 015 Admission Control Layering Gateway Routing Runtime > Consequences > Positive
sections.content:
Consequences

Positive

- Earlier, clearer shedding reduces tail latency and incident severity.
- Tenant/tier fairness is enforced consistently at the edge.
- Runtime remains protected even if gateway/routing misestimate load.
- Routing provides graceful degradation (fallback) without turning into a retry storm engine.

sections.heading: Adr Perf Canary Baseline And Thresholds > Default Thresholds (v1) > Throughput (tokens/sec)
sections.content:
Throughput (tokens/sec)

- Warning: tokens/sec **-8%** vs baseline for **2 out of 3** windows.
- Paging: tokens/sec **-15%** vs baseline for **3 out of 4** windows.

Metrics (source of truth)

sections.heading: Dedicated Throughput Slo Escalation > Evidence and logging requirements

Evidence and logging requirements

For any SEV-1/SEV-2 and any credit review, capture:

- Customer ticket link
- Incident link (if created)
- Dashboard links (throughput vs floor, saturation, errors)
- Request IDs / traces used for debugging
- Summary of customer-side traffic confirmation
